TRUE HONOURS. A bard lived, once upon a time, Of good and honest name, Who frequently dropped into rhyme, Without a thought of fame. Until one day an agent trim Appeared before this singer, And asked if he might name for him His patent new clothes wringer. And then he heard that far out West A nursery man of mcans Had called for him his very bet Superior kind of beans. Fast flocked these honours at his feet, Faster by far than dollars: And when for him was named a sweet New thing in paper collars, He asked, confused by all these brands, " What is there in a name ?" And all the pelple clapped their hands, And answered," This is fame."

"There can be no doubt of it. Yot.r Majesty has bat to command, and he will be obeyed." And the obsequious mrtiers joined in a chorus of "so say we all of us !" "Very good !" said the King; "now do you, each in your turn, take your stand on the gene of yonder throne, and bid the sea retire." His behest was obeyed, and courtier afteer courtier essayed the per- formanee, and was fain to retire baffled, amid the jeering laughter of the pos.ulece. In this manner the time was fully occupitd until the hour of flood had passed and the tide was upon the ebb, when the King ascended the throne, and bidding the waves retire, was soon left triumphantly apon dry ground, amid the plaudits of his loyal subjects. "You see, gentlemee," he said, turning to the crest-fallen c ortiers, " there is all the d;fference in the world between a regular three-ply all-wool King like myself and a lot of in:ignificant subjects like you. Let this experience teach so a humility !"—Harper's Monthly.

}ileum IN INSECTS —So marvellous are the recorded doirgs of animals that we might, even at the threshold of the animal kingdom, among the very lowest organisms Imo en, p *use to consider whether there is not intentional ad tptation of means to ends. The observations of Mr. Hi J. Ca-ter have taught us not only ihat the atinophrys pos. se's the power of selecting its food, but goes in search of it, and apparently knows when the supply is exhausted; while even the Rumba is able to distinguish and capture prey under conditions which, in higher animals, would be re- garded as eminently intellectual. The jelly-flah shows no hig`,er intelligence than may be used in carrying the larvm on the inner side of the bell-shaped body, and moving the digestive cavity alternately towards them, so as to bathe their noses in the nutrient fluid of the parent. No special intelligence is cited among any of the echinoderms; but the recently published researches concertflng the earth-worm have enabled us to appropriate the remarkable intelligence of these animals; and it is well-known that the land-leeches of Ceylon easily discover travellers advancing on the paths near which they wait, and congregate rapidly in the jungle and attack individuals in the rear of a party. Among the molltina the records of intelligence are singularly few, and, judging from our own experiments, might have been vastly augmented. Even the oyster, which, when dredged from a depth opens its shell and dies, learns, when placed in re- servoirs where the beds are occasionally left uncovered, to kelp the shell shut, and live. The inteAlgence of the rasor- fish, which every echo Ahoy lrts salted on the sea shore is well-known; but a story is told of the Roman snail which would seem to indicao affection and other mental and moral qualities, for after a healtby animal had wandered away and ' found a well stocked garden, it returned the next day for its sickly mate, and the two went off together. Cattle-fi,ll are said to recognise those who feed them, and to bear malice, as is shown by one climbing up a vertical partition, to get into an adjacent tank, in pursuit of a lobster, with Which a quarrel had previously taken place. The Duke of Sutherland has sent a cheque to all his arable tenants with an amount equal to from 10 to 25 per cent. off their forthcoming rent. Hie Grace has considered each tenant's circumstances individually, and has given the reduction to such an extent as he thinks necessary. A NEW Scanz.—We are glad to hear on trustworthy authori-y that the "new disease" Mr. Fleming is stated to have discovered is not likely to lead to any serious results. The disease in question is an affection of the tongue and some other part of the mouth, in which the former becomes much enlarged and indurated. It usually attacks only one animal in a herd, and does not appear to possfsi any con- tagious properties. It is well known in this country to veterinarians as " scirrhous tongue" cancer, hard tongue, and various other common and technical terms. Its fungus origin was demonstrated by Bollinger, of Munich, several years ago, and Professor Axe, of the Royal Veterinary Col- lege, recorded some observations and experiments relating to the disease in this country in the Veterinarian for 1877. THE FXTRAORLIINARY CONSPIRACY TO DEFRUAD DERBY. sninz FARMERS.—George Pearce, 32, milk dealer, and Charles Headen, 57, dairyman, were indi,qed that they did c &spire, by divers false irttences and suWe devices, to de- fraud a large number of Derbyshire f.rmers, at lialewood, Duffield, and other places, of milk, at various dates during the preeent year. The charge against the prisoners was that they, with others, did conspire to defraud a large number of Derbyshire farmers by means of representations that they were engaged as bond fide milk dealers at various addresses in Liveepo:lendeManchester. Advertisements were inserted in a Lumber of newspapers to this effect —" Milk! milk le:. Wanted, supply delivered at Livorpool.• Write particulars to ` Dairy,' 83, Marylebone, Liverpool." The prisoners also replied to advertisements in papers in Birmingham and other pieces offering supplies of milk. The prisoners wrote from 12, Crowtestreet, Livernool., and "Lancaster Dairy," Charles-etreer. off Miller's-lane. Manchester, and repre- sented themselves to be engaged in business. The prisoners gave bogus references, which turned out to be given by one of the long firm to which they belorged, and who wes now undergoing a long term of imprisonment. They were each sentenced to 12 months' hard labour.

AGRICULTCTRAL EDUCATION.—_The junior or elementary examination held in the autumn of each year in competition for the ten echolaeships of £2O each, offered by the Royal taricn'turd Society of England, took place on Tuesday and Ween-s.dey at tbe Bedford, Devon, and Surrey County Schools, the Agricultural and Comreercial &he& at Aspa- tri a, and the public school at Gersa, near Wetten, Caithness. In all there were thirty candidates, compared with thirty- one last veer, forty in 1880, twenty-three in 1879, twenty- nine in 1878, and thirty-two in 1.877. These scholarships ate for boys between 14 and 18 years of age, and one of the conditions laid down is that the scholar remain at school until the end of the ensuing year, or spend the time with a practical agriculturist or a land agent, or at aa agricultural college. For the purposes of the examination, local secre- taries were appointed at the various centres, the subjects co nprised in the syllabus being the same as on previous occasi)ns, viz., land surveying, cheanietry, and elementary mechanics as applied to agriculture, especially with refer- ence to the rotation of crops, the nutrition of plants and aninale, and the tnechanical cultivatiqn of the soil. SENV&GIC FARMING IN SCOTLAND—The Forfar Sewage Farm was laid out by Mesa. Bailey Denton and Co. four years back on the principle of combining surface irrigation with intermittent filtration; and 27 acres have been found sufficient to cleanse the sewage of 13.000 persona. The ex- tent of the farm purchased by the Burgh authorities was 40 acres, and its cost £4,000, with £1,500 for laying it out for the reception of the sewage. The following is a state- ment from the Forfar Herald of the income and expendi- tare in cnnection with the Orchard B trik Sewage Farm, for the year ending October 15th, 1882:—Income from crops and sand pit: Barley £l9 3s. 9d., oats £24 Os, carrots £32 4e. 9d., Swedish turnips £lO9 7e. , yellow turnips £25 193. 43., mangels £43 63. 11d., cabbages and savoys £27 IW. 63., grass and hay £l3l 18e. 3d., sand £ll 3s. 41.; total £425 21. lid. Expenditure: Railway carriage, cart- age, edvertesing, auctioneer's commission, seeds, &c., £3B is., manual labour, horse work, cic , 1215 63. 103., toole, repair, books, &c., El 14s. 6d., showing a total expenditure of £255 2a. 43., and leaving a balance of £l7O Os. 7d., which, with £3O added as rent of the house occupied by Mr. Mount, leaves £2OO Os. -7d. as profit for the year. The sewage from the town ie applied to £27 acres or thersab tuts, from which £362 7s. 103. has been realised, equal to £l3 Bs. 511. per acre. Thirteen ecree are tmltivated, which are not menured with the aewag, and the income from this acreage amonnte to £49 11s. 93., or £3 16s 30. per acre. AGRICULTURAL ARMIMETIC.—Referring to the Nairn- shire Farmers' Association for the Dostraction of &solo, which gives a nenny a head for every rook slaughtered, a writer in the West Cumberland Times opportunely recalls a conversation which to ,k place in a House of C unmons Com- mittee on the GAM,' levee in 1845, between Mr. John Bright and Mr. Grentley Berkeley. Mr. Berkeley stated that, in diericts unfrequented by rooks, bsys were employed as a substitute to hunt for that destructive foe of the farmer, the wire-worm. The hoop, said Mr. Berkeley in repay to Mr. Bright, were paid at the rate of three-halfpence per hundred for the number of wire-worms they destroyed. On being asked bow much a boy could earn at this rate of pay- ment, he said "Nicepence per day." Questioned as to the' number of worms a boy would destroy per day in earning the ninepence, Mr. Berkeley found himself in a quandary, and judged that the best way to get out of it was to go into a rage, which he accordingly did. "I am not here," he said, "to answer intricate arithmetical questions." If a boy makes 9d. per day in destroying wire-worms at the rate of lid. per hundred, how many must he destroy per day? If you find that problem too intricate for you,"- continued Mr. Bright, "will you tell us whether the boy can do the work as well as a crow ?" "A crow is worth 50 boys at such work," replied Mr. Berkeley. This was rather startling in- formation ; the matter was getting to be more interesting as the inquiry proceeded.. 83 Mr. Bright appeared to think, as be pursued the witness with the further question—" If a boy is worth ninepenee per day in destroying wire-worms, and a crow is worth 50 boys at the work, how much is the crow worth to the farmer in sterling money ?" Again, Mr. Berkeley was disposed to reply by getting into a rage. But his inquisitor was not to be outdone. Paper, pen, and ink were snpolied, and Mr. Berkeley was assisted in his calcula- tions, when it was discovered that a crow was worth to the farmer within two shillings and sixpence of £2 per day. "The bird being worth nearly £2 per day, what may be its yetrly value? was the next query. "About £700," an- swered Mr. Berkeley. He had before said that 50 would be a low average number of crows for each farm in some dis- tricts; and he was now finally asked, "What is the aggre- gate value per year to the farmer of his proper quota of these useful birds ?" This, we are told in the narrative, evolved the most startling conclusion of all; for it appeared that the farmer was a gainer of £35,000 per year by his 50 crows! Pursuing this crow business a bit farther, another problem arises. If a boy is able to make 9d. per day by killing wire-worms at lid. per 100, and a crow at such work is worth 50 boys, thus earning g 2 per day, or £7OO per year, what will have been the total loss to the Nairnshire farmers by the destruction of 4,000 crows at id. per head?

THB DALHOusia EsTaTEs.—An old Tenant writes to the Mark Lane Express :—As a farmer of nearly fifty years' standing on this property, I trust you will grant space for a few remarks on the Dtlhousielanda. Considerable changes have taken place in the ownership in the present century which more or less affected the tenantry. The lands, with the excsption of Dalhousie (which is a comparatively small property), were in the possesion of the Honourable William Mauls for almost sixty years. This noble owner was raised to the peerage at the time of the passing of the Reform Bill, and his motto was, " Live and let live." The question with that good landlord was not what a land-valuer .would make the rent, but what an honest and industrious man could afford to pay. That may now be said to have become the rule by the force of circumstancee, and it is certainly the golden rule, of doing to others what we would have them do to us. The young peer now in possession is following the steps of this noble ancestor, and in entertaining his tenantry in the parishes of Edell, Lethnot, Lochlee, and Brechin ten days ago, he won golden opinions from them. It is little more than two years since he succeeded his father, and in that brief period he has shown, by good deeds, what a landlord, whose heart is in the right place, ought to do. In drinking the health ox his tenantry he said :—" I run most anxious that every one connected with these estates should have fair play, and more than that, that every one should feel that he has fair play. I hope the steps which have already been taken, and the system which I am follow- ing out, will prove to you that I am thoroughly in earnest. No old tenant need fear of being asked to pay- too high a rent, or any small tenant in the glen being turned out of his holding against his will, for the sake of consolidating it with the next." His Lordship further referred to the new regulations on the estate, which are liberal in the extreme as to compensation for buildings, draining, manures, dzc. Hie Lordship has consented to a revaluation of farms where desired, not by the paid valuator from a distance, but by sound, practical men, in whose selection the tenantry have a voice. The leases are assignable. Many of them were sold in former days, and there was and is perfect freedom in cropping. The general provision at the end of the lease as to cropping was that the land was to be left according to the " rules of good husbandry," which, according to the alternate system in Scotland, was understood to mean that there should not be more than one-half under grain crops, and the other half in grass and green crops. The operation of the Law of Distraint may be said to be unknown on this estate. It is said that there is not a better class of tenants in all Scotland than on this (stite, and we are sure there are none who base done more in the im,.rovement of their holdings.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY DECEMB SCIENTIFIC NOTES.. Mr. Gladstone has recommended Mr. David Wingate, a 1 Lanarkshire poet, for a pension of £5O on the Civil List; and it is also stated that he did not do this until he had first read Mr. Wingate'e poems.—Academy. M. de Neuville is now in England making studies and collecting information for a picture which he is painting of the Egyptian war. He and Mr. Woodville will shortly go to Egypt, commissioned by•the Fine Art Society, to paint episodes of the late campaign. . There have been recently excavated at Pompeii six bronze statuettes, of good workmanship and excellently preservel. They are figures of Apollo with his lyre, Mercury, Escula• plus, Hercules, and two Late& They were found, topther with a bronze lamp, in a little shrine, on the walls of which is painted a figure of Fortune.

;rim ELSCT-RIC LIGHT IN COAL MINES.—Mr. Ellis Lever has offered to give a premium of £5OO to any person who will invent the best portable electric light for use in coal mines. Mr. Bart, M.P., and Mr. Crawford, the secretary of the Miners' National Union, have put themselves in com- munication with Mr. Lever for the purpose of rendering him their assistance in awarding the premium and in pro- moting the etbject he has in view. The Atheneum says that the first instalment of Mrs. Lynn Linton's story, of which we have before made mention, will appear in one of the magazines in. January. Talking of stories in magazines, it may be worth mentioning that a well•known periodical is at present embarrassed by the fafigre of a novelist, who is not at present in England, to supply the conclusion of his tale. All the chapters that he has sent have been published, and for the last two months the editor of the magazine has been forced to put in pad- ding to till the Yell Ae the publishers have paid for the whole story, illey are wondering whether its title, "For- tune's Fool," may not be supposed to appty to them, ACCIDENTS IN BLEACHING TMXTILR FABRICS —The authors having observed that in several portions of the fabric after bleaching, many yellowish spots had appeared, accompanied with rottenness of the parts so discoloured, investigated the cause. laeomplete washitg holt acid WAS at first suspected, but the position of the damaged portions did hot allow this view to obtain. An ash analysis of the parts so affected, showed that the discolonration aross from the presence of lime, which had settled upon the fabric in the night when the bath had been emptied, but the cloth not immediately washed. Contact with the warm skin of the bath had caused the lime to be dried in the fibre, wbore the acid subsequently employed only penetrated with difficulty. The final steaming caused the lime to attack the fibre, and discolour it, wherever it had deposited.—Textile Manufac- turer.

• PIGEONS--THI HO3fING INsmer.—The wonderful man- ner in which pigeons find their way over long distances, and an unknown country, to their homes, Me always ex- cited astonishment, and the deeper the question is studied the more wonderful does it appear. Bat it mast be remem- bered this is not an uncommon instinct amongst flying birds, many of which migrate every year In the spring and the autumn. Pigeons as tame birds demand our attention most of all, and their performances during the siege of Paris in 187041, when they were the only means of communica• tion the inhabitants of the city had with the outer world, brought them more prominently into notice. From an Italian writer, P. Bonizzi, we derive the following :—The hypothesis, which appears to have the foundation of truth, is that which makes the faculty of finding their way the. pendent upon the pigeons' powers of sight. To study the question, one must consider the height to which the pigeons ascend on taking flight, when they are let loose at places vary distant from their home; the possibility or not of see- ing objects at a great height, notwithstanding the obstacles presented by the evaporation 'which should come between their view and the earth; and finally, the curvature of tho earth, which would impede the view of objects in a horizon distant from the place whence the pigeons starred. When they are sent out on their flight tioey rise to a very great height, as has been noticed by all observers. They detcribe large circles round the point of departure, as if they wished to take the measure of the profundity of the horizon which is spread out before their view. At times an individual bird leaves the flock and disappears in the distance. Sometimes they lose courage or are disinclined to travel, and return to the point of departure, perching on a convenient roof. Gradually, however, it happens that the best voyageurs unite together, take a determined direction and disappear very quickly from the sight of the observers, Trois would show, therefore, that when the pigeons have determined upon a direction, they will continue and maintain that dire:. lion during the whole or their journey. Next week we shall eensider the range of vision of the birds when they rise as we have already noted. LiZtan.—This variety of canaries is one of the most beautiful of all thsekinds known, and is to called became of its resemblance to the reptile of the same name. The whole of the plumage should be dark, with the exception of the cap, which should be entirely fre3 from ticks or dark fathers. The two colours of these birds are yellow and buff, or gold and silver as they are often called. The breasts require to be dark and even in colour through- out, and entirely free from stripes of dark feathers. The wings and tail should be black to the quills, and the beak and legs as dark as possible. The principal feeture in the bird is the spangling on its back, which consists of even rows of small feathera overlapping each other. Each feather is edged with a beautiful lacing of gold or silver, according to the variety. They are rather spiteful in their n•eare, especially the nale bird, and when the hen lays he should be well watched, and, if proved to be troublesome to the hen, removed, and not returned to her until the yourne are about tan days old. Birds marked on the cap arc called "broken capped," and in good shows special classes are pr.. vided for them. On the second moult these birds lose their show plumage and become a dull colour, the feathers in the wings and tail occasionally becoming white. Renners.—Tees Low EAR.—Lop, as they are generally called, are perhaps the oldest of all the fancy varieties, and undoubtedly stand at the head so far as fancy points are concerned. They are so called because of the long pendu- lous ears which distinguish them from all other varieties, and these ears in the.show pen are regarded as very, if not all, important. At one time it was s'ze of ear and treat alone waich decided the place of the animal, so that the two-foot rule was the judge and not the user of it. Now, however, other points are considered, and rightly so, and we.hepe there is none of the cruelty practised which was at one time so common, namely, the stretching and polling of the ears in order to lengthen and widen them. The ears must always, be looked upon as an impottant point, but not so much so as to over-ride all other considerations. Twenty-two inches Is regarded as a good-sized ear, bat some have been known to reach twenty-four inches. The colours are black, black and white, gray, blue (or slate), fawn, sooty-fawn' yellow and tortoiseshell. They are large in size, and good speci- mens bring good prices. They are, however, delicate, and soon deteriorate if not kept in a warm equable temperature, and are also tender and not easy to keep. We do not re- commend the new beginner to commence with this variety, as they require a great deal of attention and skill, and we do not know that they are any more handsome than many of the hardier varieties.

Esousa TAPESTRT.—At the Royal Tapestry Factory, Old Windsor, some beautiful tableaux, designed by Mr. J. •E. Hodgson:R.A., arid intended for hall and staircase deco- rations for Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt'e mansion, New York, are being worked by the employes upon the moms of the establishment. The series comprises several large pictures —one of which is 22ft. long, and six or seven feet high— representing English sports, including deer stalking, stag and fox hunting, coursing, pheasant and grouse shooting, and salmon, treat, and bottom fishing. As illustrating the progress of the revival of the art of tapestry weaving in this country, it may be mentioned that the English appren- tices under instruction at the factory are now engaged upon portteres, with views of Windsor Castle, Osborne, Backing- ham Palace and Balmoral, and which are being woven in imitation of the old Arras tapestry.—Textile Manufacturer. WASTE.—Dr. Siemens, President of the British Associa- tion, speaking to the students of the Coventry Science Classes on "Waste," referred to the steam engine, and said that 20 years ago 1011os. of coal were consumed for every horse-power effect yielded, which had been by scientific method and mechanical skill reduced to 21bs. Without any other expenditure than that of thought and mechanical skill, greater results had been obtained with one-fifth of the , expenditure. In like manner in smelting works the amount of coal required to produce a ton of iron had been reduced from 7 or 8 tons to one-fifth of the quantity, whilst a ton of steel was produced with 3 tons instead of 14. We did not depend exactly on coal for the power of beat required. We had great stores of force, the outcome of solar radiation on the earth, in the form of water-power, wind, and tidal action. All these could and would no doubt in time be made useful for our purposes. How HEAT IS PRODUCED.—Heat Is produced when two substances are rubbed or struck together. No doubt you have often, as a schoolboy, rubbed a metal button rapidly and for tome minutes on a wooden form until the button (has been too hot to touch. Savages produce fire in the same way by taking a couple of very dry sticks mill rubbing them together until they are ignited, and we likewise use the same method when we take a match and rub its end on the wall or on the side of the box. I.: will be seen, how- ever, that the labour in the latter operation is reduced to the least possible amount by the match being tipped with phos- phorus. ,This phosphorus is very useful indeed for this par- pose,and gives BS a ready mode of showing that heat is pro- duced in many operations. If you take a stone and let it drop from a height, it produces heat from its sudden stop- sage. You cannot, however, detect that such is the case by touch alone, but if you. take the phosphorus from the tip of the match and piece it exactly where the stone will fall, you will find that the phosphorus will blaze up. Fric- tion, or the rubbing of two substances together, and percus- sion, or the. knocking of two aubstances together, are two very common sources of hew., for yon can scarcely tarn round without seeing that it is so. There, for example, is a loaded waggon coining down the hill-side. The waggoner has put the brake on; there is a dreadful shrieking noise, and you see smoke aacendinz from the wheel until he gets down into the valley. Shafting in our mills likewise re- quires oiling regifeelee etltereeise it would eoln become red- -11,4 from the friction. Oa a granar scale we hays soca-- times vast forests set on fire in the far West by the con- tinual rubbing of branches together when dry acd parched; and a vast number of meteors coming earthwards from space are supposed to never reach us, became when they enter our atmosphere with their terrible speed the rubbing against the air as they whistle through it produces heat sufficient to turn them into vapour. NOVEL DRESSING FOR WOUNDS.—Two years ago a la- bourer one day appeared who had sustained a compound fr•ctare of both bones of the fore-arm eight or ten days previou,ly, with considerable laceration. He had got a comrade to surround the whole fore-arm at once with a thick paste of peat mould, on which was laid a rough splint of wool. He was in good general health, and on c'e 'ring off the mould the wound was found to be heeling, beauti- fully, without any sign of sappuration. A Listerian dress- ing WAS applied, and the limb better fixed, and the man made a good recovery. Dr. Neuberg, of Biel, was led to in- vestigate the properties of peat mould, with reference to wound dressing, and he found that the dust resulting from the manufacture of blocks of peat with the circular saw (as ' carried on in Schltswig-Holstein), and which is very light in weight and colour, has a powerful affinity for ammonia, carbonate of ammonia, and bad smelling materials generally, and takes up nine times its own weight of water. In the infantry barracks at Brunswick it is found very useful as a ;deodoriser in privies. For dressing wounds Dr. Nenberg now uses two bags of gauze (one double the other in size wrung out in carbolic solution, and filled with mould, the mould in the smaller bag containing 21 per cent. of lodo• form, that in the larger saturated with 5 per cent. carbolic solution. The smaller bag is placed on the wound directly after disinfection of the latter with carbolic solution, zinc chloride, or iodcform, and the larger bag is placed above, the whole belng kept in place by a gauze bandage. The dress- lug remains on meetly a fortnight or more. Excellent re- • sults have been thus obtained, into details of which ,we do i not here enter. The advantages claimed for the method are • these:—L A given quantity of the mould takes up more ' fluid than jute gauze, or cotton wool. If it be slightly moistened its absorbent power is increased. 2. It has great power of absorbing products of decomposition of organic substances, and hence prevents these occurring, 3. The moistened mould is a very soft but still elastic substance and so is easily placed in the required position in the bags before applying them to the inequalities of the body. 4. It is the cheapest of known antiseptic dressings, one pennyworth being sufficient for one dressing, and still leas if the pre- paration with an antiseptic be left out. 5. It make a very suitable pad for all purposes when enclosed in gauze.

DOGS.-.-TEE MANAGEMENT OF 14-11—DI-E8;- PETB.—A few hints upon so important a question as this will doubtless be welcomed by many of our readers, for it is a fact that pet dogs, as a role, are spoiled by their owners pampering and petting them, feeding them on delicacies which are posi- tively injaarious. It should always be remembered that dogs are naturally used to plain food, and deviation from this rule is Bare to be attended with danger. As a rule, the use of meat should be avoided. Bad coats and foul breath are the sure and certain signs of a too liberal meat diet, and the toy dog suffers also from heat and irritation of the blood. Over-feeding is a very mistaken kindness, and quite as in- judicious in the case of a dog as it would be if a child were the victim. Good gravy, with some crumbled bread, bii- cults, or pie-crust soaked in it, and with a little chopped vegetables Is a good food ; so is sago, rice, or Yorkshire pud- ding. In fact, anything which is tasty, easy of digestion, and not too rich, is good for a change. Sweet biscuits can be given now and again without any ill effects, and a little liver may also be given occasionally or a treat. Milk should be avoided, as it has a tendency to produce worms. Coddling dogs is a great mistake in more ways than one. Of course, in the case of very small and highly-bred dogs every precaution must be taken to guard against chills, and much depends upon the breed selected. But it is a painful thing to contemplate the existence of many toy show dogs, who are always kept in glass cases, lest they should catch a cold or their coats should suffer. And we believe this to be I entirely uncalled for, as by proper treatment in the first in- stance these dogs can be made reasonably hardy, and if ordi- ' nary care is taken their costa can always be kept in good order. Exercise is next necessary, and we should always recommend a run every day. Draughts must be avoided, and pet dogs should always have a snug kennel indoors, where they will be quite free from these. If they sleep in a room with a brick, stone, or cement floor, the bottom of the kennel should be of wood, and a thick rug or blanket made to cover it. Cleanliness in dogs is easily taught, but a little patience may be necessary. They must be given frequent opportunities of running out, or they will certainly transgress this law. Ladies, in choosing a pet dog, should remember that a smooth-coated dog gives less trouble than a long-coated one, and a dark than a light one. With the former there is not the labour in combing and brushing the hair, and when casting the coat there is not the same amount of hair to stick about the furniture or clothes. Irri- tation of the skin is also more easily detected in the smooth dogs; and a dark dog requires leas washing than a light- coloured one.

Dr. Kern, who has filled the post of Swiss Minister in Paris for many yea:3, has resigned that post in consequence of feeble health. It is stated that great uneasiness prevails in financial and commercial circles in France, owinglo the strange errors discovered in the estimates laid before the Budget Com- mittee.

"treat ruin and suffering" hare been caused throughout the oil region in Pennsylvania by the commercial panic, but the worst of the crisis was thought to have been passsed on Saturday. The railway " war " in the north-west con- tinues.

At a meeting of the French Cabinet Council on Tuesday, it was resolvei to despatch an expedition of a pacific char- acter, under the direction of M. de Brazza, to survey the ceded territory in the Congo district from a commercial and scientific point of view, and report upon its resources. The ladies and gentlemen who were gambling on Sunday evening at Monte Carlo were startled by the explosion of a dynamite cartridge, which some person—a loser at tho tables, perhaps—had hid away in a corner. There was a rush for the door, ani in the struggle one of the gamblers WAS seriously hurt. _ _ _ _

The final -decision of the Turkish Gxvernment is that it refuses to recogni” the cession of Mosowah or any other territory on the RA Sea to any of the Powers. Accordingly the Turkish tiove:nment has resolved to send a small fleet to the Red Sea to oppose the Arabian chiefs selling terri- tories.

The floods in the Rhine and the Main are increasing and causirg immense loss and suffering. At CobLentz, accord- ing to a telegram despatched by the Empress to the Em- peror, the danger is great, and " it is impossible to foresee what the end will be." Reports of disastrous inundations have been received from Frankfort and Bonn. M. GAMBETTA WOUNDED.—M. Gatribettal was wounded on Monday by the accidental discharge of a revolver which he was handling. He had drawn the charges of the revol- ver, and while inspecting the weapon a barrel which he had overlooked went off, :And the bullet ran up his arm half way to the elbow. M. Gambetta, almost fainting with the pain' was taken to bed by his servant. It is hoped that he will be convalescent in a week.,

AN EXTRAORDINARY REvrLATION.—A New York tele- gram says that Mr. Thurlow Weed left an affidavit solving the mystery surrounding the murder of Morgan in 1827. According to tba confession of the principals, made to Mr. Thurlow Weed under circumstances of secrecy and neces- sity, the Freemasons drowned Morgan in the Niagra river, in revenge for his exposure of the secrets of the craft. In- cidental to this confession there is a marvellous story of mistaken identity. FRANCH AND MADAG&SCAIL.—It is reported from Paris that the French Government sent an ultimatum to the Malagasy Ambassadors on Saturday, and that the presen- tation of the document gave rise to a discreditable scene wiaich is described by the correspondent of the Stan/lard: The Malagasy flag was torn down by French officials, and the Ambassadors left the hotel with nothing but their money. They left Paris for London, being threatened on their departure with the immediate outbreak of war.

A BARBAROUS MASSACRE.—The Daily Teleyrap4 Vienna correspondent telegraphed on Sunday :—A barbarous mas- sacre was perpetrated last month in the province of Van. On October 11 fire broke out simultaneously in several parts of the town of Bitlis. The conflagration lasted 18 hours, destroying every house and store. The Armenian inhabi- tants, on attempting to extinguish the flames, were received by a volley of Kurdish musketry and driven back by Turkish bayonets. Several hundred Armenians were killed. The telegraph officials refused to forward messages to Van for assistance.

REVOLT IN BIIRMAH : BATTLE WITH THE INSURGENTS.— It appears from information just to hand, that an engage- ment has been fought at a place called Chatnba, in Ecua- dor, between the rebel forces and the soldiers of the Govern- ment. Chamba is a small village some 120 miles from Guayaquil, and it seems that the Government troops were victorious. The news of the battle was received on the 17th inst. at Panama, but no details of the fighting were given. On both sides, it appears, there were many killed and wounded, and the President had ordered a six days' mourn- ing for the soldiers killed in the action.

—THE FATE OF THE PALMER EXPEDITION.—Further details of the lamentable catastrophe of the Palmer expedi- tion have been received. It is confirmed that when the party were seized they were told that they had the choice between two modes of death—they might either throw themselves over a precipice or be shot. Professor Palmer "called upon Heaven to avenge his death" and took the fatal leap. He was followed by Captain Gill; the others elected to be shot. It is stated that Colonel Warren, who is investigating the matter, is of opinion that the dder to "kill the Christians" did not proceed, as the Bedouins alleged, from Cairo, but was the result of the fanaticism of two Egyptian governors. THE STATE OF EGYPT.

Reports received at Cairo from Khartoum do not confirm the previous statements that that important place was in danger of attack by the False Prophet. The Egyptian Government claims to be the owner of the bay of Tajurrah, which was rbcently "annaxed " by M. Solelllet, a French explorer and treaty maker. The terri- tory has been the subject of a special firman Qf the Sultan and a decree of the Egyptian Government. A telegram from a correspondent at Alexandria states that several soldiers of the 46th Regiment, stationed at Ramleh, on returning drunk to quarters on Friday evening, fell foul of an Arab, and beat him with their belts with such violence that he died on Saturday. Two of the soldiers are in custody. The trial of Arabi and the other prisoners has, according to the Cairo Prosecution Committee, been definitely fixed to commence on December 7. It is believed that Lord Dufierin has decided to recommend the Egyptian Govern- ment not to proceed with the charges against ArAbi of com- plicity in the burning of Alexandria on July 12 and the massacres of June 11.

The Cairo hgspital statistics for the five days from the 22nd and 26th instant, both inclusive, show that there were 307 fresh admissions, 111 discharged to duty, 112 renloved elsewhere, 7 deaths. 767 remaining in the beds. The num- ber of patients in the military horpitals throughout Egypt is 1,133, out of a total force of 12,536—rather over 9 per

,ER Sot. These returns show an improvement in the health of the troops; but the large number of fresh cases coming in is regarded as a serious feature. Ismail Pasha Eyoub, President of the Court of Inquiry. has written a letter to Mr. Broadley, the leading counsel for Arabi Pasha, in explicably strong terms. Mr. Broadley had protested against several flagrant breaches of the rules lof procedure lgreed upon, and the President, in replying to his cpmmunication, not only declares that there has been no violation.of the rules, but adds—" You are mistaken as Ito the limits of your rights, and are invited to keep within the limit of them in future."

Now that the Egyptian question has got into a condition with which Turkey is not 'allowed to interfere, and other serious matters which have troubled the Porte,hade assumed a tolerably quiet aspect, troable is again threatened on the borders of Montenegro. The Porte complains of the hostile attitude of Montenegro, and the Montenegrin Governmeat declares that if the district of Kolotochin be not immedi- ately given up, Montenegrin troops will be sent to occupy it. The situation bears a disquieting aspect, but little ebul- litions of this kind are, unfortunately, not uncommon on the confioes of the Turkish Empire.

div.head: IRADE NOTES.
div.p: IRADE NOTES.

BILLS OF SALE AND FAILURES. In the week ending November 25, 1882, there were 213 bills of sale in England and Wales, a decrease of 897 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted nambered 201, a decrease of 55. The total for portion of year to November 25, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 40,422, a decrease of 5,539 the failures gazetted number 9,609, a dsc,ease of 886.—Stubbs' Mercantile Gazette. A meeting of delegates representing the house coal minus of South I'Vales and Monmouthshire was held at Nelson Bay oa Saturday, at which the forthcoming conference at Leeds with regard to the question of restricting the output was condemned, and resolutions were passed in fassotie of the nine hours' system and the compulsory prohibition by Act of Parliament of anybody working in mines except those who had served the necessary apprenticeship:to the duties. THREATENED IRONWORKERS' STRIKE IN STAFFORDSHIRE. --On Monday there was a great deal of complaining amongst certain of the South Staffordshire ironworkers, and at some works they were hesitating to resume on the night turn. They declare that the award of Alderman Avery does not meet their case with the fulness which the condition of the labour market justifies. They assert it should have given them a 71 per cent. rise from the end of October, instead of only a3d rise from January 1. It is hoped, however, that the threat of a strike will not be r a .ried Out. THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE.—The amount of buying going on in this market continues extremely small, and if anything seems to get less. The numher of inquiries*stir- ririg on 'Change on Tueslay was very limited, and there was an absence of actual business of importance. Pig iron is generally held pretty firmly for late rates so far as local and district brands are concerned, although an easier tone Prevails in outside markets. For delivery into the Man- eiester district Lancashire pig iron is still quoted at 495. to 503. less 2 ; Lincolnshire at 495. to 50s. less 4; and Derby- shire from 51s. to 525. less 2. Finished iron shows more weakness than pig iron, and the difficulty of getting speci- fications for iron already sold for shipment is seriously affecting some of the large works. Where manufacturers are kept going it is mainly with deliveries on account of old orders, and, although sales are not actually pressed at lower figures to secure new orders, makers in many cases would be open to offers. For bars delivered into Manches- ter district £6 10d. to £6 12s. 6d. is about the average figure, but for a good specification a little under £6 103. would be taken in sonic cases.

TITTER LABOUR MARK RT.—The labour market shows few important changes. In the North of England the coal trade continms in a good position, and in South Wales and Mot.- moutbshire the miners are opposed to limitation of oat-put; meanwhile, in the Forest of Dean the coal trade shows s3nie revival. In the northern iron trade a reduction of five per cent. in wages has been awarded. In South Wales the iron and steel works are briskly employed. Tinplate workers in the same district are somewhat unsettled. At the leading northern ports iron shipbuilding remains as active as it has been for some weeks past, and shipwrights for the Govet n- aunt dockyard at Chathatn are being advertised for. The textile trades are on the whole maintaining an average amoueit of employment. At Macclesfield there is a strike of silk weavers. At Kidderminster traile is improving, and m9st houses are now busy, and throughout the Huddersfield district employment keeps satisfactory. .At several points in the United States, specially Chicago, St. Louis, wages in the iron trade have been reduced, Assisted passages to South Australia have been resumed.—Labour News.

THE LANCASHIRE CCAL TRADE.—During tiiT:Pst week the coal trade has shown :a tender* towards improvement. Orders for house-fire coal have been coming in rather more freely. There are also indications that the stocks taken in by eonsumers for manufacturing purposes are being gradually worked off, and this will bring into the market an accession of orders for the lower quilities of fuel. Owing to the recent stormy weather having kept vessels away from Liverpool and Garston, a good deal of coal on order for shipment hss been thrown upon the home market, and to effect temporary tilles prices have been irregular. For the general trade, however, the market is fairly steady ; the prin&pal firms in ihe Manchester district maintain their full list rates, and al- though in the West Lancashire districts there has been a pretty general giving way of 6d. to al. per ton in round coals upon the fall advance asked at the commencement of the month, it is not likely that the downward movement will go beyond this. At the pit mouth prices average about as under :—Best coal, 103. to 103. 61.; seconds, Bs. to;8s. Gd.; quotations above these figures being now only exceptional; common house coals, 75. to 78. 6d.; steam and forge coals, 6s. Gd. to 75.; burgy, 53. to ss. 3d.; bet slack, 4s. to 4s. 3d.; and common sorts from 3s. 3d. to 3s. Gd. per ton. Coke con- tinues in g,od demand, at full rates.

div.head: POACHING FFRAY IN CHESHIRE.
div.p: POACHING FFRAY IN CHESHIRE.
A GA.MEKEEPER AND A POLICEMAN WOUNDED.

A serious affray between a gang of poachers and several policemen and gamekeepers has occurred on the Bostoek estate, near I\liallewich. Guns being beard at night in the covers, head keeper Myles and a number of watchers went in search in one direction, while James -Hooke, under keeper, Robert Niddie, and four policemen frho were on duty near the place, went in another direction. Myles's party disturbed the gang at work, who made off in the direction of the police officers and the other members of the party. Cross- ing a meadow they were confronted by the police, whom the poachers began to stone. The officers and watchers joined in the pursuit, when two of the gang of poachers, after using threats, deliberately knelt on the ground and tired into the advancing group of men, who were only a few yards off. The contents of one gun were lodged in the calf of Niddie's leg, inflicting a severe wound. The officers and watchers then dashed in, and came at close quarters with the poachers. The latter, treizrig the barrels of their gnus, began to club the officers and watchers, and in the course of the desperate fight which ensued police-constable Hodgkin. son received a blow on the head, which penetrated the skull. Two of his teeth were knocked out, and he was also bruised about the face. One of the poachers, John Johnson, of Northwich, was captured on the spot, but the rest of the gang ebt away. John Jones, alias William Aldesley, was arrested early on Sunday morning as be was entering Northwich. Later two men, named Emmanuel Hanker and Thomas Sandbach, were captured at Castle Northwich. The injured men lie at Northwich in a critical condition. The four 'men—Johnson, Aldesley, Sandbach, and Hankey—have been positively identified.

div.head: PROJECTED SIIIP CANAL
div.p: THE PROJECTED SIIIP CANAL

1 The plans and sections in connection with this irnportan ; project have during the present week been deposited with ; the Clerks of the Peace for Lancashire and Cheshire in ! readiness for the next session of Parliament. Messrs. G. ; Faulkner and Sons, Manchester, have been trusted with the work, which, it must be acknowledged, has been very artistically done. The intended navigation commences at the Old Quay Docks, Runcorn, and takes the course of the Ruricorn and Latchford Canal to Walton, where the first set of locks is to be constructed. From thence it followsinearly the course of the river, passing throttgh the parishes of Grappenhall, Runcorn detached, Lymm, Warburton, Bow-. don (close to the Mill Bank Paper Mills), and Flixton, near the confluence of the Mersey and Irwell, where the second set of locks is ta be made. From this point the canal will continue along the river side by easy curves through the parish of Eccles to Barton, where the third set of locks will be formed, immediately above the Barton aqueduct.. The waterway is thence carried on to the vicinity of what is now the Manchester Racecoui se, where it is intended that docks, covering an area of 70 acres, shall be constructed. In connection with the works and in addition to the diversion of streams and provision for public roads there are five railways to be dealt with. It has been admitted ever since the scheme was started that this was the most serious matter to be considered. The railways that will be affected are the London and North-Western Company's main line from Crewe to Preston; the Great-Western line from Chester to Warrington; the London and North- Western line between Stockport, Warrington, and Gar- , stun ; tbe Cheshire Lines railways from Stockport to Warrington, and between Liverpool and Manchester. The intention is to carry all these railways over the canal by bridges at such an elevation as will permit ocean-going vessels to pass beneath, except in the case of the Stockpolt, Warrington, and Garston line, which it is -proposed to carry under the stream. In order to obtain the i requisite gradients tke lines will, of course, have to be taken up, and re-constructed for a considerable distance on either side of the proposed bridges. The construction of the canal commences, as we have said, at Runcorn, but beyond that, between Runcorn and Garston, the bed of the river Mersey will be efficiently dredged, and a deep channel maintained between training walls to be specially constructed for that purpose, in place of the present variable and otherwise un- satisfactory channel. Messrs. Falkner are also preparing tLe book of reference, which will extend to nearly 300 pages. It will contain a description of all the property affected by the proposed works, together with the names of each owner, lessee, and occupier. A glance at the plans and reference book enables one to realise the magnitude of the enterprise, and the vigour and efficiency which have so far characterised the efforts of the promoters.

RUNCORN (2ND) VERSUS EGREMONT.—This match was p7ayed at Runcorn, on Saturday last, and a most enjoyable game ended in favour of Runcdrn. Egeemont kicked off, and a litt:e loose play eneld'ed Dunbavand ti score. Egremont had to act on the de:enaive several times, Fisher pertormiag his duties very well. filarne capital kicks were exchanged between Ellaby and Wainwriselt, when Gatens, Ford, and Sherlock effeoted a nice dribble, Cox running up and gaining a try; but the place kick was again a failure. Luring the second half, a much faster game was played. Egrentont seemed to improve, but this did not preyed T. Riley from running in. J. Postman took the place and kicked to Wainwright, who essayed a drop at goal, and aim. et succeeded in his efforts. Clarke and Bur- rews followed up, the latter player touching down. J. Roberts was instrumental in taking the ball to neutral territory, where Ellaby dropped back to J. Pownall. J. Pownall returned, and thrice in succession these two players exchanged some heavy kicks. As matters were now equa!, both teams strove hard to make headway, and in twenty minutes further play the visitors succeeded in securing-;their second goal, which in three minates t.me, was followed by James Blackey securing an equalising point for the hmse trans. EARIXSTOWN ASSOCIATION V. Sr. HEL-ENS —A match be- tween the representatives of the Earlestown association and Sr. Thomas's (St. Helens) football clubs was played on the gamed of the former, at Wargrare Moss, Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon last. The ground was very soft and slip- pery, and, owing to the mud, many of the players presented a singular spETtaele at the conclusion of the game, which was not played out owing to a dispute. There was a good attend- ance of spectators. The Earlestown cap-ain won the toss, and chase to play with the station goal at the back of Ills team. The visitors set the leather in motion shortly after three o'clock, and the match was evenly contested for some time. The home team, however, quickly asserted their superiority. Alters quarter of an hour's play the game was all in favour of Earles- town. Simms on the left wing made some excellent runs, and the St. Helens goal was frequently endangered. The home backt and half-tracks well tag-sported the f ‘rwards. and half an hour from the kirk off Eaalestown sects, ea a corner kick. Nothing tangible resulted, but a'ter five minutes further play, the right wing players made a good MI with the ball, and B miter st•nt it between the updghts amid applause. Just before half time was called, Bowker again score i with a splen- did "screw." shot, and ends were changed with the score two t none in favour of Earlestown. On the re-commenaewent of the game the home eleven severely pressed their opponents, and in ten minutes Shaw seared a third goal, and about ten minutes later Dagnall added a fourth. At this print the visitors claimed a free kick for alleged "charging" by one of the Earlestown players, and as the umpires gave a decision contrary to the St. Helens team, the St. Helens players left the field 23 minutes from the ffsish, thus leaving the home team winners by four goals to none. RUNCORN V. BIRICRNFINAD PARE (A TRAM) —The Runeorn football team journeyed to the Park at Birkenhead on Satur- day, where they m-t an exceedingly strong team. There was a field full of spec-atone but they had apparently not gathered for the legitimate enjoyment of the game. Their language was at times most violent, and the game was carried on with the gieatest difficulty. This is very surprising. Runcorn spectators will certainly record the return team a more cordial ception. The leather was started by the home team, and the home territory was strongly invaded by the Runoorn forwards, who pressed Birkenhead very heavily. Wilson and Morgan made a good attempt to rele-ve the pre sure, but to no purpose, and the excellent forward piay of Cox, Wright. and Atherton soon traneterred the play in close proximity to the home lines. H. Andrews splendidly wriggled through the paek and eroseed the line. The place proved unsuccessful. Some very fast play was the scene on both sides. the scene of ac:lon being the centre flag, when Larkin put Ins fine run, being almost on the point of scoring before he was brought down. Playing then following on the home goal line they touched down. Following up their drop out, tbe visitors' 25 was Invaded. Johnson put in some short runs, and the centre flag was passed. A long punt by Larkin rested the leather In touch in the home 25 Hughes made progress towards the home line; passing to Mason, the corner flag was reached, bell goleg in touch. Williams and Wilson nicely relieved the apparent danger by a smart run, which the latter ended by a long punt. Broady returned so effectively-that a touchdown was again resorted to by Birkenhead. Williams quickly dropped out from 25 yards flee. and Wilson following up quickly, the visitors' 25 was entered. The back play of the Runcorn men prevented their opponents scoring up to half time. On the change of ends Hughes re-started from centre, and the home 25 was again entered. Morgan shook off the Runcornians by short punting, and Johnson making several short runs, the leather finally rested in touch. Following this some fast play ensued, during which both positions were alter- nately threatened and relieved by Mergau. Blood, and Wilson on one side; Cox, Hughes. Wright, and Andrews on the other. Atherton, who bad plaeed a good forward gune,earried the bail across the line, the plwe kick failing. The visitors followei up quickly, play being confined in the home quarter, when Andrews piekng up smart, dodged his way through the pack and added the third try, no goal being placed. Play became extremely difficult, the spectators lining the goal line, and not a few in the field of play. The home team teemed to rouse up a little, play ensuing in the visitors' half. Clarke played the ball well, finally kicking in touAr. Wright and Gatley were Instrumental In transferring the noel black past the centre flag, when, by a combined rush of the visitors, Wilkinron added the fourth try, the place being again unsuccessful Immediately afterwards "no side" was celled, Runcorn winning not a very agreeable game, viz., four tries, four minor points, to Birkenhead nil. Teams :—Full beck, W Hughes; three quarters. Broady, Larkin, end Johnson; half backs. Andrews and H Hughes (captain), Wright. Cox, Atherton, Joule, Page, Mason, Clarke. Gatley, and Wilkinsen. ferwards. Birkenhead: Blood, full back; Davidson, Madge, and Fairley three quarters; h Llf bricks, Williams and Morgan; Madge, Wilson, Williamson, Newton, Hood, Duncan, Hampson, Graham, and Brown, forwards.

CHIME IN IRELAND.—The CHIEF SECRETARY for IRE- -14-MD made a statement on the subject of crime in Ireland, lue reply to an inquiry as to whether the Government could eye any information about the horrible assassination of a Policeman on Saturday night. Mr. Trevelyan pointed out the distinction between the general state of Ireland and the OPecial question of violent and organised crime in Dublin. As to agrarian outrages the returns for the current month Would, he said, fall below 100 for the first time for 28 Mouths. As regards murderous crime in Dublin, the autlabrities had now reached a stage of open conflict in Which all the servants of the Queen were determined to do their duty, and he trusted the country would recognise the heroic conduct of the brave men who had the opportunity ef showing what stuff the Dublin police were made of, and 'also the courage of the gallant sergeant of rifles, who stood by the police in circumstances more trying than those of an erdinary battle. t THE BAY OF TAJOURA.—Sir CHARLES DILICE informed Baron de Worms that the Government were not aware of .• any such cession as that of the Bay of Tajoura having been made to France by the Sultan of Laita, and said they Were distinctly of opinion that Tajoura Was part of the territory of the Khedive. Mime—Mr. ASHMEAD BARTLETT repeated his inquiry as to whether the Russians were in Merv, to which Sir C. DILKE answered that he could not say, but the Government had no reason to think they were. NEW MEMBER.—Mr. Tomlinson took the oath and his eetst for Preston. • PROCEDITRE.—On resuming the consideration of the Rules of Procedure, Mr. GLADSTONE moved the 13th rule, - Which provides that the first seven and the last three of the resolutions already passed should become standing orders of the House.—Mr. STANHOPE moved to omit the Closure re- solution. and Sir J. LUBBOCK to omit the second, relating to motions for adjournment during question time.—Mr. GLAD- STONE said he was not disposed to despair of the working of the second resolution, notwithstanding what had taken Place. He thought they wanted longer time to see whether It could be made to work. In the exceptional circumstances in which they found themselves, he thought they ought •' not to give too much weight to what had happened. As to * Int resolution, he denied that the Closure had been carried, as was asserted, by a party vote, and declared that if the Rouse had not been favourable to it the Government would have accepted the failure of their plan.—Mr. Stanhope's amendment was defeated by 137 to 90, and Sir J. Lubbock's did nct go to a di.vision. The motion of the Prime Minister Was agreed to. GRAND COMMITTEE.—The House then proceeded VS con- eider the question of Grand Committees. The suggestion Of the Premier was that limited and special business in Committee which was now taken on the floor of the House should be delegated to Committees out of the House, and he proposed to commence the experiment with reforms of the law and measures relating to trade and shipping, which had always been beyond party strife. He proposed that the • number of members on each Committee ehould be from 60 to 80, that the appointment of Chairman should rest with ' the House, that the Committee should meet at the same ' time as the select and private committees. It was intended to take one step forward and give the House an opportunity ' fef forming a safe and clear judgment as to whether they Would take another forward step.—Sir RICHARD CROSS , Moved that it was not expedient to consider the matter at the present time.—Mr. Norwood, Sir H. Holland, Mr. Lebow- chere, Mr. Forster, and other speakers followed, and the debate was adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. ,V THE COST OF THE EGYPTIAN WAR.—Mr. GLADSTONE Made his promised statement on the expense of the Egyp- tian war, in answer to a question by Colonel Stanley. It Would be necessary, the Prime Miaister said, to ask for a ' farther sum on account of our military expense. He could not yet say whether it would be asked for as a supplemen- tary estimate or an additional vote of credit. The sum originally voted was £2,300,000. It was now proposed to ask for an additional sum of £1,060,000. The estimated expense of the Indian contingent was £1,880,000. The actual expenditure had been £1,140,000. The gross amount to be borne by England, including transport at home was . £4,560,000. THE Coo.—Sir C. DILKE, in reply to Mr. Jacob Bright, • laid the Government were very anxious for the freedom of Commercial intercourse which had hitherto existed on the • Congo between this country and that part of Africa, and • the matter was at present under their most serious con- Sideration. - THE STATE OF IRELAND: MICHAEL DAVITT'S SPEECH.— Mr. TREYELYAN, in reply to an hon. member, said the speech ; Of Mr. Devitt at Navan had been under the consideration of : the Government, but no steps had yet been taked in regard to it. No further arrests had, he believed, been made in Pnblin. Mr. Field had passed a better night than was expected, but his state was most critical. THE ADMINISTRATION OF THE IRISH LAND ACT.—The Chief Secretary for Ireland was interrogated as to the Working of the Land Courts, and made a statement as to the Proposed reconstruction of the Courts. It was to the effect that the Court valuers had been appointed with the view of increasing the despatch of business, that the hopes of the Government in this respect had been disappointed, and that it had therefore been determined to attach to each Court four main sub-commissioners instead of two, an arrange- ment which it was eexpected would lead to a very, great act eleration in the number of cases decided.—At a later Period of the evening Mr. 4ISSON asked leave to move the Mjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing the matter, which he asserted was of "urgent public , Dortance." The right hon. gentleman having obtained the Support of more than 40 members proceeded to raise a debate on the subject. He contended th it the decisions of the administrators of justice in Ireland were about to be set aside by the Government oa account of political , considerations, and suggested that if the Chief Secretary had power to promise that the administration of an Act Would be varied until it satisfied his political friends, it Mig'ut be used as a vast engine of political corruption. The neurt valuers were, he said, being got rid of, not because they valued unfairly, but from clamour, to please the politi- cal friends of the Ciovernment.—Mr. FORSTER was glad to see the course the Government were adopting. It would , Cost a little more money at first, but the work would be done quicker, and therefore in the end it would be economical.— Mr. C. RUSSELL thought the Government had acted wisely • h putting an end to an experiment which, if it had been per- Severed in, might have been disastrous to the working of the Land Act; but Colonel TOTTENHAM insisted that what the Government wished was that there should be a general reduction of rents in Ireland.—Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out ' that he had from the first deliberately opposed the appoint- Ment of Court valuers as a cumbrous method of procedure, and as unlikely to contribute to general confidence. Ho assented to the appointments for two reasons propounded by • great authorities, but they had failed. They therefore pro- , Posed to substitute a system under which, with a-limited e increase of present cost, greater justice would be given to the Land Act, by causing its provisions to be adopted with at greater effect over the whole surface of the land. At the conclusion of the right hon. gentleman's speech, the Speaker r etired, and was not able to resume the chair, owing to indis- , Position. The Deputy-Speaker (Mr. Playfair) therefore took /te place of Sir H. Brand, and the debate was resumed by ear. PLUNKET. It was continued by Mr. RICHARDSON, Mr. • G'DONNELL, Mr. O'SnAuonNEssv, Lord G. HAMILTON, and • others. It ended in the rejectioa of the motion without a division, and the House then resumed the discussion of the Procedure Rules. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. . TEM SPEAKER.—The Speaker was again unable, through Indisposition, to appear in the House of Commons when tlif embers met yesterday afternoon, and the Deputy-Speaker look the chair. Tete Away IN EGYPT.—A question from Lord E. Cecil brought out the fact that the "War Office had obtained the consent of the Treasury to make a special extra allowance 3s• per day to each officer serving with the army oceupa- ', • loh in Egypt, in order to meet the additional expense entailed up o them by residence in that country. As to the rank and file no such enlargement of expenditure was corn- : puleory unon them, and consequently their pay will not be ; tneinented. The money devoted to officers' expenses will included in the extra charges spoken of by the Prime uunister on Tuesday night as likely to be borne by Egypt." EGYPTIAN Amlns.—Sir W. LAWSON endeavoured to , obtain the promise of a day for the discussion of Egyptian affairs, but Mr. GLADSTONE slid there was to his mind no reason why anything except a vote of censure should justify the Government in asking the House to interrupt its busi- tioas to discuss that matter. f.• GRAND COMMITTEES.—The consideration of the resolu- * 0,11 appointing Grand Committees" was then resumed. ue Government declined to accept amendments extending ;Tie number of committees beyond two and endeavouring to :tiMit the times at and during which the committees shall these propositions being negatived by a majority of the C. Dream took the opportunity, on a remark Vi ettnn Mr. W. H. Smith, to deny in the most emphatic man- net the accuracy of his reported statement that measures LT re by these reforms intended to pass through the House L'lthout due consideration—"as through a bill-spinning tinclaine." The arrival of a quarter to six o'clock, when a „ tes close on Wednesday afternoons, caused the post- ! leorn , ohne, , ant of the discussion before any definite result was mew. 4.4 HOUSE OF COMMONS—THURSDAY. • 4R CUBAN ReremEes.—Mr. ASHLEY said the report of Committee' of Inquiry as to the case of the Cuban refugees 414,r1Y condemned the conduct of the Gibraltar authorities. se, ,314131 PASIIA.—In reply to Mr. Bourke, Mr. GLADSTONE -,e4tu that reasons of public interest still existed which pre- ‘v,!nted the Government from offering any facilities for a ''excu,s_sion on the surrender of Arabi Pasha. DAVITT'S SPEECIL—S H.' W. HART DYKE called il.retetion to Mr. Davitt's speech at Navan last Sunday, and FLETCHER to a speech made by Mr. Healy, M.P., in tha,ntY Carlow on the same day.—Mr. TREVELYAN replied tee' the Government had given their earnest attention to 2:4o2Peeches of Mr. Devitt, Mr. Healy, and Mr. W. Red- If such speeches continued to be made there was no at r Or peace and order in Ireland. If the speeches made it-Tehlic meetings ot the National League continued to be elaou", ,8114 e. strain as those made during the last week he el,erellits,feel it his duty to advise the Lord Lieutenant-to Prebibiet his power, under the Prevention of Crimes Act, to beers the proceedings. div.p: were not within the scope of the Act. He was advised that the latter part of Mr. Healey's speech was indictable, but he was recommended by the Attorney-General not to prosecute. It was, however, a serious question whether such speeches should be allowed, and application would be made that the speakers should be bound over to good be- haviour.—Mr. O'Donnell having asked a question with re- ference to the proclamation of Dublin, Mr. TREVELYAN said the proclamation was not directed against peace-loving citizens; on the contrary, it was issued with the view of protecting them, and another proclamation giving this assurance bad been published that morning. A MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT PREYENTED.—RepIying to Mr. Parnell, Mr. GLADSTONE said he did not feel justified in asking the House to depart from the business immediately before it for the purpose of permitting a discussion on the Irish Land Act.—Mr. PARNEEL afterwards moved the ad- journznent of the House for the purpose of discussing the working of the Land Act, but his proposal was only sup- ported by 37 members. PROCEDURE —The House resumed the consideration of the question of procedure.—An amendment, moved by Mr. O'DONNELL, and supported by Mr. PARNELL, providing for the appointment of a Grand Committee, consisting of Irish members, "to facilitate the transaction of Irish business by the House," was strongly opnosed by Mr. GLADSTONE, and was defeated by 94 votes to 22.—Considerable discussion then took place on an amendment by Mr. GORST, and on an appeal from Sir RICHARD CROSS, the PREMIER promised to introduce words into the resolution providing that no bill should be referred to the Grand Committee, except by express order of the House.

Ann Howard and William Brough to were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness.—Elizabeth Howell, a young woman, was mulcted icn lOs and costs for a similar oleace. A farm of 800 acres in the parish of Docking, in West Norfolk, has just been let at 2s. 61 per acre, the tithe-rent charge on which is 7s. 6.1. per acre. Duty is an angel, reverently beloved, that walks beside the man, with solemn steps; and common life is a pith shining before bins more and more; and the future is a mist which he will pass through, and so be nigher to God; and if to-day the world feels round him like a temple to worship in, then to-morrow there will be a farther world for him to pass on into, and it will be the holy of holies. A noble lord took leave of Louis 'XIV., just before he went as Ambasesdor to a foreign Court. " The most material in- junction I lay upon you," said the King, "is that you pur- sue a line of conduct directly opposite that of your predeces- sor." "Sire," replied the noble Lord," you may depend upon my acting in such a manner as to make it perfectly unnecessary to give the same instructions to my successor.'" A HORRIBLE DISCOVERY.—A fearful accident took place at the foundry of the Brymbo Company, near Wrexham, early on Tuesday morning, which caused the death of Robt. Oldfield, aged thirty years, married, and who leaves a widow and four children. The facts are as follows. When the men employed at the kneplow, in the foundry, were about to commence work, they discovered something in the kneplow, which, on closer examination, was found to be a man's re- mains, he having been literally roasted to death. It was with the greatest difficulty that the only remains of the un- fortunate man were extracted, they being nothieg but cin- ders. It is thought that the deceased had been in the place named since six o'clock on Monday night. Oldlield's work was to attend at the kneplow, but it was not his turn on duty on Monday night.
