div.head: EXAMINER, rSATURDA Y, DECEMBER 2, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, rSATURDA Y, DECEMBER 2, 1882.

MISCELLANEOUS. • The yacht Pandora, with Sir Stafford Northcote on board, sailed from Portsmouth on Monday morniag. Mr. Henry Irving has handed Mr. Creswick a cheque for £550 as the result of-the special afternoon performance on Wednesday of "Much Ado About Nothing." With all possible privacy the remains' of the late Earl of Harrowby were placed in their final resting place at Saudon Church, six miles from Stafford, on Saturday. The Right Hon. J. Chamberlain and Sir C. Dilke arrived at Sandringham on Saturday afternoon on a visit to their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales. In the election of a representative in Parliament for Cambridge University, the votes of Lord Rayleigh and Lord Henniker were rejected by the Vice-Chancellor. On Saturday the Albert Mills, at Savile Town, Dews- bury, and the property of Messrs. Porritt and Senior, were destroyed by fire. The damage is estimated at £25,000. Alfred Heins, a corporal in the Wiltshire Regiment stationed at Woolwich, has been committed for trial, charged with the wilful murder of a comrade named John Edgar, by stabbing him. Early on Saturday morning a large shop in the carriage , works of the London and North-Western Railway at Wol- verton was burnt down. Upwards of 100 " coachea " were destroyed, and the loss is estimated at £lOO,OOO. Clevedon Court, the seat of Sir A. H. Elton, Bert., was destroyed by fire on Monday. The flames spread with great rapidity, and Lady Elton had hurriedly to escape. Only a small portion of the library, but most of the furniture, was saved. On Monday, at Willenhall, Mr. Reuben Plant, proprietor of the Beacon Colliery, was fined in several cases, the aggre- gate of the penalties amounting to £2l, for numerous breeches of the Mines Regulation Act. Mr. S. Smith on Monday accepted the invitation to be- come the Liberal candidate for Liverpool, and Mr. A. B. Forwood having been formally adopted as the Conservative candidate by the Executive Committee of that party, the active work of the contest has commenced. In reply to a resolution of the South Shropshire Liberal Tenant Farmers' Association, urging upon the Government the passing of a measure for the assimilation of the borough and county franchise, Mr. Gladstone has replied to the effect that he hopes the question of county franchise may be dealt with by the present Parliament. Lord Berwick, who had attained the age of 80, died the other day at Attingham, Shropshire. The deceased peer was in the army from 1817 till 1855, and he served in the Burmese War in 1825-6. He is succeethled in the peerage by his nephew Richard Henry, son of the late Hon. and Rev. Thomas Henry. On Saturday, Louisa Jane Taylor, a widow, about 40 years of age, was charged on remand, at Woolwich Police Court, with the wilful murder of Mary Ann Tregellis. an aged woman, at whose house in Plumpstead she was staying as a visitor. The circumstances of the case have been fully published. The prisoner was committed for trial. ALARMING ACCIDENT IN A THEATRE.—During the per- formance at the Canterbury Theatre of Varieties, Seuth Lon- don, on Saturday night, one of the occupants of the gallery, Wm. Jones, aged 20, either overbalanced himself or was pushed over the front rail and fell head foremost into the pit. He was conveyed in an unconsuious condition to St. Thomas's Hospital, and on inquiry it was reported that there was scarcely, any hope of recovery. TEMPERANCE IN BRITISH CHURCHES.—In 20 dioceses of the Church of England there are over 220,000 in the temper- ance associations connected with the Church, with upwards of 3,000 abstaining clergy, including fire bishops and seven of the Queen's chaplains. The Wesleyan Methodists have 800 abstaining ministers, the Congregationglists 730, the Bap- tists 520, the Established Church of Scotland 200, the Free Church 300, and the United Presbyterians 220. Tim CHANNEL TUNNEL.—Mr. Shipton, the leader of the "delegation" of workingmen who have been sent to Paris to prove that the whole mass of the workingmen of England are in favour of tha Channel Tunnel scheme, has had the courage to lecture the Parisian ouvriers on their readiness to "descend into the streets." The English trades unionist pointed out that his fellew-countrymen endeavour to gain their objects by peaceful means, and he would no doubt be able to give many striking instances of their success. THREATENING MR. GLADSTONE.—John Norris Saunders was charged, on remand, at Bow-street, London, on Tues- day, with sending a letter threatening to murder Mr. Glad- stone. The facts of the case have been already published. Mr. Poland, for the prosecution, said that siace the last occasion it had been ascertained that the prisoner's state- ments as fo his having been confined as a lunatic were cor- rect. All the facts would be placed before the jury at his trial. The prisoner, who denied any enmity towards Mr. Gladstone, was then committed for trial. A MURDERER HANGED.—Edward Wheatfield, a sailor, was executed at York at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning for the murder of Peter Hughes, a fisher lad, aged 16. At the trial the culprit maintained stolid indifference, but he displayed a different temper during the last few days, though he made .no confession of his guilt. On Monday night he rested quietly, and on Tuesday morning showed singular coolness and self-possession. He died without a struggle. Reporters were present. Efforts had been made for a reprieve but they were unavailing. William Clegg, 28 years of age, single, employed as stoker at the well-known Lowmoor Ironworks near Brad- ford, on Monday committed suicide in a most horrible man- ner. About six o'clock in the morning he walked to the top of the charged blast furnace and threw himself in as the flames were bursting out of the top. A. few minutes later all that could be seen of the body was a few bones.

THE OPENING OF THE NEW LAW COI:MTS.-Mr. Shaw- Lefevre has informed a deputation that her Majesty will, on Monday next, after arriving at Paddington, go down Constitutional-hill, St. James's, Pall-Mall, past the National Gallery, and along the Strand to open the New Law Courts, reaching there at twelve o'clock. She will be accompanied by the Duke of Albany and Princess Beatrice, and will be met by the Prince and Princess of Wales and the Dukes of Connaught and Cambridge. The Bradford School Board election has resulted in the return of the whole of the seven Unsectarian candidates. The Roman Catholics have returned their only candidate at the head of the poll, the notninee of the Women's Electoral Association occupying the second position. The Church party nominated seven candidates, but returned only five. The two candidates supported by the Property Owners' Association did not poll more than 1,200 votes each, and were absolutely last on the poll. Out of a total of 32,000 burgesses only 18,000 recorded their votes. A TERRIBLE TRAGEDY. - Ellen Carver, an English woman, who nine years ago settled at Rolm with a married man named Holland, has killed her two children and at- tempted to poison herself. She had seven children by Holland, but the only survivors were a boy aged two years and an infant girl. Holland, on going home on Tuesday night, found the door locked, and on forcing it he saw the children lying dead on the bed, while the mother seemed to be expiring. There is, however, a chatice of her recovery. She has confessed the act, but has assigned no motive. The neighbours describe her as an affectionate mother, but as having latterly shown much uneasiness at her irregular position.

FORBIDDING THE BANNS.—During morning service at St. Jude's Church, Liverpool, on Sunday, the banns of mar- riage between a young couple were published for the third time, when an elderly gentleman rose at the end of the church and said he wished to forbid the banns The vicar, the Rev. E. J. Fitzroy, replied that the objection would be received in the vestry after service. The gentleman after- wards said that he was father of the bridegroom, and haled in a written statement objecting to the marriage on the ground that his son had no income and Ito means of main- taining himself. The bride was without fortune, and con- sequently a future of utter misery was before the couple. The gentleman concluded by saying that both he and his son were Frenchmen, and by French law a father had the right to prohibit the marriage of his children. CAT'S MEAT FOR A. WIFE.—At the Stratford Police Court, on Saturday, Thomas Slade, aged 39, was charged with deserting his wife and four children. A relieving officer stated that prisoner's wife applied for relief on July 13th, on the ground that her husband had left her and four chit- dren destitute. He gave her an order for admission. Pri- soner's wife deposed that she was brutally ill-treated and ' beaten by her husband. He left her and the children for days without money to get food with, and beat her in a shameful manner. She kept the home together hertklf by working hard for some time, but owing to his beating her about the face so much she could not see for several dip, and then everything went. At one time the prisoner came home—after keeping her without food for two days—and brought a halfpennyworth of cat's meat, which he threw at her, saying, "Take that; that's quite good enough for you." (Sensation.) He could get plenty of work if he liked, but was lazy.—Prisoner, who made no reply to the charge, was committed for a month.

THE "Nor Ail INcinErr."—The Milan incident would have led to further loss of time in the House if the Speaker had listened to a suggestion that Mr. Millman, the clerk at the table referred to by Colonel Nolan in his state- ment of Tuesday night, should have an opportunity of giv- ing his version of the story at the Bar. The Speaker, however, decided that sufficient had been said, and that the best thing that cotakl be done was to let the subject drop. The Observer says :—" Mr. Millman's story is, we under- stand, a somewhat remarkable one, showing that the list from which the Chairman of Committees named obstructive members had been drawn up by a prominent member of the Irish party and sent to the Chairman, with a request that on grounds of personal convenience the Irish members would be glad if the process of naming might be gone through at the earliest possibla moment." TERRIBLE RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN SCOTLAND.—A fright- ful accident took place on Monday evening on the Macduff and Turniff branch of the Great North of Scotland Railway. The train which left Macduff at 4 p.m. fell through a bridge near Auchterless. The broken bridge is an iron one, with wooden cross beams. The height was about 18 feet above the road, and the length of the bridge about 40 feet. Two third-class carriages, a van, and three waggons fell into the gap, but the engine passed over in safety, and a first-class carriage in the rear kept the metals. As the accident hap- pened in a sparsely-populated part, it was some time before succour could reach the injured, whose cries for help were pitiful. The first accounts of the disaster were meagre and contradictory; but it seems to be accurately ascertained now that five persons have been killed and 11 injured, some it is. feared. fatally. The Board of Trade have been communi- cated with, and it is believed that owing to the character of the accident they will, acting on the precedent of the Tay Bridge case, hold a public inquiry instead of, as is usnal in Scotland, a private investigation. It is stated that the bridge was regarded by the people of the district as a vely unsub- stantial one.

The yield of the Lowestoft Herring fishery up to the pre- sent time shows a decrease of £40,000 as compared with last year, a deficiency not likely now to be made up. Whilst following the North Warwickshire hounds near Leek Wooton, on Tuesday, Dr. Lyon, of Quorne House, Leamington. was thrown at a fence and killed. Mr. H. C. Raikes was declared at the final close of the poll on Tuesday at Cambridge, to have received 3,491 votes, against 1,301 which were given to Professor Stuart. Inspector Hughes, of the Metropolitan police, T division, was found dead late on Motaday night in a ditch at Sunbury, I with his neck broken. He had evidently been thrown from his horse. _
During Lord Wolseley's leave of absence, General Hawley, Deputy Adjutant-General, will transact the official business of the Adjutant-General's department at the War Office.

The difficulty between the Braes crofters and Lord Mac- donald has been settled by the crofters binding themselves to pay the rent, with a request that the questionof amount should be submitted to arbitration.

Robert Nicoll, a member of the Dunfermline Town Council, who occupied premises in High-street in that town, which were destroyed by fire on Sunday morning, has been committed to prison on the charge of wilfully setting fire to the premises A young man named Ernest Lodge, of Kingsheath, Wor- cestershire, was on Tuesday remanded at Birmingham on a charge of stealing £4OO worth of human hair. It is stated that German girls cultivate their tresses for the market, and fine hair, 33 inches in length, realises a sovereign an ounce.

Early on Tuesday morning, Isaac Haggott, a platelayer, in the employ of the Great Northern Railway Company, wis run over by an empty passenger train near Bradford and cut to pieces, while engaged in repairing the rails. The remains of the deceased were collected an taken to the mortuary. THE ALLEGED MURDER DT ITALIANS.—At the Leicester police court, on Triesday, Dominic Mossorella, an Italian, was committed for trial at the assizes on a charge of wilful murder of James Green, on the night of November sth. Guiseppe Valrona, his companion, was committed for un- lawfully wounding James Gavin at the same time and place. Mossorella was subsequently also committed on the coroner's inquisition.

A YOUNG MOTHER CHARGED WITH STARVING HER CHILD.—At Halesowen, on Tuesday, Annie Law, aged 20, was charged with killing her infant child, aged four months, by starving it to death. The evidence alleged that the prisoner habitually neglected her child for two months, and that death was attributed to starvation. The prisoner at- tacked the witnesses, and said that they wanted burning to death. She was committed for trial.

Writing to a Glasgow paper, Viscount Folkestone con- tradicts the statement made regarding his recent speech at Salisbury concerning a suppoped resignation of Mr. Glad- ' stone, and asserting that Sir Wm. Harcourt had made him his confidant. The Home Secretary also writes character- ising the statement as a gross and palbable falsehood, and denouncing the writers who concoct lies of this descrip- tion. LORD BRA.I3OIIRNE'S DESERTION OF HIS PRINCIPLES.— The first general meeting of the "Liberty and Property Defence League" was held in London, on Wednesday, under the presidency of Lord Bramwell. Lord Brabourne spoke, as an independent political observer,in commendation of the League. He said that he had been driven from the Liberal party because it had deserted its principles, and had shrunk from joining the other organisations against which he had been so long in arms He further informed the meeting that Liberal doctrines had been "left behind" by the present leaders of that party. FIRE AT BOLTON.—On Tuesday morning, about one o'clock, a fire broke out in the packing-room of the works of Messrs. Dobson and Barlow, machinists, Bolton. The torporation fire brigade and the brigade belonging to the firm were speedily on the spot, and five jets were soon at work on the flames. A strong wind was, however, blowing briskly, and this hindered the efforts of the frremen. In two hours the flames were got under. Damage was done to the extent of £lO,OOO. It is covered by insuiance. Several firemen were injured by the falling debris. The building was completely gutted. There is no clue as to the caus.?, of the fire.

LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL AND THE REPRESENTATION OF MANCRESTER.—On Saturday a deputation of Conserva- tives from Manchester waited upon Lord Randolph Churchill, and besought him to become one of their candidates at the next general election. The noble lord was assured that he had excited much enthusiasm in the city, and that he would be a tower of strength at the election. Lord R. Churchill read a reply, in which he referred to the " emotion " with which he had listened to the speeches of the deputation. He realised fully the importance of the position to which he was invited. He censured the leaders of his party for their "systematic neglect" of opportuni- ties for damaging the Government, and intimated that if we were on the eve of a general election he would contest Man- chester; but he was not certain that Woodstock, on his re- tirement, would not go over to Liberalism, and, on the whole, he was not able "at the present moment " to accede La the flattering request of the deputation. LORD SALISBURY IN SCOTLAND.—On Saturday, the Marquis of Salisbury was present at a meeting of the Mid- lothian Conservative Association, when the Countess of Dal- keith received the gift of a portrait of her husband, the Earl of Dalkeith, whom Mr. Gladstone defeated at the general election. Lord Salisbury was, on Tuesday afternoon, pre- sented with the freedom of the city of Edinburgh. The Lord Provost, in presenting the burgess ticket to the noble Marquis, said be felt that all his lordship's endeavours had been actuated by a desire for the public good. Lord Salis- bury, in reply, said he knew he could not claim from all those present an agreement upon what some might call his peculiar views, but there were questions upon which men of all parties might think together and work together. He went :oa to point out the growing danger of the tendency to centralisation, which all good citizens should resist. In the evening, Lord. Salisbury was entertained at a private banquet by the Scotch Conservative peers. Loss OF A STEAMER AND TWELVE LIVES.—The steamer St. George, of Glasgow, from Swansea for Nantes, with coal and copper, foundered on Wednesday morning about 25 miles off Portreath, on the North-east coast of Cornwall. Ten of her crew and the engineer's wife went down with the vessel. The remainder, numbering eight hands, got into a boat, and they had:' got near the beach, when they were upset in the surf. Assistance was at hand, and with the aid of the rocket apparatus and other means, seven of the eight were saved, but the other man sank, making a total loss of 12 lives. The survivors landed at Portreath. A later telegram from Penzance states that as far as can be ascertained the following persons were drowned in the steamer St. George :—Captain Maclean, merchant service : James Carley, Mr. Cruickshank, engineer; Mr. Atchison, second engineer; two firemen, unknowm; Mrs. Cruickshank, wife of engineer; and Patrick Owen, steward. TERRIBLE OCCURRENCE IN GLASGOW: A MOTHER AND Two CHILDREN BURNT TO DEATH.—An appalling case of fire and lose of life occurred in Glasgow early on Tuesday morning, by which a woman and her two children were burnt to death. A man named Hutchison, a machinist, went to b;s home in Kent-street, East-end, on Monday night, but could not gain admittance. His wife, aged 25, is alleged to have been drinking for some time. The husband proceeded to his mother's house, in the next street, and slept there all night. About two o'clock, on Tuesday morn- ing, a fire was discovered to have broken out in the house where the woman and children were sleeping. On the arrival of the fire brigade the men succeeded in extinguish- ing the flames, and were about to retire, considering the affair but a trifling one. On a closer inspection of the bed, however, the burnt remains, almost cinders, of the mother and daughter, aged three years, were discovered, and what are supposed to be those of the infant aged eight months. It is conjectured that Mrs. Hutchison, while under the in- fluence of drink, capsized a paraffin lamp in the bed aud set the clothes on fire.

THE MADAGASCAR AFFAIR: DEPUTATION TO EARL GRANVILLE.—EngIand is directly involved in the contro- versy that has arisen between France and Madagascar. Lord Granville on Tuesday informed an influential deputa- tion that in 1859 the two nations agreed that neither Power should do anything in Madagascar without consultation with the other. He then stated that, as he understands the matter, France now makes three claims—one affecting French subjects, of which he knows nothing; the second, that foreigners should be allowed to own land in Madagas- car; and the third, far a French Protectorate.. The second claim, he said, was objected to by the Malagasy Govern- ment as contrary to the municipal laws of the country, but the English and French Governments rest their claim on treaty rights. As to a French Protectorate, he knows of no treaty on the subject. It is clear that, under the arrange- ment of 1859, France has no right to establish a French Protectorate without England's consent, and it wculd be highly disadvantageous to England were Madagascar treated as Tunis has been. Lord Granville guarded himself by saying that he spoke unofficially, and that what be said was not binding upon the Government; but his utterances at least show that Her 'Majesty's Ministers are alive to the situation.

THE QUEEN AT Nrrunt HOSPITAL.—The Queen, accom- panied by Princess Beatrice and the Duke of Albany, paid a visit on Wednesday to Netley Hospital, where the sick and. wounded who served in the Egyptian campaign are now under treatment. Her Majesty drove from Windsor Castle to the Great Western Railway Station, where the Royal party were joined by the Duke of Connaught, who drove from Bagshot Park. Her Majesty left by special train at eleven o'clock, and travelled by way of Slough and Reading to Basingstoke, and thence over the South-Western Railway to Southampton. Netley was reached at half-past twelve, and the Royal party were driven in an open carriage to the hospital. In attendance on her Majesty were General Sir H. M. Ponsonby, Major Egerton, the Hon. A. Yorke, the Marchioness of Ely, and Lady Waterpark. The road to the hospital was lined with spectators, and the 2nd Hants Volunteers, with their band, kept the route from the en- trance gates at Netley to the hospital. On reaching the hos- pital her Majesty was received by General Sir Chailes Pearson, Surgeon-General Holloway, and the medical staff. The Royal party were conducted all over the buildings, and her Majesty addressed several of the men in kindly terms, whilst she personally decorated all those who had been wounded in the campaign, pinning with 'her own bands the medal to the breasts of those who were unable to leave their beds. After the visit, which occupied nearly two hours, the Royal party left the hospital and drove to the residence of Sir Charles Pearson, where luncheon was partaken of. Her Majesty returned from Netley at 3-45, arriving at Windsor shortly before 6 p.m. The weather was fine, and on the route to and from the hospital her Majesty was heartily cheered.

The contest at Liverpool has begun in earnest, Mr. A. B Forwood (Conservative) having consented to stand in opposition to Mr. Samuel Smith, the Liberal candidate. The Duke of Richmond and Gordon, president of the Royal Commission on Agriculture, has recently offered to the tenants on his English estates a lease for 14 years, tp take effect immediately The condition of the Duke of Edinburgh has now so im- proved that His Royal Highness will be able to resume his customary avocations within the next day or two. The steel mills belonging to the Lackawaana Iron and Coal Company at Scranton, Pennsylvania, have been closed indefinitely. Over 1,000 persons are thus thrown out of employment. An Exchange Company's Paris telegram states :—M, Bazin, the editor of the Egalite, has been arrested, and further arrests in connection with the International are expected to be made. Mr. A. M. Dunlop, who contested Merionethshire at the last general election, has written to the Cambrian News to say that he has severed his connection with the Conserva- tive party, and will henceforth do all he can to advance the principles of Liberalism. Two men named Darcy and Keogh were arrested at Kiltulan, Loughrea, early on Thursday morning, on a charcT of having murdered there a man named Connor, in April, 1831. They were 14 months imprisoned as suspects on the same charge, and are now remanded. A LOST WIFE.—On Wednesday, in the Court of Queen's Bench,Dublin, an application by Hermann Carl von Islieroth for a habeus corpus, directing the Rev. Canon Seymour, Mrs. Seymour, and others to restore his wife, whom he alleged .had peeb spirited away and kept in duress, was re- fused, the Court bolding that he had made no case proving where the lady was. _ _ _

It has been arranged that Mr. Gladstone's visit to his constituents shall take place between the 14th and 21st of January. He will address four, perhaps five, meetings, namely, three of his constituents in Edinburgh, Dalkeith, and Midcalder, a banquet given by the Scottish Liberal Club, and a meeting of the Edinbtargh University students, who are members of the Rosebery Club. _ _

According to the notices published in the London Gazette, the number of private bills to be brought forward next ses- sion is 253, which is a decrease of 70 as compared with last year. The total number of applications th the Board of Trade for provisional orders is upwards of 212. or 129 more than last year. This increase is owing to the large number of provisional orders relating to electric lighting which are to be applied for. It is proposed, in respect to the assistance given by the Oldham limited companies to the Ship Canal project, that they should contribute £1 per 1,000 spindles, which would give (as there are nearly eighty companies in the Oldham district) about £9,000 towards the guarantee fund. There is little doubt, says a correspondent, that the proposal will be generally carried into effect. A shocking accident occurred at the Midland Station, Sheffield, on Monday. A young man, named Pilkington, in the employ of,Messm. Spiers and Pond at the refresh- ment rooms, was crossing from one platform to another when he endeavoured to get between two carriages which were moving. He was caught between the buffers and was killed. At Dublin, on Thursday, a man was coramitted for trial for burglary at a tradesman's establishment. A policeman heard a noise, and found all the doors forced, the till robbed, ' and a jemmy lying on the floor. No person, however, was visible until the officer ran his sword up the kitchen chim- ney, when the prisoner, who was concealed there, surren- dered. He appeared in collet covered with soot. On Wednesday night an explosion ef gas occurred in a house connected with the new Royalty Theatra, Blackburn. A painter named Wilson was making gas to work the lime light in the theatre, and when it began to pass from the retort to the purifier an explosion took place from some unknown carse. The oven and fireplace were broken down, all the windows on the ground floor were forced out, and Wilson was blown across the room, but was only slightly injured.

Great alarm was caused at Waterhead, Oldham, on Thursday morning, by the water breaking through the south corner of Lower Strinesdale reservoir. Between six- teen and twenty yards of the embankment was washed away, and along the channel thus formed, a torrent rushed five feet broad and as many deep. Fortunately the resident 'engineer was on the spqt with a body of workmen. The water in the reservoir was let off, and a terrible catastrophe avoided

A LITERLRY WOMAN'S ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SUICIDE.— At Leicester County Police Court, on _Monday, a widow, giving the name of Ann Robinson, from London, was charged with attempting to commit suicide. The prisoner, a woman of literary attainments, was found by two con- stables attempting to. drown herself. She explained that Ehe attempted the rash act through idleness, and she could refer to Sir Stafford Northcote and other eminent men in London if she had an opportunity. She was committed for trial.

A diamond merchant named Gompertz, whose place of business is in Hatton-garden, received a visit in October from a man named May, who introduced him t one Hart, or Menes, saying the latter desired to sell some diamonds. Gompertz went to the Midland Railway Hotel and gave £6OO to these two men before he had been shown any diamonds. They left him, apparently to fetch the jewels, and never returned. The same night the two men were found in the continental train at Charing Cross. May escape I, but Menes VMS caught, and found Co have upwards of £6OO in his possession. At the Central Criminal Court on Wednesday, he was sentenced to two years' imprison- ment.

The news connected with the arrest of Faad Pasha --a-t Constantinople turns out to be very serious. A charge has been brought against Fuad Namyk Husrel (aide-de-camp to the Sultan) Kranil (ex-Minister), and even against Behrem Agha (Chief Eunuch) and Said Pasha (late Minister of Foreign Affairs), of having been engaged in a conspiracy to depose the Sultan, to seize him as he was going to the Mosque, and place upon the throne his youngest brother Pachid. An inquiry is being conducted at the Palace. By way of precaution a great number of Circassians and others have been arrested, and the Daghestan Regiment, which kept guard at Zieb, has been dissolved and shipped off to Constantinople. GAMEKEEPER SHOT BY POACHERS.—EarIy on Wednesday morning a serious encounter took place between two game- keepers of the Earl of Stair and a number of poachers, on his lordship's estate, near Gervan, Ayrshire. The poachers and the gamekeepers came upon each other at a plantation, when the former turned upon the hitter. One of tie poachers discharged his gun at one of the keepers named James Rennie, who fell, it is supposed, fatally wounded. Another of the poachers discharged his gun at the other keeper, but the shot did not take effect. The Procurator- Fiscal and sheriff's clerk left Ayr at one o'clock on Wednes- day to take the dying man's deposition. It is expected that the poachers will soon be•arreste4. A CLERGY7.ILAN ON CARD PLAYING.—At the meeting of the Chorley Board of Guardians, on Wednesday, the chap- lain, the Rev. 0. de L. Baldwin presented a report, in which be suggested to the Board that the moral state, at all events, of the imbecile inmates of the workhouse would be amelio- rated if they were allowed the indulgence of a few harmless games, such as draughts and cards, which he would supply. The chaplain went on to say that he specially mentioned cards as being, by reason of their endless variations, and the little intellect required to play them, specially adapted to the imbecile mind ; in fact, they were invented for the recrea- tion of a lunatic king. The Guardians gave the permission asked for.

ALLEGED FORCIERY AN) MISAPPROPRIATION OF TRUST FUNDS IN SCOTLAND.—The Scotsman of Thursday published an announcement that forged bills to the amount of .£3,500 had been discounted by the Commercial Bank of Scotland, and drawn by an Edinburgh accountant in the name of a Danformline coalmaster. The accountant in question is now said to be Mr. Donald Smith Peddie, for whose ap- prehension a warrant was issued on Thursdey in Edin- burgh. Mr. Peddle, who is influentially connected, has been trustee for a number of friendly societies, and is co-defender in an action for divorce. The exposure con- sequent on this has, it is stated, resulted in Mr. Peddio's disappearance, .and subsequent inquiries go to show that £25,000 trust funds have been misappropriated, chiefly belonging to the United Presbyterian Church. CONDITION OF TIIE PRIMATE.—The Archbishop of Can- terbury's weakness continues to increase, and it seems im- possible that the end can be much longer delayed. The members of his Grace's family are constantly nith him, and during the last few days he has had an interview with several friends, including the Bishops of London, Rochester, Truro, Winchester, Lichfield, and Dover, the Dean of West- minster, Canon Freemantle, the Dean of Durham, Canon Knollys, and one or two others. Dr. Kennion, the newly- consecrated Bishop of Adelaide. visited Addington on Thursday morning after his consecration in the Westminster Abbey to receive the Archbishop's benediction. It is not probasble, owing to his increasing weakness, that his Grace will now be able to see any ether friends. He is in no suffer- ing and sleeps much. His Mental powers, when he is awake, seem to be in full vigour. THE PULLMAN CAR Drusun.—Colonel Yolland's report on the cause of the burning of the Pullman car at Leeds, which has been issued, reached the Coroner on Thursday afternoon. The Government Inspector says that the cord communicators in Pullman cars appear to be of very little use, as passengers have great difficulty in reaching them, unless they go on to the platform at the end of the car. He points out, also, that this system of communication is not sanctioned by the Board of Trade, and therefore all railway companies who continue to use it are liable to penalties. He is satisfied that although tne witness, Mr. Cranston, swore he did not go to sleep, he is mistaken, and that in blowing out the reading lamp a spark had either flown and set fire to the curtains or risen to the inflammable materials above, and so caused the accident. Colonel Yolland is further of opinion that if the driver of the engine had pulled up imme- diately he received the signals, the life of Dr. Arthur would have been saved. div.head: CRIME IN IRELAND.
div.p: CRIME IN IRELAND.

The Horne Rule League is dissolved, its objects being merged in the programme of the newly-established Irish National League. Mr. Patrick Egan, Land League treasurer, has forwarded £l,OOO, the second remittance of a like sum, to the Dublin Mansion House for the relief of evicted tenants, it having been certified by the secretaries to the fund that a similar amount had been subscribed by the country since the pre- vious draft was sent. THE ALLEGED DEFECTIVE DEATH SENTENCE.—Among the Parliamentary papers issued on Saturday morning was a report of the sentence passed by Judge Lawson on Patrick Walsh, as transcribed from the official shorthand writer's notes. His lordship directs that the prisoner be taken from I Galway prison "to the place of execution, within the walls! of the prison within which you may be then confined, and I that you be buried within the precincts of the prison; and may the Lord have mercy on your soul." The London correspondent of the Birmingham Daily Post says—"l understand that the Irish Executive and the Home Office are in joint possession of very serious infor- mation with respect to the designs of the Fenians who still I lurk in Ireland. Mattes have now reached a critical state 1 between ruffianism and authority. Ruffianism means to die 1 hard, and by way of striking a harder blow has a scheme on foot for moving its scene of operations to this country. The Home Office is forewarned, and is now taking steps to forearm the local authorities in various parts of the king- dom where danger is threatened." The police are busily engaged in sifting matters which are still cropping up in reference to the Phcenix Park mur- ders. There is no doubt, the Dublin correspondent of the Observer says, they have important evidence, which, it is stated, has arisen from the arrest et Delaney for the attempted murder of Judge Lawson. Rumour says the police are in possession of information which, it is alleged, would bring hcme guilt to certain parties who are reported to be still in Her Majesty's dominions. It would not be a great surprise to certain parties in well-informed circles to see within a month or two three men Idaced upon their trial for being concerned in the Phcenix Park murders. The police are most sanguine that their efforts to capture and convict the assassins will be crowned with success.

THE THREA.TENED DISTRESS.—It has been officially re- ported to the Government, through resolutions of boards of guardians in Ireland, in many cases forwarded to the Chief Secretary, that widespread distress is apprehended in that country during the approaching winter months. The dis- tricts most seriously affected through want of employment for farm labourers and the failure of the potato crop are Sligo, Ballina, Swinfori, and the greater portion of the county of Galway. There is at present much destitution at West 'Clare, attributed to the fact that the small farmers had sown the ordinary potato instead of the champions, the former having in almost every instance proved a total failure; and to the same cause is attributed the present "deplorable condition " of the usually distressed locality throughout Connaught. It has been ascertained by several of the local boards that, owing to the continuously heavy demands upon the Irish in America to sustain the Land League Eunds, there has been a considerable falling off in the remittances to " struggling relatives" in Ireland, and this has reduced many among the latter te the condition of being unable to purchase new seed, at the same time oblig- ing the consumption as food of that held over from the past season. THE CITY PROCLAIMED.

- The city of Dublin has been proclaimed, under the curfew clause of the Prevention of Crime Act. Members of the Detective Department on Tuesday pursued inquiries with the view to discover the destination of the cir on which the would-be assassins of Mr. Field escaped, and a reward of £5,000 has been offered for information leading to the arrest of the intended assassins.. The soldier Danvers, who rendered such timely assistance when Canstable Cox was murdered on Saturday night, is to be substantially rewarded.

div.head: THREATENED ATTACK ON A HOSPITAL.
div.p: THREATENED ATTACK ON A HOSPITAL.

About half-past ten on Monday night, large mobs con- gregated in the neighbourhood of Jervis-street Hoqpital, where the man Dowling, who shot Constable Cox, is lying wounded, and their threatening aspect caused great alarm to the constables on duty, and to the Sisters of Mercey who attend the sick in the hospital. Large reinforcements of police were sent for, and paraded in the vicinity of the institution. The object of this assembling of a mob is not known. Some people assert that it was intended as a covert movement to get off the police, so as to rescue Dowling while the constables were dispersing the crowd. There is a good deal of excitement in the city. Bodies of police patrol the locality, with swords drawn. The mobs dispersed upon the arrival of the constables, a large force of whom took up a position opposite the entrance to the hospital. It is thought the fears of the Sisters of Mercy exaggerated the condition of things, and that there was, in fact, no intention to break in. Guards of constables are now placed at the appproacbes of the hospital, and bodies of police patrol in the adjicent streets. A BAILIFF DANGEROUSLY WOUNDED.

Another man has been stabbed in Dublin. His name is Thomas Mallow. He has been employed by the Emergency Committee, and he was serving a process in his avocation of bailiff in a house in Gardiner-street, on Monday night, at seven o'clock, when three men attacked him with knives. He was stabbed in the back of the head, the wound being very dangerous. Two men, named Birmingham and Brady, have been arrested in connection with this occurrence.
THE "HANGING GALE" CLAUSE OF THE ARREARS ACT.

IMPORTANT DECISION. - An important decision was given on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. Commissioner Litton, under the Arrears Act, which, if not reserved, will do away not only with a large amount of arrears due to landlords, but also with the difficulties under the so-called "hanging gale clause," which would otherwise to a large extent nullify the Act. It is unfortu- nate that this decision has only been arrived at on the eve of the expiration of the time limited by the Act for inde- pendent applications by tenants. The case before Mr. Litton was a test one, affecting 1,200 others on the estate of Sir John Leslie, in the county Monaghan. The rents were usually not paid until long after titey fell due, at irregular times, varying from three months to nearly thirty after the gate day. The contention on the part of the landlord was that the rents were not demanded till the expiration of twelve months after the gale day, that this constituted a twelve months hanging gale, and that the word" paid" in the proviso of the Act should be read as equivalent to "demanded." Mr. Litton said it would be better to abandon the use of the term hanging gale, as there was no such term in the Act. A hanging gale meant a gale still left unpaid at each payment of rent. The Act of Parliament referred to some usual day of payment, but here there was no usual day,. nor even usual short nericocl of time. It was possiblethat this language was adopted' by :the Legislature in the proviso to minimise the mischief which the proviso would introduce. It lay upon the landlord, in his opinion, affirinatively to show that the tenants were excluded from the Main proviso C,f the Act, but this bad not been done, nor according to his (the Com- missioner's) interpretation of the Act did the evidence sup- port the landlord's contention. In this case the rent was paid in January 1882, and the tenant sought to have it re- garded, according to the main provisions of the Arrears i Act, as applied to payment of the rent which accrued n 1881, but the landlord sought to have it declared a payment against the arrears previous to 1881. The investigation de- cided in favour of the landlord, and the tenant now came in to show cause against making absolute a conditional order for dismissing his claim. In the Commissioner's opinion, the investigator was wrong and the cause shown by the tenant must be allowed. He would ask the Treasury to allow costs to both tenants and landlords. Counsel for the landlords asked to have a case stated for the purposes of ap- peal. If the decision was right there was not an estate in Ulster but was outside the proviso.—Mr. Commissioner Litton: If the decision is wrong there is scarcely an estate in Ulster that is not outside the Act. A case can be stated.

TriREE TERRIBLE OUTRAGES. Crime in Ireland has during the last few days appeared to be centred in Dublin. That city has just been the scene of three murderous outrages, one at least of which is evidently the deliberate work of a secret society similar to that which planned the Phcenix Park tragedy. In the first case a de- tective IGas shot dead, one of his assailants being seriously wounded. A special juror, who was foreman of the jury at the trial of Walsh for the murder of Police-constable Kavanagh, has been, it is feared, fatally stabbed under cir- cumstances akin to those which attended the deaths of Lord F. Cavendish and Mr. Burke: A bailiff, employed by the Emergency Committee, was serving a process when three men attacked and stabbed him. In the cases of the detective and the bailiff there are various arrests, but the assassins who attacked the juryman drove off in a car, which was lost sight of after an exciting chase

div.head: SPECIAL JUROR STABBED.
div.p: A SPECIAL JUROR STABBED.

The details of an attempted a..ssassination on Monday evening resemble those of the Phoenix Park murders. Hav- ing aimed at the life of a judge, and then killed a police- man, the society which plans these outrages determined that their vengeance should next fail on one of the Dublin special jurors, who had done his duty by finding a verdict in one of the capital cases sent under the Prevention of Crimes Act for trial in tile Irish Metropolis. The case was that in which Michael Walsh (whose brother had been previously convicted for the Letterfrack murder) was found guilty of the murder of Constable Kavanagh, who had rendered himself active in tracing the Letterfrack murdere-s. The trial came off in Sep- tember, and amongst the juror( was Mr. Denis J. Field. Mr. Field, who is 60 years of age, and very near sighted, has his private residence at 14, North Frederick-street. Ou Mon- day evening, at six o'clock, he left his place of business, and proceeded homewards to dinner. Frederick-street is a con- tinuation of Rutland-square, at the top of Sackville-street, and is a much frequented thoroughfare, as it forms one of the direct entries to the northern suburbs. That street some years ago obtained notoriety, for it was when passing through it that Talbot, the policeman who entered the Fenian organisation in order to betray its members, was assassinated. Mr. Field had almost reached the door of his house at a quarter-past six, the street being then pretty well thronged by persons returning home from business. Two respectably dressed men drove up on a car, one of the or- dinary city licensed vehicles, guided by a licensed jarvey. One of the occuuants of the c:r sprang down on to the foot- path beside Mr. Field, when the latter was a few yards from his own door. Then the car was driven on to the corner of North Frederick-street and Hardwicke-street, about eight yards further on, the driver and the second man remaining on the car. The assassin who bad jumped down carried a sword, which he had drawn before leaving the vehicle. Mr Field:did not see his danger, and instantly the fellow stabbed

Ihim two or three times with the sword. The suddenness o the attack took evey one by surprise, and there was a cry of horror from the spectators as the victim sank to V:* ground. But the assassin was determined to complete his work, for as the vroanded man lay at his feet, bleeding, he again I plunged the sword into the prostrate body several times. ITwo young men, who were going home after their office work, saw the gentleman on the ground, and rushed for- ward. Toe murderer, even as they were approaching, I plunged the sword twice inlo the bxly of Mr. Field, then I brandished his weapon, and ran to the corner, where the car Wss waiting for him. Springing to the seat the car was then driven rapidly down Hardwicke-street (which runs at right angles to Frederick-stieer). The two young gentlemen raised cries of " Murder," and one of them, being a swift runner, followed the car for a considerable distance, but he had to give up the chase, as the driver increased his pace to a furious rate. Some other persons joined in the chase, and the vehicle turned into Dorset-street. The assassins were about to leave the car, but looking back they saw the pur- suit was being continued by a number of persons who had joined those who had witnessed the fearful transaction. Then the horse was whipped up again, and the car was observed to wheel round into Synott-place, where both it and its Occupants were lost sight of. It is scarcely possible that Mr. Field can recover. He has seven wounds, two in the breast, two in the throat, one very deep wound in the head, and one at each side.

Telegraphing on Thursday afternoon, a correspondent says :!--While the Lublin police have so far failed to arrest any person concerned in the attempted assassination on Monday night, their inquiries have been attended with results which hereafter may prove important. It seems that nearly a dozen persons were witnesses, and were on Wednesday interrogated by the chief of the detective department, and though the nature of their evidence has not been disclosed, it is known that some of them testified their ability to identify the desperadoes. One of the latter it would appear dropped his hat, which was picked up by a stranger, and the police are now trying to discover the 1 possessor of this, what may be an important clue. Under the Curfew Clause of the Crime Act it is neeessary to appoint a number of special mag- istrates for the different districts of the city. This work was being:proceeded with througheut Wednesday by the Government officials, and during Thursday. Another important proclamation will probably appear in the next Gazette placing the saburbs of Dublin under the Curfew , clause, there being there places of resort for suspected per- sons. Before the special magistrates these persons arrested as suspicious strangers will be taken and either committed for trial or discharged. The intimidation of jurors has already had a most serious effect. A proposal is made that all those who have been summoned to attend the special commission next week, should hold a conference beforehand and decide on some united action. If this is not done it is expected that those who can afford to do so will stay away from the Commission, and that their less favoured brethren will be victimised. The opinion is growing that under the present circumstances it is not fair to call upon Dublin men to try the agrarian cases from the country. The Express suggests that some such place as Bal. fast should be made the venue of the trials. Fenian assassins mould not there have the sympathy or apathy of the peep'e to reckon upon. The sturdy and loyal men of the north would not suffer murder to be done in their streets, and never stretch out a hand to protect the victim or arrest the mur- derer. Whatever steps may be taken in this respect tie Ex- press is certain that no Government has a right to expect ce-operation from the citizens in the jury box unless it is ' prepared to defend them from acts of lawless ruffianism. The proclamation of the city under the Crime Act was resolved upon, it would appear, after continued representation of the necessity of such a proceeding byEarl Spencer,and it is believed that Mr. Gladstone was opposed to it until the last outrage on Monday. The deficiency of the Dublin police force is a serious difficulty. The total available force for the city proper is only 881, but of this number constables have to be stationed in all the ceuits, churches, theatres, and other places of entertainment and resort, also to watch public- houses and to protect persons and places which are exposed to special danger. When the Commission Court sits, there are 40. When a rescue was threatened at Jerris-street Hospital, 30 men had to be pried there. At the Viceregal Lodge alone there are now close on 30 men. All the judges, the under-secretaries, the law officers, and other officials of Dublin Castle have to be protected; and when, allowance is made for all these requirements, and for a sick list of 40 emeslehles, thc total etreng,th will be reduced one-fourth or one-third. some iwetiLY-latP army pensioners and ex-constables are employed as con- stables in aid, and these will now be reinforced by men from. Manchester, Liverpool, Glasgow, Birmingham, Bristol, and other large English towns. Regarding 'detective Cox's mur- der, it is stated that counsel for the defence at the trial of the prisoners will raise a question whether, as a matter of fact, the bullet that killed the detective was not fired by one of his own comrad,,s. The defence will probably be that in trying to shoot Dowling when struggling with Cox, one of the detectives shot his comrade, and that the position of the fatal wound bears out this theory. A DEFECTIVE MURDERED. Shortly before midnight on Saturday some detectives on special duty in Middle Abbey-street, Dublin, were watching a number of men who were engaged in suspicious move- m2nts. The officers upon coming up to the party noticed that one carried a loaded revolver. A constable named Cox stepped forward to seize this man, who immediately faced round and discharged his revolver at the head of the police- man. The bullet entered the officer's skull and he fell to the groend. The shot was instantly followed by a dis- charge of three barrels of a revolver by Sergeant Eastwood, which all took effect, and the assassin was secured. He turned out to be Christopher Dowling, a gasfitter, residing near Dublin. While Eastwood was engaged with Dowling he was seized from behind by a Irian, and both after a struggle fell. The officer recognised this fellow as James Devine, and during the struggle addressed him by name in order that there should be no mistake as to the identity. Devine was captured by a soldier who was passing at the time, and who cowed the miscreant by pre- senting his bayonet at his breast and threatening to run him through if he moved. The Constable Cox and the wounded prisoner were conveyed in a cab to the hospital, where it was found that the officer was dead, and that the assassin had received dangerous injuries, but that there is a possibility that he may recover. Devine is an ex-suspect and a returned convict, but Dowling had not been known to the police before Saturday night. Cardinal M'Cabe referred to the erreadful crime on Sunday, and highly commended the police for their vigilance in frustrating " some abominable plot in which a gang of conspirators were certainly engaged." The murder of Constable Cox in Dublin was the subject of inquiry on Wednesday both in the Coroner's Court and at the Police Court. On the suggestion of counsel for the Crown the investigation by the Coroner was restricted to the question of the cause of death, and it was very short, the verdict being simply that the death of Cox was caused by a gunshot wound. Some littld additional evidence was given before the magistrate, and at the conclusion of it two men named Woodward and Ryan, who were in custody were discharged, but the other prisoners? Poole and Devine, were committed for trial at the Special Commission which will commence its sittibga in Dublin next Monday.

div.p: SATURDAY, DECEMBER 2, 1882.

Two of the most atrocious crimes which it has been our painful duty to record have taken place in Dublin within the past few days. It may be possible to ass;gn a motive for the attempted assassination of Mr. FIELD, but so far as regards the murder of Police- constable Cox, it would seem as if a thirst for blood only was at the root of the crime. Ihe worst of the outrages which have darkened the pages of Irish history during the past two or three years of agitation have been committed in the country, and for the most part have been agrarian in their origin, there has been a comparative immunity from crime in the Irish capital; but ever since the murder of Lord FREDERICK CAVENDISH and Mr. BURKE in Phcenix Park, the city of Dublin has been pretty well crowded with assassins and cut-throats—villains of the deepest dye—the emissaries of secret societies, whose main object seems to be to shed,blood, and if possible to set the law at'defiance. The haunts of these miscreants have now become known to the police, and with the view of rooting them out a special detective force has been formed. This is well-known to the murderous gangs who now infest the city, their move- ments are closely watched, and it is because they know the police are on their track that they find it necessary to play a desperate, and, we trust it may be found, a losing game. The murder of Police-Constable Cox, which took place in Sackville-street—one of the most frequented thoroughfares of Dublin —on Saturday, is one of the boldest, as it is one of the most defiant, which has beep com- mitted during the present agitation. Cox, along with other five constables, had, it .seems, been detailed for special detective duty on the evening of the day in question.

!They were following up—at a very early hour, too—a group of suspicious persons with whose foul intentions they were evidently acquainted. The band of ruffians found their movements were observed, and in a state of desperation they turned and fired upon their pursuers. The officers closed with the band, and a sanguinary struggle ensued at close quarters, the result being that one of the officers—Cdx —was killed, while one of the men who led the attack on the constables was seriously wounded. Another of his adComplices named DEVINE was secured by the aid of a soldier, whose brave conduct is deserving of the recognition which it will doubtless receive. It is to be hoped that the other assailants are by this time in custody. and will receive their just deserts. The attack on Mr. FIELD resembles in many respects the Phcenix Park murder. This gentleman, like Lord FREDERICK CAVENDISH, would appear to have been specially marked 'out for the assassins' knife Mr. FIELD, it may be remembered, was, as luck would have it, foreman of the jury at the Dublin Commission Court who tried and convicted young WALSH of the murder of a police-constable at Letter,- frack. Mr. FIELD is one of the most respect- able tradesmen in Dublin, and on Monday afternoon he left his office about the usual hour—six o'clock. It is not quite clear whether he was watched all the way from his office to his home, but just as he was about to enter his dwelling, a car—as in the case of the murder of Lord F. CAVENDISH—drove up. From this vehicle two men jumped down, and with a dagger, a knife, or some other deadly weapon, stabbed Mr. FIELD SO severely in several places that his life Is despaired of ! The assassins having, as it happens, only ! partially accomplished their cruel object, lost no time in getting on to the car again, and it was driven off at a rapid pace. It is said that I the conveyance—on which other men were , seated—was followed for some distance by a young gentleman who witnessed the crime, but he was unable to keep up with the vehicle, and it was very soon lost to sight. So far the ! miscreants—as in the Phcenix Park tragedy —are at large; let us hope the handsome reward offered for their apprehension will result in their detection. It is rather a singular coincidence that just at the very moment when we begin to congratulate ourselves on ,an improvement in the state of Ireland, ohe or two outrages are perpetrated which completely dash our hopes. This was the case when under so many promising circum- stances Earl SPENCER and Lord FREDERICK CAVENDISH assumed the Government at Dublin Castle; it is the case again just after Mr. TREVELYAN in the country and Mr. ! GLADSTONE at the Mansion House have pro- claimed to the world that crime in Ireland is on the decrease, and that the Land Act and the Arrears Act are productive, and have been I productive, of the most beneficent resu:ts. It would seem, however, that there exists in Ireland a class who will never be satisfied, and who have declared war to the death against all law. By the assassination of Mr. FIELD they revenge themselves for the con- viction Of WALSH ; and by the murder of Police Constable Cox they endeavour to strike a blow at English rule, It is a credit to the Dublin Police that under these trying circumstances they Axe showing a degree of , vigilance and bravery which will do more than anything else to effectually wipe out the : aspersions which have been at times cast upon ' their faithfulness to duty; and if, as Mr. I' TREVELYAN hints, those attacks upon them may be expected at the present time, a dis- play of personal courage such as that of Saturday evening will do much to prevent their repetition. As a rule, assassins have some regard for their own safety, it is not often they are so bold as DOWLING, DEVINE, and their confedel-a:c, and '1 liey are made to feel they cannot pursue illir murderous deeds with itnynnity they will soon l)ecome , quiescent. Within the past few months , punishment has followed swifc and sure on ' the heels of crime ; and if the mu derers of Constable Cox and the ass_issins of Mr. FIELD are spe:oily brought to jus• ice, as we sincerely hope they will, crime in Ireland will I very soon be extirpated. To all lovers of law and order it must be a source of regret that Mr. MicHkEr. DAVITT has seen fit at the present juncture to indulge in intemperate and inflammatory language. Speaking at Navan on Sunday, Mr. DAVITT—and be it remembered that, though a convict, he com- mands the respect of the Irish people— I affirmed that he would never again beg for starving Irishmen if they paid in the shape of rent the money that ought to be employed in purchasing food. He went on to say that I "the time will surely come, unless wise and just legislation should,. ere long prevent its necessity. when these people on the mountain I slopes of Donegal, the bleak stony hillsides I of Connemara, and the marshy slob lands of i the west and south-western coast will have to be told in self-preservation to march down upon and take possession of the rich soil of the now depopulated plains whereon to make I existence possible, in accordance with divine intention and the requirements of Christian civilisation." Not content with this, Mr. DAVITT advised a general strike against rent until next May, and suggested that out of the sum thus saved a National Relief Fund should be established—if the Government did not provide support for the necessitous and starving poor, of Ireland. Having declared his belief there was no peace, or finality, or honesty in the Land Act, Mr. DAVITT con- cluded with a fierce denunciation of land lordism. On the same day Mr. HEALY, M.P., described ,the British Government as "an organisation of so many pirates and brigands." Language such as this is absolutely inde- fensible. It is certainly not calculated to inspire the- people with confidence in the Government. To us Mr. DAVITT'S utterances appear to carry with them a direct invitation to set the law at defiance. This is the more to be regretted in Mr. DAVITT'S case as he has usually been very guarded in what he has said. The speech is under the consideration of the Government, and what may be the result is as yet unknown. We hope, how- ever, there will be no prosecution, as the adoption of such a course would, we are sure directing attention to the speech —be productive of a great deal more harm than good.

THEATRE ROYAL RUNCORN.—The drama "Shamus O'Neil" has occupied the boards of this place of amuse- ment on four evenings during the past week, and there have been large audiences nightly. The piece is descriptive of certain phases of Irish life, and it is full of striking inci- dents, which were effectively represented. The histrionic ability of Mr. Ottley's company is beyond the common place, and the theatre is well worth a visit to witness their per- formances. Fresh attractions are announced for next week. Four, MOUTHED Pintsolfs AT Rl:moon:sr.—Hannah Radford, a young woman, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, with using profane language in Church-street, on Saturday, the 18th November, and she was fined 10s. and costs, 9s. 61, or in default 14 days' hard labour.—A labourer named Thomas Parks, was summoned on a similar charge, the offence being committed in High- street, on the 23rd November. He was fined 103 and costs. SINGULAR FATALITY TO A HORSE AT HOUGHTON GREEN.—A. horse, belonging to Mr. Charles White of War- rington, met with its death in a singular manner on Mondayl evening, at Houghton Green. Whilst Mr. White's man was transacting some business in the farmhouse of Mr. George Jackson, the horse was standing outside, and suddenly a well, which was paved over, and had been covered for some years, gave way, and the horse went down, hindquarters first. Assistance was at once obtained, and every effort used to liberate the animal, but the well being only 3 feet diameter and about 27 feet deep, it was wedged so tightly that it soon died, and it was not until twelve o'clock at noon on Tuesday that the carcase was extricated from the 1 singular position. ALLEGBD ASSAULT AT RUXCORN.—At Rnneorz Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. W. Bankes, Mary Cox was charged with assaulting Mary Jane Garnett, the younger, and Isaac Law was sum- moned with assaulting Mary Jane Garnett, the elder.—The complainant lives in Penketh-lane, Runcorn. On the 18th November Mrs. Cox struck Garnett the younger, on both sides of the face when the,elder went to her door, and asked Mrs. Cox why she had struck leer girl. Mrs. Cox replied that she would jump on her if she came into the street. Law then came up, and struck Mrs. Garnett, and also pulled her shawl from her shoulder.—Ann Percival said Mrs. Cox never struck the girl.—Law stated that before he struck Mrs. Garnett, the latter pushed him, and sent a quantity of water in his face.—The Bench dismissed both the cases, as the evidence was so unsatisfactory. WESLEYAN HOME AND FOREIGN MISSION: WIDNES BRANCH. —On Sunday two sermons were preached in Victoria-road chapel, on behalf of these missions by the Rev. J. Eglinton, of Warrington. On Tuesday evening the annual meeting was held in the, same chapel. Mr. J. Robin- son presided, and there were also on the platform the Revs. R. Harper (superintendent minister), J. Tessyman, T. Peters, and Fowler (deputation). The Rev. J. Tessyman read the repart, which showed that the income of the Liver- poet district(in which Widnes is included) was £7,93653.10.1., being ate increase of £923 on the previous year. The income of the Widnes circuit was £ll 7s. 2d., made op as follows : —Cronton £l9 Bs. 6,1., decrease 1 19s. 91. ; Moss Bank £1 155., decrease 3s. 4d.; Hale Bank £5 17s. 7d., increase I 3s. 7d. ; Ditton £l2 Bs. id, increase £8 14s. 11d. ; Farn- I worth £4 us. 91., increase £3 Bs. 81. ; Albert-road £Bl Sc. 101., increase £1 2s, 21. ; Oakland-street £ll 12s. id,l decrease £1 us. 81.; Victoria-road £54 3s. GI, increase £6 7s. 31.—The Chairmen, in a short address, expressed his regret at the falling elf in the attendance at missionary meetings, and, said he could remember the time when the missionary meeting was the jubilee of the church. The Rev. T. Peters said in spite of the fact that there was some lukewarmness in the cause discernable, the missions were I progressing, as were also things in this "moving age." The Rev. William Fowler, the deputation, also delivered an address.—The meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

HALTOI4I MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.—Mr. Harrison r2ad a paper to the members of this class on Tuesday ev en- iag. It was entitled "Vivisection." BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPEOVE3IENT CLASS. —At the weakly meeting on Wednesday, the Rev. E. J. Robinson read a paper on "Psalmody in church service." There was a good audience. THE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT RUNCORN.--011 Monday afternoon, this popular preacher and lecturer will deliver a , sermon in St. Paul's Chapel. In the evening he will lecture in the Public Hall, ind there will probably be a crowded gathering. THE ADDITIONAL GUARDIAN FOR WIDNES.—As was hinted last week there is to be no contest for the vacancy on the Baard of Guardians. The Ratepayers' Association have withdrawn the name of Mr. Samuel Sadler' and Mr. Matthews, the nominee of the Owners and Occupiers Association, will therefore fill the vacant seat. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK. —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday, Mr. G. H. Danby, clerk to the Widnes Sclaool Bard, prosecuted the fallowing persons for , breaches of the Education Act, and a fine of 5s was imposed in each case :—Thomas Buckley, James Rawson, Francis Boyle, James Carr, Elizabeth Hyland, Dennis Malone, Jas. Hynan, Maria Casey, Henry McGee, John Riley, • Roger Harrison, James Talton, Noah Bate, Thos. Molyncux, Jas. Welsh, Mary Purcell, and John Sproson. VOLUNTEER BALL AT WARRINGTON. —The unfavour- able weather was doubtless the reason for the small attend- ance at the annual non-commissioned officers' ball, held on Monday evening at the Drill Hall. As usual the room had been tastefully decerated for the occasion, and the gyrations, which commenced at eight p.m., were kept up till three o'clock the following morning to the music of the band of the corps. The ball altogether was most enjoyable. Amongst the officers who put in an appearance during the evening were Lieutenant-Colonel Greenall and Captain Bolton. ABLB• BODIED BEGGARS AT RtnaeonN.—On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions James' Green, a strong looking fellow; was charged with begging.—P.O. Bossons said that on Saturday night he CM the prisoner in Mersey-street, acting in a somewhat suspicious manner, as if he were beg- ging."' When he reached the witness, he asked him for a copper. Bossons told him that he had asked a policeman, and took him into custody. He became very violent, and a struggle ensued, but with the assistance of Inspect's'. Hol- lingsvorth he was locked up. In his pockets were found 3s. 51-al., all in cappers, and some scraps of beef.—Superia- tendent Williamson said there had been frequent complaints about able-bodied men like the prisoner begging, and so difficult was it to detect and apprehend the vagrants that he had to send men out in plain clothes.—The Bench committed the prisoner, who protested that be only accosted the officer as a joke, to gaol for 14 days. MOVING THE WR.ONG COURT: A WIDNES CASE.—At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. Arthur I Sinclair and Alderman M'Bryde, the case of William Garton , Dixon, veterinary surgeon, St. Helens, against Charles Fowler, son of Mr. James Fowjer, of the Central Hotel, Widnes, was called on. Mr. Massey appeared for Ildr. Dixon and Mr. Husband appeared for Mr. Fowler. Mr. Massey said this WAS an action under the Employers' and Workmen's Act, 1875, but their worships had no jurisdiction in the matter, and he must ask to with- draw it. He supposed Mr. Husband would consent.—Mr. Husband said that as his friends client had make a mistake, and brought a civil action into a criminal court, he must ask far reasonable casts, as he (W. Husband) and two witnesses had come from Widnes to obey the order of the court.—The Clerk said that as the magistrates had no jurisdiction in the case, they had no power to grant costs. —The application was consequently refused. div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOUS.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOUS.

At la,t ! After years of waiting, patience has oh- tained her reward, and the " slope " on the Runcorn , aide of the bridge is actually commenced. More than ! six years have elapsed since the desirability of the im- provement was advocated at a Commissioners' meeting. I "Great bodies move slowly," the truth of which has ' been amply sustained by the London and North- Western Railway directors; and yet I cannot help remarking that an accident or two and compulsory compensation has a wonderfully quickening power. I venture to suggest that the enterprising Runcorn Gas Company would confer an inestimable boon by opening an exhibition of improved gas illumination, Ihaving for its arena the whole length of the footway ; of Runcorn bridge, and specially invite the chairman land directors of the Railway Company to see the leffect upon the majestic and magnificent stracture. At the present time the bridge is illuminated by a ; single burner—consuming about five feet of gas per I hour—placed at distances of over a hundred yards each, and yet I opine, there are few lengths of either rail or roadway yielding a larger return over working expenses. As I cross after nightfall I can hear the 'tramp, tramp, tramp of the benighted traveller long before I can discern his form, allowing full play to , the imagination in the conjuring up of scenes of I robbery and violence. 1 I suspect seine of the E sclestonians, as well as Newtoniaus, were on Saturday last let into a secret by the magistrates sitting at the Newton Town Hall. It is generally supposed, at least by a dishonest I section of the community, that if a person succeeds in getting into arrears with his rent, all he has to do is to make a " moonlight " departure, and he will evade all further trouble. This is not so. At the • Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, a person named I Owen Boyle was summened for removing his goods from a house in Earlestown to another at Haydock I whilst owing rent to the amount of £1 2s. 31, and , this it appeared he heel done in order to evade pay- ment, and failing that seizure. The magistrates, how- ever, informed Royle—and through him the public— that taking goods away clandestinely did not free a person from liability or the goods from seizure. The t goods can, the magistrates said, be seized wherever Ithey are taken, and they added that people by such • removals not only did not free their goods from the , liability of distraint, but they gave the landlord power to distrait' for double the amount. That is a wrinkle which it is worth while to know by people of a dis- honest turn, for it may save them a great deal of un- necessary trouble. The House of Commons this week got through the whole of the new rules of procedure, which have re- ceived the sanction of the House almost in the form in-wlaich they were introduced by the Government. The House is now engaged with the consideration of the scheme for the institution of Grand Committees, BO as to relieve it of much of its business, and I have 'no doubt that this also will be sanctioned, as it is obvious that it must result in a great saving of time. It is an old saying that a coach and four may be driven through any Act of PktriiNmeut 4e4 we have had ample illustration this week that without very I much difficulty rule No. 2 may be set at naught. .This rule gives to forty-one members the right of in- sisting upon the adjournment of the House being moved after questions and 'before the orders of the day "in order that a definite matter of urgent ' public importance" may be discussed. The decision of what is of " urgent public importance" is left with the member who moves the -adjournment, and from the experience of this week it it evident mem- bers have not only no difficulty in deciding themselves what is of "urgent public importance," but they very easily persuade forty other members to think with them. Although the present is a very considerable improvement on the old rule, still it wants amending if it is not to, be abused, and I think it could not be better amended than by leaving tho Speaker, and not lan individual member, to decide what is matter of " urgent public importance." To me it is rather remarkable that my Lord IBrabourne finds it necessary to so frequently apologise 1 for his desertion of the Liberal party. His ILordsbip on Wednesday attended a meeting of the Liberty and Property Defence Lague, I held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, and there he was at his old game apologising for his conduct. He says he changed his views be- I cause the Liberal party had deserted the principles of I freedom, and he added that Liberal doctrines had been left behind by the present leaders of ,that I party. Assuming that this is all true, which of course deny, I think it much more to the point if Lori I Brabourne would explain how he arrives at the con- I elusion that "no one could be more outside of politi- cal parties than himself, for he was driven out of one party by reason of their recent legislation, and he had I ! shrunk from joining the other political organisation 1 I against which he had so long been in arms." Lord Brabourne "outside political parties ! " Why, it is i absurd. If any one will take the trouble to examine Lord Brabourne's votes in the House of Lords, it will be found he always votes with the Tories; awl if any lone will read his speeches in that House it will not be difficult to see he is in close alliance with the Opposi- tion. After all, I dare say had Lord Brabourne—or , rather, Mr. Knatchbull Hugessen—obtained a seat in I the Liberal Cabinet, he would have been a Liberal 1 yet. 1 It must be a matter of disappointment to Her 'Majesty's Opposition that the cost of the Egyptian war is not considerably more than it now turns out to ' be. From the first commencement of operations they harassed the Government about their estimates belie..ill I much under the mark, and since the conclusion of t; , campaign they have been impatient to ascertain what 1 the total cost has been, in the hope, I presume, of I getting a cry to take to the country. A Liberal ' Government, however, shows its economy in war I expenses just as it does in everything else; on the ;other hand, Conservative Governments are so much I given to spending that they imagine this must be the case also with every Government in power. What • are the facts with regard to the Egyptian affair? The original estimates were for £3.300,000, made up of £90,000 for the War Office and £1,400000 for the Admiralty. The supplementary charge as estimated to the eat of October is £1,060,t000, made up of £750,000 for the War Office and £310,000 for the Admiralty. The two sums, therefore, already authorised and esti- mated to be required amount together to £3,360 coo. But then there is the cost of the Indian contingent. The charge of this contingent was originally estimated at L 1,880,000 ; the expense, however, has been only 11,14c5000. The total charge for the operations of the war, and including transport home, is only £4,500,000. In a petty-fogging little campaign in which the Conservatives embarked the cost was nearly five times that amount. The charge from the sat October is expected to be borne wholly, or in part, by the Egyptian revenue; and .it is not yet decided what proportion, if any, of the La 500,000 India will be called upon to pay. Under all the circumstances I think there is reason for cone ratulation that so much has been done in so short a space of time and at so small a eost to the British tax-payer.
