HAGUE'S MINSTRELS AT RUNCORN.—Crowded audiences greeted the minstrels on their appearance in the Public Hall on Monday and Tuesday evenings. The eccentricities of the various, performers in word and action kept the audience in an almost continual roar of laughter. The songs and choruses were given in good style, while the clog dancing of Mr. Tom Ward met mith universal approbation. ALLEGED BRUTAL ASSAULT ON A MOTHER AT RUN.. CORN.—Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. W. Bankes, Robert Moores, a young fellow, who is no stranger to the police court, was brought up on remand charged with assaulting his mother, Eleanor Moores. It appeared that the prisoner got married on Sunday, and left his mother to reside in the Halton-road. The Tuesday following the mother and son met in the Masonic Hotel and quarrelled. It was alleged that the prisoner struck her under the chin and knocked her down. The face of the prosecutrix bore evident signs of severe illusage, being much scarred and discoloured.—The prisoner was again rein tab(' until Mon- day, although the prosecutrix wished to withdraw the I charge.

div.head: WIDNES CRICKET CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CRICKET CLUB.

The annual meeting of Widnes Cricket Club, for the pur. , pose of electing officers for the ensuing year, and transact. ing other business, was held in Simms Cl•cSi Hotel, Widnes, on Monday evening. The night was wet and boisterous, and consequently few members were present. Mr. H. W. Deacon presided, and there were present the Rev. G. Bond, Messrs. J. White, Kyle, J. Pritchard, D. Forster, W. H. Longton, H. Lea, W. Farrant, R. Moore, T. Upward, W. J. Moorland, J. Stone, Brown, J. Heyes, IL Parkes. It was stated during the evening that it was of great , importance that it should be widely known that young teen under 20years of age were admitted to the club as playing members, at an annual subscription of 10s 6i. Mr. FORSTER read and moved the adoption of the balance sheet, whitsh had been previously published. The motion having been seconded. , The CHAIRMAN, referring to the financial position of the clh, said he understood that Mr. Forster had rEceived about five guineas of special donations which the committee ha decided to try to raise. Mr. White had kindly promised to get up a concert, by which he hoped to realise £2O. Much of the expenditure of last year would not occur for a cen- tfcterable time. He thought from the subscriptions the club had, and perhaps an increased number., of bowling members and next year, they would be able to wine off the debt. But in the meantime he thought it was the duty of every member of the committee to try and wipe off the balance. The report was tl-cn alcpttd. The CECAIRKiN read the hon. secretaries' report as fillows:— -

' In presenting our annual report we have to call attention to the fact that although we ale in debt yet, that we Ii eve never he'ere had the cricket ground an bowling green in such ex- oellent condition. We have usually been obiged to spend a considerable sum of money at the beiginoiag of each season in ge' Ling the ground into playin4 order, but the field committee expect that very little, if any, money need be spent before next season. We regret that the report of the average committ4e showed such unsatisfactory results as regarded the season's cricketing. Tue +art that no fewer thin seven second eleven matches were not played because a team could not be get to- gether would serve to show that the interests of the junior playing metilloers have decreased. This is very much to he re- gretted, for unless the :v 'linger members take an interest in the affairs, the club Twist lose much of its value. We re:ton-emend this subje:ct for the consideration of next season's committee, and hope that some means may be found t induce playing members to join the club and take an active ieterest in its • affairs. The number of bowling members has considerably in- creased, and with the really good ground the club now has, we think that we may at least expect that the number of sub- s2rib,rs will not deerease. No doubt that next year a large number of mains will be arranged. The officers and committee n realigning their post beg to thank tbe members for their support " The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report. Re- telling to the small number of second eleven matches which had been played during the past sefson, Mr. Deacon said the number of playing members should be increased. The ebb had a large subscription list—about.e9o—which meant a Large number of men, and it seemed a pity if they could not get sufficient men to play matches on Saturdays. The club ought to be able to get sufficient young men to make two or three or more elevens, bat they could not make more than one, and could not even always get Gne. He announced that he thought the gentleman who filled the office of secretary ought to be more active than he was, and wished to resign the appointment he held, in order to give way for some one who played in matches. ' Mr. PRITCILARD seconded the motion for the adoption of the report, which was carried. The CHAIRMAN said they were all aware that the presi- ident, Mr. Gossage, had recently been male ied again, and LI thbught it WAS only right that the Cricket Clnlo should pass some resolution congratulating him upon the marriage. He had been president now for a very great number of years. Me had always taken a veiy great interest in the affairs of the club. He did not know anything about the financial deficit of the club at present, and he (Mr. Deacon) was quite sure that when he did he would help them as he had always done hitherto. He moved the following resolutions : That the Widnes Cricket Club begs to offer te its president, Mr. F. 11. Gossage, the most hearty congratulations on his marriage,and trusts that the future will bring much happiness to km and Mrs. Gossage. That the members beg to express their appreciation of. Mr. Gossage's kind help since the early days of the club's existence, and bole that ke may long to , spat ed to be president of the club. Mr. FORSTER seconded the proposition, remarking that he should like it to take the form of an illuminated address. It was explained that Mr. Gossage would appreciate the simple resolutions quite as highly as a more elaborate , address. The resolutions were then unanimously passed. On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, Mr. F. H. Gossage was re-elected president. The Rev. George Bond, Major Cross, and Messrs. J. L. Muspratt and Eustace Carey were appointed rice-presidents.—Mr. Forster having resigned the post of treasurer, Mr. Pritchard was appointed to fill the post, on the motion of Mr. WHITE, seconded by Mr. KYLE. —The Rev. G. BOND moved the re-appointment of Mr H. W. Deacon and Mr. W. H. Longton as hon. secretaries. He expressed the hope that Mr. Deacon would not persist in his intention of resigning the post of secretary. Mr. Deacon's name was closely identified with everything in Widnes, and be thought his withdrawal would be a mis- fortune to the club. (Applause.) After some conversation Mr. Deacon consented to retain the post, and the resolution was adopted. The committee were appointed as follows:—Dr. rown, Messrs. James White, R. Moore, M. T. Coyier, A. Kyle J. Hoyle, H. R. Colquitt, I'. Deakin, Dainteth, Moreland, T. Callon, John Farrant, C, H. Watson, F. Young. I Mr. LONGTON moved that the committee be empowered to engage a *professional or ground man at their dis- cretion. I The motion was seconded, and Mr. WHITE made a few remarks, pointing out that in the present financial position of the club it would bo best to engage a ground man for a salary of about 258. per week. IDr. Bnows moved an amendment that a professional be enkaged, and that Mr. Briggs fill the post. ' Mr. JAMES HOUGH seconded. I A 1 After a short cliscassien the amendment was withdrawn and the original motion carried. , This concluded the meeting.

CONCERT BY THE BAPTIST CHORAL UNION AT WIDNES.— A concert, having far its object the raising of funds with which to erect a new Baptist Chapel in Widnes. was given in the Drill Hall on Wednesday evening, by the Baptist Ceoral Union. The services of a strong company of vocalists had been secured, and the concert was a decided success. The vocalists were Mr. George Barton, Mr. S. J. Edwards, Miss Parry, Miss Maggie Evans, Miss Fanny Gardner. Mr. Daniel Jones was the conductor, Mr. Street presiding at the harmonium. ORATORIO AT BETHESDA. CHAPF.L, RrNCOIIN.-011 Tues- day evening, Farmer's sacred oratorio, "Christ and His soldiers," was performed in Bethesda Chapel, Runcorn. Independent of the object for which it was given—to pro- vide funds for the reseating of the orchestra of the chapel —the oratorio succeeded in bringing together a large , audience, despite the other attractions claiming the atten- tion of the townspeople on that night. The body of the ; church was comfortably filled, while the gallery was crowded. We have previously commented favourably on • the dramatical graund work of the music. which is worthy of the theme of which it treats. It is divided into two parts, the life of Christ and the life of the Christian, and affords abundant scope for the band, the choir, and the soloists, the light and shade of the piece coming with a varyiug cert. stancy which had a charming effect. The chorus, 'which included representatives from almost every choir in the town, was under the able leadership of Mr. Wm. Handley, who is well ktown as an experienced musician. Mr. C. Powell directed the band, and Mr. J. Ravenscroft officiated ,at the piano. The principals 'were Madame ! Laura Haworth, Miss Annie Richardson, Mr. C. ' Palliser, and Mr. F. Fairhurst. During the entire ; performince of the first part of the programme the effect of ,the choral music, and of the solos, was greatly detracted from the extremely discordant instru- mentation at the band. At times all harmony was destroyed, and the audience until almost the conclusion of the first part was cold and unsympathetic. Mr. C. Palliser was the first to awaken any enthasiasm in the audience by a masterly rendering of the solo "When I survey the wondrous cross," although earlier in the evening Madame Haworth had sung the bright solo "Hark, the glad scaled with a force and expression worthy of recogaition. ! Unfortunately the faulty instrumentation prevented a happy realisation. "Jesus Christ is risen to-day" was solo and chorus, in which Madame Haworth and the choir were very successful. It must be ceded that the sieging of the choir, as an amateur performance, was highly creditable, alike to themselves and the conductor, and gave evidence of very careful training. The cherus "Cleft are the rocks" was a difficult performance, cleverly given, but marred to Borne degree by imper- fect instrumentation. In the second part of the programme their efforts were heard to greater advantage, and the choruses "Soldiers of Christ arise " am". " ‘l, he are those like stars appearing," were pleasing prces of ' vocalisation. Miss A. Richardson succeeded in winning the sympathies of the audience at the commencement, and her first effort, "By Jesus' grave," was rewarded with loud ap- plause.. In the second part, she received an entlateiKtic encore for her rendering of the solo "Rock of Ages.' IV: iss Richardson has a voice of great music-it power, whlcb she uses with good taste and effect. Mr. Palliser renewed his success in the first part of the programme in the secousl by his rendition of the piece "The Son of God goes forth W. war," his clear and tasteful intonation being very pleasing:. An interesting part of the evening's programme was the ap-. pearance of Mr. F. Fairhurst. He possesses a somewl at highly-trained and clear voice, and he gave intelligent in- terpretations of the solos which fell to him, lacking, perhaps, in dramatic force, A perfect musical gem was the quartette, "Jesusdied for us," by Madame L. Haworth, Miss- A. Richardson, Mr. Palliser, and Mr. Fairhurst. The haw- monious blending of the voices was delightful and, in response to an irresistible encore, the piece was repeated.

WE CAN CHARGE WHAT WE LIKE.

c—OM-no-n with other householders, I have received an assessment paper for inhabited house duties, in ,which the rent or asst.ssed value is £35. Assuming this to be" an obvious error" (for my rent is £32 103.) that the surveyor of taxes is asthorised to rectify, I called at his office to point it out. There, a young gentleman who heard my business gave me some information. The rent, he found, was £32, the poor rate assessment £3O, and the assessed value £35. The latter, he said, was the highest rateable value. I certainly thought it was, for the house is barely worth £3O a year. Venturing to enquire upon what basis the assessment was made, I was given to understand that they certainly received a statement of the poor rate valua- tion, but were not at all influenced by that. As for rent', they didn't care what rent I paid ; that, of course, was a matter of utter indifference. "In fact," said the young gentleman, "We can charge what we like." You can? "I asked with much astonishment at the revelation. My young informant, with a graceful inclination of his bead, said "we can," with a polite manner that might imply "and we do, and with much satisfaction to ourselves." Ido not know that this little incident requires any comment. If it is the case that the inhabited house duties in Warrington are assessed by some young men in the Inland Revenue Office, upon the simple rule of charging "what they like," it certainly explains some anomalies, but hardly in a way that can be considered highly satisfactory to the ratepayers of this heavily-taxed borough.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, _ F H T ALLAN. _ F. H. T. _ _

ANTIDOTES AGAINST DRUNKENNESS. Sir,—Swan, in his "Speculum Mundi," says:—"The egges of an owls, broken up and put into the cup of a drunkard, or one desirous to follow drinking, will so work with him that he will suddenly loath his liquor, and be displeased ever- afterwards with drinking." In Spain, according to the / experience of Mr. Howard Saunders, a stork's egg is believed to have the same effect. Mr. Samuelson, in his "History of Drink," records how the Egyptians believed in the efficacy ofmabbage seed as an antidote. Athenceus would seem to confirm this, as, according to the latter, "wherever a vine- yard has cabliages growing in it, there the wine is weaker." But Mr. Ward will find the firm and consistent practice of moderation the beat antidote to excess of all kinds. The fate of the modefn glutton, the drunkard, or of the professed abstainer, who too often falls a victim to the insidious and growing habit of secret dram and drug drinking, merely accentuates afresh-in these days the moral conveyed in the classical story of the blight of Dmdalus and Icarus. All those engaged in the temperance movement should peruse 'The History of Drink," and read carefully (and between the lines) the medical journals. Raise the tone of the "amusements of the people," and the morale of those who patronise or attend them will improve in proportion. The Archbishop of York struck the right key-note when, in the course of a sermon preached to workingmen at Middles- borough, the other day, he spoke strongly of the sporting, drinking, and other debasing pastimes by which, as he said, they were ruining themselves. "Slavery over men's bodies had been abolished," he added; "but there were other bonds of slavery from which he was not so sure they were alto- gether free." Meanwhile, the " Blues " and the "Total Totalites " deserve all honour and credit. But time alone will test the question as to the physical possibility of an entire Northern nation being able to dispense with the heat_ giving and other stimulating properties derived from fruits and cereals by distillation or fermentation.—l am, sir, (he.,

THE HARE ON TRADE TOKENS, SIGNS, deo. Sir,—Though in truth we have often been invited, in passing, to partake of the hospitality of our own particular clergyman, it was not to partake either of hares or raiebits, so we have had no experience of the taste of an otter,which "Anglo-Scotus " says is no bad substitute for either—if we understand him aright. But, being "abroad," in a wider sense than perhaps he meant, we did one day drop into the hostelry known as the Smoking Rabbit (Lapin que Fume) in St. Denis, with a brother Scot from Chili, who was in fact, no cold-blooded animal, but a very warm- hearted companion while we were together. He was, in fact, Scott by name and Scot by nature. We met on the field of Waterloo; and until he saw a " thumb " volume of Childe Harold, thought himself the only Briton in the party; and when we parted it was with a promise to meet again in Paris. We rode, after seeing the Rhine, by the merest chance, in the same train as, and the next carriage to, the Prince of Wales and Duke of Edinburgh, when en their way to join the Queen, when she unveiled the statute to the Prince Consort at Gotha, and after a variety, of remark- able incidents, such as eating raw herrings preserved in milk (St. Patrick's trout) we left the train and returned from Ingleheim to Coblentz. In. crossing the Bridge to Ehrenbreitstein we met on the bridge, with one solitary com- panion, the Crown Prince Imperial of Germany. What a chapter of accidents! But sure enough, on reaching Paris, we met in the Rue de Rivoli our whilom friend the Chili- Scotsmen, who rushed up, to the surprise of the passers-by, to shake hands and say how do you do. But to the point, nothing would satisfy him but we must go to see the Cathedral of St. Denis; and sure enough we did see it in all its magnificence and in the glory of an autumn after- noon, when the sun shone through the gorgeous stained- glass windows, filling the church with a golden glory that made us think we were in a second Alhambra. There was no necromancy about the place then as we hear there is now, and to judge of the answer given to our friend by the hostess of the aforesaid hostelry the natives are as hard- headed as some of our countrymen are said to be. To make himself agreeable ter madame the hostess, he incautiously hinted that if he were not a Scotchrnan he should like to be a Frenchman, to which she replied promptly and rather dryly that there were good and bat of all nations—which made us think she was by birth as well as by name a descendant of her celebrated namesake, Madame Lafarge. However, a good look at the interior satisfied us that there was neither smoking hot rabbit nor other viands to our taste, but that, in fact, the sign was one of those subtle things, half joke, half earnest, for the rabbit might be enjoying a • pipe, as it was shown on the sign, like the former "Pig and Whistle," in St. Helens, the proprietor of which, by-the-bye, we knew from earliest boyhood. But this (Lapin que Fume) was an unsatisfactory beast, and so we left it. As " Anglo Scotus" ie for the time being going to leave the hare to those who are fond of coursing, and going to give us some- thing anon about the blunders of printers, a subject he is eminently weld qualified to deal with, most people have had to lament such vagaries as the "good devil "now and then indulges ; and talking of trades or handicrafts made us take down a volume of Servian folk lore in which we had seen an account of "The trade that no one knows," and in which we find the inevitable "hare and hound." The pith of the story is that a peasant's son de- termines to marry the king's daughter, and she is willing enough if only he will learn "the trade that no one knows." This again reminds us that the Crown Prince of Germany aforesaid is a printer by trade, for from the highest to the lowest in Germasy they learn trades. So after many most remarkable adventures the peasant succeeds in gaining the object of his desire. One incident as proving the assertion of "Anglo-Scotus " to be true, that "the hound is the natural enemy of the hare," we will quote :—" After travelling for a long time, the young man came at last to the palace of the king whose daughter he wished to marry. When he saw the palace, he was exceedingly sad, and remembered the words of the princess ; for after all his wanderings and sufferings he had learnt no trade, and had never been able to find what trade it was that no one knows.' Whilst con- sidering what be had better do, he suddenly recollected the halter, the key, and the iron chain, which he had carried concealed about him ever since he left the castle of the four giants He then said to himself "Let me see what these things can do!' So he took the halter and struck the earth , with it, and immediately a handsome horse, beautifully - caparisoned, stood before him. Then he struck the ground with the iron chain and instantly a hare and a greyhound appeared, and the hare began to run quickly and the grey- hound to follow her. In a moment the young man hardly knew himself, for he found himself in a fine hunting dress, e!' riding on the horse after the hare, which took a path that passed immediately under the windows of the king's palace. Now, it happened that the king stood at a window looking out, and noticed at once the beautiful iereyhmiud which was chasing the hare, and the very handsome horse:which a huntsmen in a splendid dress was mounted on. The king was so pleased with the appearance of the horse and the greyhound, that he called instantly some of his servants, and sending them after the strange rider, bade them invite e him to come to the palace. The young man, however, hearing some people coming behind him calling and shouting (the usual concomitants of the race ground) rode quickly behind a thick bush, and shook a little the halter and the iron chain. In a moment the horse, the greyhound, - and the hare had vanished, and he found himself sitting on the ground under the trees dressed in his old shabby clothes, cite.," and so forth, the whole being a strange . mixture of romance and reality.—Yours truly, Newton, November, 1882. NEWTONIAN.
LONDON MISSIONARY SOCIETY.
MEETING AT WABRIN. GTON.

The anniversary services in aid of the London Missionary Society, were held in Wycliffe Congregational Church, on Sunday last. In the morning the Rev. J. Peill, from Mada- gascar, occupied the pulpit, and in the evening the Rev. J. Yonge preached to a good congregation on missionary work. There was a good attendance at the meeting of the anxilliary held in Wycliffe Church,on Monday evening. Mr. Z. Armitage occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Revs. J. Peill (deputation), E. Moore, J. Eglinton, and J. Yonge (pastor). The CHAIRMAN remarked that the commonly-conceived notion about missionary meetings, he supposed, was that the deputation came there for the purpose of inspiring them with missionary zeal, but he ventured to think that this was altogether a mistake. The deputation might come there for another purpose, and one which he thought he, at any rate, was quite right in expecting, namely, that they should encourage him in his work. It must be borne in mind that Mr. Peill, and all those who had consecrated their lives to this service, had not learnt their lesson and their duties from a different doctrine to that which those present had to control them. They were all subject to the same command, and if they did not see their way to devote themselves in the way in which many had done to the missionary work, they had no less a duty to perform, and that was to main- tain a lively interest in the missionary work, and it might be to stimulate those engaged in active work. They were not to look to the missionaries entirely to inspire and encourage the growth of the missionary zeal, but rather to gain what they had from the Gospel itself —" Go ye out into the world and preach the Gospel to every creature." If they were not able to do it in person, at any rate they could do it by their sympathies and their contribu- tions. Mr. Peill came to them from a place which was one at the present moment of great interest. Momentous things were happening in regard to Madagascar. Within the last day or two events seemed to have taken a far more serious turn than was anticipated, and they could not see what the issue would be. But they would listen to what Mr. Peill had to say, and he hoped there would be some expression of opinion, that their sympathy would be on the right side, and that the evil which now threatened it would be averted from the island of Madagascar. For what might be considered as a gauge of their interest in missionary work, they looked at last year's collections. There were collections from morn- ing and evening congregations in November last year £24 14s 9d, and public meeting held in the week £5 8s 10d. There was collected in the Sunday schools during the year ending last November £3O 15s, and a similar amount was contributed by Mr. Murray. This year, so far as they had gone—that was to say the collections at the Sunday services and Sunday school contributions—the amounts were each in excess of those of the previous year. The excess was very small, and did not represent, he thought, what should be considered their interest in missionary work; still, it was an encouragement to _be able to say that the amount subscribed so far at the various services in connection with this auxiliary showed a slight increase upon those of the previous year. Let them hope that the result of that, meeting would still further improve the total sum which they would be able to send up as their subscription to the missiemery society. There was every need for subscriptions larger than they were able to give, and he thought if their zeal and earnestness on behalf of missionary work were what they ought to be, and what they should expect them to be if they were true believers in the Lord Jesus Christ, the amount would be greater than the sum which they were now able to send. _ _

The Rev. J. PEILL, after givin2; a summary of the results produced by the preaching of the Gospel in Madagascar, and speaking of the progress made in that island, referred to the dispute at present existing between net French and the Malagasy. He said the difficulties unfoilunately were now at a very critical stage indeed, in fact, he was afraid that the French had decided upon their course, and that it would go very ill indeed with the Malagasy Government. Adverting to the French claims, he said they claimed a strip of country on the north-west coast of Madagascar about 300 miles in length, and including the best harbours in the island. , The claims bad not been stated by the French Government fully, but they heard that they claimed a suzerainty over the whole island. At any rate they knew as a fact the French claimed this part of the country, but how far inland they claimed was not known That was an indefinite item, and it meant having once got a footing they would advance and advance until they get possession of the whole island. The claimed was based on , the cession by some tribes of the North-west coast of the island to the French in 1840. No demand had been made on the .part of the French since 1840 to enforce their sup- posed claims. The people had acknowledged the Queen of the island as their sovereign. The people along the coast claimed by the French actually paid tribute which, with custom dues, had amounted to the sum of £B,OOO per annum, to the central Government of the Queen of Mada- gascar. Strange to say the French had never objected to their paying that tribute, and not only that, but the French ships calling at the ports on that part of the coast bad paid the dues of the Hoven Government. If since 1840 the country had belonged to the French, it was inexplicable that they themselves should pay custom dues to another sovereign. (Hear, hear.) In .1808 a treaty was concluded between France and Madagascar, and no reference whatever was made by the French to the claims now advanced. Pro- bably they never would have referred to it even at the present time but for the aggressive spirit which seemed now to be showing itself in France. He then referred to the un- justifiable treatment of the Malagasy envoys in Paris, and proceeded to speak on the right of our Government to interfere in the matter. He gave one or two reasons. First of all there was a great power bullying a little one—(hear, hear)—and he maintained that not only was it politic, but the very spirit of Christianity, that they should visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, help the helpless, stand by those who were trodden down, and do their best to help them. (Hear, hear.) t'ut on that ground it seemed to him a great shame that a strong civilised power like France should treat the envoys of Madagascar, with whom they had a treaty, in this way. Another argument was that we had interfered again and again, and therefore our Government had stand- ing ground for -acting as mediator between the French and Malagasy at the present time. It was a 'critical time, and they who loved the Malagasy and saw the results of their efforts, prayed that God would over-rule these things for the good of the church there. He thought our Government might be prevailed upon to use its friendly influence with the French in order to stop these high-handed proceedings. (Applause.) The Rev. J. EGLINTON said he rejoiced in the brotherly feel- ing ever shown to him by their excellent and gifted pastor, and his dear friend Mr. Yon,e, and had always sympathised with this great work of Christian missions.' As to Mada- gascar, he trusted the appeals made in reference to this in- teresting country would find a ready response until the Government exerted .a friendly influence. (Hear, hear.)

The Rev. J. YONGE said he thought they would reel, after listening to the statements which Mr. Pal had given, that it was the duty of Christian people and Christian communigea like themselves to do all they could to encourage our Government to take some practical steps on this important matter. He hoped at the various mis- sionary meetina which might ba held at the present thse up and down the country, a similar line or procedure might be adopted to that which he proposed to submit for their adoption that evening. There needed to he excited a strong Christian public opinion upon this case, and our Government, he thought, needed to be made to feel that in any action to which they saw their way, they would have the sympathy and support of the people of all Christian denominations. Of course, our Government folind itself in a very delicate position at the present time in a matter like this, remembering the sensitive condition of affairs which exists between us and the French people in connection with the Egyptian crisis. He thought they would feel Her Majesty's ministers had peculiar difficulties just now in dealing with the matter. Still he hoped the Government might be able to see its way to the expression of such an opinion, and to the offer of such services as might tend to obviate the present difficulty, and, if possible, stop anything like hostile action on the part lof the French towards Madagascar. He moved, I "That this meeting views with deep regret the claims made by the French Government to the north-western portion of the island of Madagascar, and the treatment received by I the Malagasy envoys in Paris; it further believes that these claims, if insisted upon, will destroy the independence of the Malagasy people, and seriously injure the cause of Protestant missions in the island, until now so eminently ssccessful, as well as prejudice British interests in Mada gascar ; and further believes that this is a case in which arbitration on the part of a neutral and friendly power could be most advantageously applied. Therefore, it moet respectfully urges upon Her Maj-!sty's Government the de- sirableness of using its friendly office on behalf of the Malagasy people, in order to aid the peaceful solution of the present dispute." The Rev. TitomaS RIPPON briefly seconded the motion, which was heartily carried.
The Rev. J. YONGE expressed the obligation of the meet- ing to the Rey. J. Peill for his admirable addresses on Sunday and that night, and to the Chairmnn for presiding, and the meeting terminated. •

div.head: MEETING AT LYMM.
div.p: MEETING AT LYMM.

Special sermons were preaebed in Lymna Congregational Church, on Sunday last, on behalf of the London Missionary Society. The Rev. J. Bedell (pastor) preached in the.morn- ing, and the Rev. J. Fein (missionary from Madagascar) in the evening. The annual meeting in connection with the society was held in the Congregational School, on Monday. The Rev. J. Bedell presided, and he was supported by the Rev. J. Peill (from Madagascar) and Mr. R. Dutton. Tke CHAIRMAN, in the course of his address, said that the

total collections last year amounted to £l2 is. 5d., widows' fund £2 ss. 101, and the young folks' new year offerings £9 (less expensas Os. 3d.), making a total of £23 is. The collections on the Sunday this year were about the same as last year, but unless they got some £4 or £5 that night the total would be below that of last year. As far as the whole society was concerned they had this year an income of £112,000, and were net in debt to the treasurer. This in- come, however, did not come up to the Bible Society, which was £194,000. But with the £112,000 thAY la id been enabled through God's help to do a good. work. Fot instance, there was glorious news from Africa. It was stated at the beginning of the present year 20 New Guinea men had joined, making a new church numbering about 00 or 40 members,
The Rev. J. PEILL said he wished them to convey them- selves over the s?a about 12000 mile 9 to Madagascar. It was an island about four times the size o!England and Wales,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY DFCEMBER 2, 1882. DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY DFCEMBER 2, 1882. DISTRICT NEWS.

inhabited by Various tribes of people, but there was a con- siderable admixture of African blood. It was in 1820 that their mission was commenced at the capital there, and in 1873 a party of missionaries were sent to that place, of which he was one. On landing they pushed their way across the plains, made through the Belt Forest, and reached the high table land of the interior, and then came to the capital, which had a population of about 100,000. On arriving they were told that their station would be about 30 miles west of the capital, but they resided in the capital about six months in order to become acquainted with the language, after which time two of them found themselves in charge of about 80 churches. The speaker then went on and described the difficulties which he and his friend Mr. Pickersgill ex- perienced at the commencement of their work, after which he gave a few statistics showing the present position of the society in Madagascar. He said that they had 1,200 churches, and some 300,000 native adherents, or people who attended chapels, and who were neither Christians nor heathens. They had 70,000 church members; and 862 elemen- tary schools, with about 60,000 children receiving elementary education. The natives had contributed about £40,000 for educational purposes, and for the spread of religion; and no less than 20,000 Bibles had been sold to them. He then adverted to the difficulties which beset the miisionary work from French interference, and spoke at length on the French claims for a greater portion of the island.—Other speakers followed, and the meeting closed with the usual vote of thanks.

ANTROBUS. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY FARM LABOURERS AT ANTROBUS. —On Tuesday, at Daresbury Petty Sessions, before Messrs. E. Greenell and J. Marson, two farm labourers named Patrick Donoghue and Thomas Burke, were charged with. stealing £3 18s. 61., the property of Patrick Hooson, at Antrobus, en the 24th November. The prosecutor is a farm labourer, employed by Mr. Percival at Antrobus, and on the 23rd November be slept in the "Irish house" with several others, including the prisoners. Before going to bed he counted his money, and found he had £3 18s. fn., which he placed in his trousers pocket, and put the trousers under his heal Next morning, when he awoke, he found that his money was gone, and that the men had left. Evidence was given that Burke Was the last man in the bed with prisoner, but the Bench thought there was no evidence against the prisoners, who were discharged. CAUGHT IN A HEN ROOST AT ANTROBUS.—John a collier, from Bilston, was charged before Messrs. E. Green. all and J. Marson, at Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with stealing four game fowls, value 355.' the property of William Plumb, at Antrobus, on the 16th November. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—The prosecutor said about half past five on the morning of the 16th November he got up and went to the place where his fowls were kept. He there saw the prisoner in the act of killing one of his game fowls. The prisoner jimped out of the pen, but he caught hold of him, and retained him until a young man came to his assistance, when the prisoner was taken to the police station. On examining the pen he found that three other fowls had been killed, and that there was a basket near containing a bar of iron, a collier's lamp being also in the pen.—The prisoner said his attention was called to the pen by a crow- ing cock, and as he was very hungry he thought he would steal a fowl to make his breakfast.---He was committed to IKnutsford for two calendar months witi. hard labour.

div.head: 9TII LANCASHIRE (WARRINGTON) RIFLE VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: 9TII LANCASHIRE (WARRINGTON) RIFLE VOLUNTEERS.

The annual prize distribution of this corps took place at the Drill Shed on Tuesday evening. Colonel Greenall presided, and he was supported by Colonel Bertram, Cap- tains Bolton, White, liepherd, Ridgway, and Widdows, Lieutenants Gooch and Thompson, Drill Instructors Blease and McCoy, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mr. Robert Davies, and Mr. J. R. Buckton.

The CHAIRMAN said they had met that evening according to ancient custom—for that was their 2ard prize distribution —to receive the prizes which the gentlemen around him, and others, had given for competition. Their thanks were due to those gentlemen for the continued confidence they reposed in them, and they hoped they would never do any- thing that would cause them to withhold those prizes. They were assembled that evening to take stock, if he might so speak, of their proceedings during the past year. They knew that men in business took stock in order to know how they stood, and they were met there for the same purpose that evening. With regard to what the Army had done, and the respect. which it had won for England abroad, he would leave that to the gentlemen who had done them the honour of coming there that evening. He was sorry to say that the strength of the corps during the past year was less than that of the previous year.. That was accounted for by a circumstance which was known to them all, and which must be a cause of regret to all of them. The corps numbered this year 578, against 608 last year, and there were 528 efficients against 592 last year ; but, at the same time, the non-efficients were less this year than last, being 50, against 60 last year. The money earned this year amounted to £937 15s. 6d., and last year to £1,045. While he regretted that the number of the corps was leas, he hoped that this did not mean that the young men in Warrington were losing interest in it. It must, ho admitted, be very discouraging to the men when they came on parade to find that there were no officers to meet them. He saw, as he walked the streets, plenty of well-made, smart, and good looking young gentlemen, and he would be only too glad if they could see their way to join the corps as officers. (Applause.) It had always been his aim to keep down the expense of the corps, and he might tell them that their subscriptions were only ono-half of what they were some years ago. There must be subscriptions of a certain amount to meet the expenses which were nsces- sitated, such as the expense of the drill Equarters. He might tell them that during the year they bad gained a new title for their regiment, owing to the altera- tions which had been made by the Secretary of State for War. They were now nailed "The Prince of Wales' Volunteers." (Applause.) He thought that was a title they would all be proud of, and one which none of them would desire to be changed. They had this year sent nine men to Wimbledon, but he still had to complain that the Queen's Prize had not been brought to Warrington. (Laugh- ter.) It would be a proud day for him, and a proud day for Warrington, if they could hail one of their men as the winner of that prize. A prize worth £7 had been won by one man, and most of the others had made their expenses. He did not think the corps took that interest in shooting that was taken by the regiments throughout the country; but their disadvantage was that they had not a good range. (Ap- plause.) It was not from the fault of the officers not look- ing out. The difficulty was to gain the consent of the land- owners for the use of the laud. Bad shpoting was not confined to the volunteers alone, and he was afraid that suf- ficient time was not given to one of the essentials of a soldier, namely, that of shooting. It was no use giving a soldier a good weapon unless they gave him time for practice. After referring to the recent campaign in Egypt, he said he oould not help alluding to the fact that ha had had the honour of marching side by side with the men of that gallant brigacte who stormed Tel-el-Kebir, and took it by the bayonet. He was sorry to have to report the decease of one of tkeir officers Captain Hogarth. There was another matter of which he had to inform them, and that was that before several months were over they would have to part wiih their esteemed and worthy adjutant, Colonel Bertram. He wished they could have retained him as their adjutant as long as he lived. (Hear, hear, and applause.) At the time Colonel Bertram entered the corps with him, an officer could stay with the corps a lifetime, but under the new regeinte an adjutant had to retire after arriv- ing at a certain age. He could only hope that whoever might be his saccessor he may prove as worthy an adjutant as Colonel Bertram. (Applause.) Referring to the finan- cial condition of the corps' he said that they were in a better state that ever they had been before • and, in conclu- sion, he apologised for the unavoidable absence of Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P., the ex-Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Mr. Stubs, Mr. Marson, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, Mr. Gornall, and Lieutenant Buckton. Col. Greeuall having presented his prize, Captain BOLTON presented that given by Mr. McMinnies‘ M.P., who, he said, took considerable interest in the corps, but owing to his Parliamentary duties was unable to be with them that evening. Lieut.-Colonel GREENALL, in calling upon Mr. Robert Davies to present His prize, said he did not believe that gentleman had missed attending a single presentation from the first, and a more loyal and attached friend the corpahad not. (Applause.) Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, in presenting his prize, remarked that the volunteers were a body of men numbering, he believed, about 200,000, and they were supported at an expense of about 50s per head. It must be gratifying to know that they had been trained, and that if ever they were called upon for home defence they would be ready. He had heard with regret of the sad news that one of their officers had been taken away in his early youth. He was also sorry to hear that Colonel Bertram, an old Crimean hero— (applause)—was about to retire. • The Rev. S. WILKINSON said, in presenting his prize, he believed the volunteer movement had been the means of doing a vast amount of good in the country, and that the drill and discipline which it gave their young men must have a wholesome effect. A great number of those who formed the volunteer corps were employed in sedentary occupations, and the drill and exercise they had to undergo did them a vast amount of bodily good. Mr. Joirsa WHITE, in presenting the prizes, remarked that the volunteer force had become a recognised it not a neces- sary force of the country. Some people still said volun- teers did nothing; but it was in the fact of being always ready to do something if required that their strength lay. (Applause.) There was, he admitted, a necessity for a batter shooting ground. Risley Moss and Rixton Moss were bang cultivated, and he did not know of any ground suitable for their purpose except Cuerdlev Marsh. He did not see why there should be any difficulty about a proper range being obtained there, as it was easily accessible to Warrington. He should be very glad to render them all the help he could in obtaining a better shooting ground than the one they had at present. (Applause.) Mr. BUCKTON said he had the honour of having a son in the corps, but he was unable to be present as he was 200 miles away. He had not forgotten the corps, and he hoped to be be able to with them at the distribution:of the prizes next year. He urged upon the volunteers to endeavour to be- come better marksmen. (Hear, hear.) The CHAIRMAN expressed his obligation to Mrs. Qaekett for her kindness in presenting a prize' which had been given for several years. (Hear, hear.) He regretted that the Rector, owing to indisposition, was unable to with them. (Hear, hear.)' Captain RIDGWAY presented his own prize and that of the Finance Committee, and in doing so , remarked that the corps laboured under a disadvantage in the shortness of their range. He had hoped when they got the one at Lymm that all would have gene on smoothly, but, unfortunately, it had been .taken away from them. If they could only have one at Cuerdley Marsh the station at Pidler's Ferry would be very suitable, in fact more snitable than the one at Lymm, and they might have a range of from 800 to 1,100 yards without any difficalty. (Hear, hear.) Good shoot- ing was now necessary, great changes were taking place, and they could not tell how soon they might have to defend their oountry, not in a foreign land, but at home, owing to the existence of the ship canal at Warrington. (Laughter and applause.) There was a possibility that in years to come a foreign fleet might anchor at Bank Quay, and then the volunteers might be required to pour a volley upon them from the shore. (Laughter and applause.) He concluded by referring in feeling terms to the retirement of Colonel Bertram who, he said, had gained the respect of every men in the corps, and whoever followed him would have a diffi- cult place to fill. (Applause.) Colonel BERTRAM, in presenting Mr. Stub's prize, thanked the varbus speakers for their kind remarks. He had spent a very pleasant time with the corps, so much so indeed that he sometimes thought he could hardly have done his duty and have been strict enough, or he would have met with more opposition. However, things had gone off smoothly and pleasantly, and he should always look back with pleasure to the time spent amongst them. (Ap- plause.) , Lieutenant THOMPSON said there had been a good deal of I talk about the ship canal, shooting, Ste., but in presenting the doctor's prize he would say that the health of the vgimsnt was vsav good. (Laugh*er.) They had not had one case that had called for his aid. (Applause.)

div.head: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRICULTURE. MR. G. W. LATHAM ON LAND CULTIVATION.
div.p: CHESHIRE CHAMBER OF AGRI- CULTURE. MR. G. W. LATHAM ON LAND CULTIVATION.

The annual meeting of the Cheshire Chamber of Agri- culture was held at Crewe on Wednesday; Mr. H. J. Tollemache, M.P., presiding. There was a large attendance. Embodied in the report of the Council were the following recommendations, which the Chamber was asked to approve of:—

. (1) That compensation should be made to outgoing tenants for improvements made by them during tenancy, which, either in whole or in part, are in existence at its termination. That such compensation be measured by the increased agricultural value of the holding, which increase has been caused either by actual money outlay or by the general condition and cleanli- ness of the soil, and is due to the expenditure and skill of the tenant. That in ease of dispute the amount of compensation be settled by arbitration, or if neither landlord nor tenant should desire arbitration, by allowing the tenant to dispose of his interest in the holding to an eligible incoming tenant, against whom there are no reasonable grounds of objection. (2.) That notice to quit an agricultural holding be extended to twelve months.

(3.) That to carry out the previous and other proposals it will be nece ju dge, with to give powers to the County Court with the assistance of competent assessors, to settle matters in dispute :tetween landlord and tenastt expeditiously and economically. (4.) That there should be granted full liberty of cultivation, cropping, and sale of produce, subject to a power to be given to such court, to restrain any acts of the tenant which would be injurious to the landlord, and to assess damages, if any, to the extent to which the acts complained of have reduced the letting value ct the land.

(5.) That the law of distress be abolished, subject to a power to be given to such court to allow, in case of non-payment of rent, the re-entry of the landlord, on such terms as it shall consider equitable, or to place the tenant under terms as to payment of rent. _ _

long discussion followed.—Mr. G. W. LATHAM said he regarded clause No. 4 as being the most importr.nt in the resolutions, because it allowed a tenant farmer to do the best he could for the land, subject to his paying the penalty in case he did not cultivate the land properly. He could con- ceive nothing fairer on both sides than the terms proposed— compensation by the landlord for unexhausted improvements, and that the tenants should be required to recoup the land- lord if he had in any way damaged the letting value of the land. (Hear, hear.) He thought that landlords ought to exercise great care in the selection of their tenants, and not be so ready to let their land to an unskilled person merely because he offered a higher rent for it. Landlords should seek to obtain men of skill and judgment, good practical far- mers. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. TOMKINSON, of Willingtou Hall, said that the land system of the country requirel in many important points considerable amendment. The bonds which at present so greatly bound down the tenant- farmer must be loosed ; he must be given freedom of cultivation, security for capital invested, and those special privileges which had hitherto been claimed by the landlord under the law of distress must be abolished.—The Chairman said he could not agree in the provisions of the measure drafted by the Farmers' Alliance, and so far as these resolutions represented that bill he should oppose them. lie confessed that it was universally ad- mitted now that compensation ought to be granted to tenant farmers; and he quite agreed in that, if a suitable bill could be framed that would deal satisfactorily with the question. Ha could not support the sale of the tenant-right by the out- going tenant; that was a step on the principle of Irish legislatiou. IL e deprecate], too, the creation of courts for the purpose of dealing with disputes between landlord and tenant, as such a step would encourage litigation. He would prefer to leave such matters to the mutual good feeling of both parties. He hoped somebody would move an amend- ment to the propositions.—No amendment was, however, proposed, and the report was adopted in its entirety.

The Rev. Canon Barclay presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. There were present the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, John Lockwood, Messrs. Robert Ashton, J. Darbyshire, C. Rigby, W. Jack- son, J. Mclntyre, W. Pickering, Henry Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk), J. G. Bride (medical officer), and Javies Farrington (nuisance inspector).

div.head: NITISiNCIS:-WIIO IS RESPONSIBLE?
div.p: A NITISiNCIS:-WIIO IS RESPONSIBLE?
The NIIISINCE . IssPEcroa (Mr. Farrington) reported as follows:

On the 27th Sep`ember last, I received a complaint from the engineer to the London N. W. and G.W. Railway Companies respecting the emptying of a sewer at the bottom of tke slope on the side of the railway near to Daresbary Station. Such complaint was laid before the Sanitary Authority on October MIL and it was decided that the clerk and inspector inspect the place together. Such inspection took pace on October 18th, but as nothing could be an ived at by inspecting the out- let of the sewer only, we agreed that I should examine the drainage of the surrounding premises with a view to ascertain- ing from which the sewage emanated, and also to ascertain when and by whom such sewage was made to empty at the point in question. I have since made a thorough examination, and have obtained sn.th particulars and information as I have been ablo, anal now beg to submit the same for your informa- tion and consideration :—lt appears that when the Town Pit was la existence the whole of the premises situate in that por- tion of the village were drained into it, also the water from the road flowed therein, At the time the railway was cut, pro- vision appears to have been made by the Railway Company for the overtlaw from the pit, by putting in a receptacle and an , Iron syphon under the metals, the size .of such syphon being four inches in diameter. Some few years ago the pit was donel away with, and since then the sewage has been flowing through a pipe which empties on the railway side. lam in- ' formed that the late Mr. Dutton obtained the sanction of the company to make the present outlet, owing to the pre-men- tioned syphon having become blocked. Another informant states that the sanction of the company was only given to en- able Mr. Dutton' to run the pit dry to remove the solid matter therefrom. Alter the nine was put in, the pit was filled up and the pipe retained, and has since been used as a sort of main cutlet for the sewage from Mr. D. Dutton's resid,nce and villa adjoining theretn, also from premises belonging to Mr. Bow- cock, also from the premises owned and occupied by the Rev. G-. Heron, and those occupied by Mr. Fairclough. and a coti-age belonging to Miss Milner, the road water also ficivr.s in the same course. The questions at issue are ' Who is responsible for the pipe being where it is; and if it is to be removed, who should bear the cost of such removal and replacing the syphon?" There is no doubt but the construction of the railway has cut off the natural fall for drainage, and a four-inch syphon Is quite inadequate now when the pit is 'abolished. Mr. MCINTYRE moved, and Mr. C. RIGBY seconded, a motion that the railway company be written to with respect to the nuisance.—Carried. MEDICAL OFFICEL''S REPORT.
Mr. J. G. BRIDE, the Medical Officer of Health, read his monthly report. It contained no observations Df public in- terest.

The Indian contingent left London on Wednesday, and embarked at Tilbury on board the Ganges for India. "CHRIST BEFORE PILATE!' —A. QUESTION OF COPYRIQIIT.—Mr. Terrell moved on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Chitty, on behalf of Messrs. Agnew, for an injunction to restrain Mr. Whiteley, of Westborne drove, from parting with', a reduced copy of the picture "Christ before Pilate," the copyright of which was in the plaintiffs. The picture had been deposited with Mr. Whiteley for exhibiticn for the pur- pose of sale, and the plaintiffs required an injunction to restrain Mr. Whiteley from parting with it. Mr. Whiteley had expressed his willingness to have an injunction against him, the plaintiffs fearing that the owner of the picture would apply for and obtain repossession of it. Justice Chitty granted an interim injunction over Friday, with leave to serve short notice of motion for that day. EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY Acr : HEAVY DAMAGES.—In the City of London Court on Tuesday, an important case lender the Employers' Liability Act was heard. The plaintiff was an elderly woman named Stokes, living in Tooley-street, and the defendants were Messrs. Barber and Co., of Brewers' Quay, Lower Thames-street. The case for the plaintiff was that her husband, who was employed by the defendants, met his death in August last through certain defects in their plant. For the defence it was argued that it was the duty of the workmen to protect themselves by seeing to the condition of the machinery complained of; but t'oe jury found for the plaintiff, and awarded her ,gl.4S4elbei'Lng equal ' to three year's earnings of the husband,

div.head: ASHTON.
div.p: ASHTON.

CREATING A DISTURBANCE.-012 Saturday last, John Pritchard was apprehended at Ashton, on a charge of being drunk and disorderly and creating a disturbance on the same evening. He was brought before H. Mayhew, EN , at the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, and was ordered to pay the costs. VISIT OF AN OLD CONGREGATIONAL PASTOR. The Rev. G. S. Spencer, of Birmingham, pastor of the Ashton Congregational Church so far back as 1139, has paid a visit to the scene of his early labours. On Sunday last he twice preached in the Congregational Church, and there were large congregations, many persons coming from a distance to hear their respected friend and former pastor. LIME LIGHT EXHIBITION.—In aid of funds being raised to be devoted to the purchase of prizes for the day scholars attending the Stubshaw Cross schools, a lime light exhibi- tion of pictures, representing scenes in the "Pilgrim's Progress," and places of interest in Jerusalem, the Holy Land, Arctic regions, &c., was held in the school on Mon- day evening last. There was a good attendance, and the exhibition was greatly enjoyed. OPENING OF A NEW WESLEYAN MISSION ROOM Air S'ennsile.w Coss.—On Sunday last special services were held in connection with the opening of a new Wesleyan mission room at Stubshaw Cross. The morning preacher was the Rev. J. M. Wamsley, of St. Helens, and the evening preaeher the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, of Earlestown. On the, same day a Sunday school was also started. On Thursday evening a public meeting was held therein, and there was a large attendance. The chair was occupied by the Rev. J. M. Wamsley, and he was supported by the Rev. J. M.Fairbourn, Messrs. Howard, Parkinson, and Brown. The meeting was an interesting one, and an extended report in connection therewith is held over until our next issue. SIOCKING FATAL ACCIDENT IN AN EARLESTOWN COL. LIERY.—About three o'clock on Monday afternoon last, a shocking fatal accident occurred in the Bickershaw seven- foot mine At the Mesnes Collieries, belonging to Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Co. The deceased was named Peter Martland, a lad 12 years of age, who had been employed as a drawer at the pit named, and whose father, William, Martland, is a check-weighman at the same colliery. it seems that the lad 'garland was returning from his work, and was making his way to the pit bottom, when some waggons filled with coal running on a tram line knocked him down and passed over his body, killing him almost in- stantaneously. An inquest was held at the Ram's Head Inn, Stubshaw Cross, on Thursday forenoon, before Mr.: Barker, deputy coroner. The inquiry lasted about two hours,. the jury ultimately returning a verdict ef "Accidental death."

THE GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MOVEMENT.— A fortnight's special Gospel Temperance mission was commenced in the Congregational Schoolroom, Gerard-street, on Monday even- ing last, but the movement has not met with the same success that has attended similar efforts elsewhere. There was a ' good attendance, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. H. Wilson, who was supported by the Rev. G. S. Spencer, of Birmingham, and Mr. Lee, ot Stubshaw Cross. After the meeting had been opened, the Chairman spoke of the cir- cumstances under which they had met together, and stated that a committee of management had been formed for the 'purpose of carrying on that mission. It would be conducted in that schoolroom for a fortnight, and afterwards continued in connectien with other places of worship, at such times as the committee might decide. He impressed upon them the importance of being thoroughly united in the work, and said that the success of the movement to a great extent depended upon the people connected with the different places of worship all lanai no-. He pointed out the origin of the Blue Ribbon Army, and traced its history up to the present time. The Rev. G. SI Spencer and Mr. Lee also addressed the meeting, at the close of which 35 persons donned the bit of blue. A similar meeting was held on Wednesday evening, and another will be held this (Saturday) evening. On Tuesday and Thursday special Gospel addresses were given by the R2V" G S Spencer, and will be continued during the following week. The singing, &c., is being conducted by the United Gospel Temperance Mission choir. FRODSHAM.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR LT KINGSLEY.—This bazaar was held at Kingsley on Wednesday, and was opened by Mr. Peter Hall. A variety of useful and fancy articles were offered for sale, and the sum of .218- 133. Bth was realised.

FANCY BAZAAR AT FRODSRAM.—We would refer our readers to the advertisement of a fancy bazaar to he held in connection with the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Frodsham, on Thursday and Friday next. The decorations will repre- sent shops in the early English style of architecture, and will be well worth a visit. GOLBORNE.

NEGLECTING TO SEND A -CHILI; TO SCROOL.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday last, Ellen Howard, of Go'borne, was summoind for neglecting to send her child to school as required by the Elementary Education Act.— The case was adjourned for a month to see how the child attended the school in the meantime. TEL MEETING AND ENTERTAINMENT AT EDGE GREEN. —On Saturday afternoon last a public tea meeting and entertainment were held in the Edge Green Primitive Methodist schoolroom, the proceeds of which were to be devoted to a fund being raised in connection with a pro- posed bazaar for the reduction of the chapel deLt. About 120 or 130 persons sat down to an excellent tea, but at the substquent meeting the number of those present was•con-- siderably increased. Mr. John Sproston occupied the chair, and he was supported by the Rev. R. Crewdson and Mr. R. Yates, of Golborne, both of whom delivered interesting ad- dresses, Mr. Crewdson, at some length, spoke on persever- ance as being a necpssity of success and of steadiness in connection with religious work. During the evening a lIUM-- ber of songs, recitations, dtc,, were very creditably given, the selections by the choir being especially noticeable. Mr. James Prescott presided at the organ. At the close of the meeting the Rev. R. Crewason thanked all those who had contributed to its success. HAYDOCK.

SERTICE OF SONG AT THE WESLEyAN METHODIST CHAPEL. --A very interesting service of song, entitled, "The Pil- grim's Progress," .was given in the Wesleyan Msthodist Chapel, on Monday evening, in aid of the funds for the enlargement of the Sunday schools. The weather was some- what unfavourable, however, and there was not a large attendance, it being smaller than that anticipated: But this did not in any way detract from the interesting character of the service or flee succeas which attended the efforts of the choir, who gave the musical selections in a most creditable manner. The connective readings were given by Mr. John Fairhurst, who at the commencement alluded to the" Pilgrim's Progreso" and its writer' and went on to point out that the object of that meeting had' claims upon them, inasmuch as it was for increasing the comfort and convenience of both scholars and teachers in their schools. From beginning to end, the singing of the choir was much appreciated, the singing being unusually effective. Mr. Wm. Briscoe presided at the harmonium. ENTERTAINMENT AT ST. JAMES'S SCHOOL—Another of the series of entertainments in aid of the funds of St. James's schools was given in that schoolroom on Monday evening last. Though owing to the unfavourable weather the attendance was not quite so good as formerly. Ihere was, however, a goodly number of persons present, including the Rev. H. and; Mrs. Sherlock, the Rev. H. and Mrs. Mason, the 141'ses McCorquedales, Miss Watkins, Dr. and Mrs. Hayward, Mr. and Mrs. Turnball, Mr. and Mrs. Wal- don, Mr. and Mrs. Edwin Jackson. The programme was a pleasantly waled and interesting one, and the entertainment was a success; and it is said, one of the most enjoyable of those hitherto held. The pianoforte accompanists were Messrs. .U. and J. Leyland, and A. Simms. The first piece was a pianoforte duet, " Wilbetm Keller," by the Misses M. and J. Turnbull, which was followed by tha Rev. H. Sherlock (vicar) singing "The , village blacksmith," which was meritoriously encored. He responded by repeating the last verse. Mr. Arthur L. Evans effectually sang "Polly," after which the Rev. J. Lovell I (curate of Newton) received a hearty encore for his song, "Brown eyes and blue eves." The Rev. H. Sherlook, then read "My account with Her Majesty," after which a choir of school children, under the leadership of their efficient master, Mr. Weldon, gave "Murmur; gentle lyre." Mr. Waldon then read an amusing selection from "Andy Andy," and the Misses Pennington and Leyland sweetly gave the duet, "Flow on, thou shining river," bringing the first part of the programme to a close. The second part was opened by the Misses J. and A. Turnbull giving a piano- forte duet, consisting of selections from Beethoven's works, after which Mr. J. Leyland sang "The thorn." The song "The poodle," by the school children, was effectively rendered, and received a merited encore, nal the Lancashire sketch, entitled "A fowl way of dressing game," by Mr. TiArnbull, created wuch

amusement. Ur. dames Hunt then gave the song, .4 The Bay of Biscay," which was followed by the 11:1:e*t. J. Lo v .611 receiving much applause fore his song, "The Boilen story." An encnre was demanded, and as a response he I read a selection fronthe " Harly Burly." The programme concluded by Mr. Arthuel,Evans being warmly encoied for his song, "Alladdin," after which the Rev. 11. Sherlock , moved a hearty vote of thanks to the Rev. J. Lovell: and 'other friends, who had kindly given their services. The F motion was seconded by Mi. Edwin Jackson, and heartily I accorded.

div.head: KIcIITSPORD.
div.p: KIcIITSPORD.

At black marble timepiece, designed to represent the frontage of the Madeleine in-Paris, has been presented to• Mr. W. Ff. Ingham by the congregation of Knutsford Parish. Church as a token of their high appreciation of the valuable assistance he has rendered in connection with the musical services^of the church for two years.

LITTLE LEIGH. STEALIITS, A TURKEY AT LITTLE LEITHL—At Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. E. Greenall and J. Marson, a man named Walter &Lid, described as a labourer and poacher,. was charged with stealing a turkey, value 12s. ed., the property of John Turner Cowap, at Little Leigh, on the 20th November.—The prisoner was on the prosecutor's premises on the evening of the day named, and was seen by the servant to leave with a turkey under his coat. On the constable visiting the prisoner's house, he found the head and wings of a turkey, which were identified by Mrs. Cowap as the property of her husband.—The prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was committed• to Knutsford for two months, with hard labour.

div.head: NANTWICIL
div.p: NANTWICIL

HORIIIDLB CONDITION OF AN IMBECILI3 WOMAN AT NANTWICII.—At the meeting of the Nantvrich Local Board, on Saturday, the Inspector (Mr. Gentry) called attention to a house in Beam-street, one of the principal thoroughfares of the town. On many occasions there had been an attempt made to gain an entrance. These had failed'until Novem- ber 10, when the inspector and Sergeant Warvrickpbtained access. They found sitting by the fire an imbecile woman, in a shockingly neglected state and utterly uncared for. In the living part of the house there were found four large vessels containing old buttermilk and other slops in a state of fermentation, and another vessel containing pigs' meat. In the pantry, where food was kept, was a pail full of putrid stuff. Things were worse in what had been a milk-house. The stench was abominable. Upstairs, things were quite as bad. Dr. Fox, medical officer, went next day, but the house was locked. It is stated that the sister of the poor woman left a considerable amount of money when she• died.—A member of the board said screams had been frequently heard proceeding from the house.—lt was understood that unless the woman was looked properly after, farther pro- ceedings will be taken. _ _

div.head: OVXR.
div.p: OVXR.

_ The recently elected Mayor of Over, Alderman Ji Slater, attended church- on Sunday, accompanied by the local police, fire brigade, and representatives of the volunteers. Theßev. E. Woodyatt was the preacher. BEGGING. - At Over Police Court, before Mr. Slater (Mayor), two beggars were brought up last Friday, by P.C. Leather, Moses Evason, mechanic, from Northwich, and Geo. Stokes, from London, both charged with begging in High- street, wore sent to Knutsford for seven day's with hard labour.

div.head: RAINFORD.
div.p: RAINFORD.

STRAYING Cows RAINFORD.-011 Monclay, at the St. Helens County Petty Sessions, Thomas Woods, an elderly man, was charged with having allowed two cows to stray on the highway, near Rainford, on the 21st ult. An ofßeer stated that he found the cows straying on a road which leads from Rainford-road to Moss Bank-lane. The road was a public highway, and was kept in repair by the Rain- ford Local Board. Mr. Thomas, who represented the defen- dant, said his client was a farmer, and had lived in the neighbourhood of Rainford for about 78 years. The cows had been pasturing in a field adjoining the road ;in question, and, owing to someone having opened the gate, they had strayed out on to the road. He mentioned that this road was very little frequented, and it was quite a custom for the neighbouring farmers to pasture their cattle upon it. A fine of Is and costs was imposed. CONCERT AT CRANK Scnoms.-011 Friday evening, a very successful concert was given in aid of the above schools by the following St. Helens artistes :Miss McCar- roll, Miss Maud Dennett, Mr. C. Grime (Wigan), Mr. Geo. Barton, jun., Mr. R. B. Husker, Mr. Frederick DE.innett, and Mr. W. G. Foreman. The openin glee, "Hail, smiling' more," was very well received; after whieh Miss McCar- ron sang "Tell him I love him" with much feeling, and for which she deservedly received an encore. Mr. G. Barton, Jun., was very successful in his rendering of "Good night, beloved." The next piece on the programme was -a humorous glee, " Beware,' by the glee party; so well was it given that, on being recalled, they responded with the give, "I know a lass, a fair one," whick received great applause. "Sailing" was next sung by Mr. Fred. Dennett, who did full justice to it, and on being endored repeated the last vers^. Considerable amusement was caused by Miss McCarroll and Mr. W. G. Foreman in the duet "Very sus. pinions," which was exceedingly well given. Miss Maud Dennett next gave "The blind girl to her harp," which was very creditably sung, especially so as it was her first appearance as a soloist. Mr. W. G. Foreman caused roars of laughter in his song "Waste not, want not," "Sweetly blows," a very nice glee, and admirably given, brought the first part to a close. The glee, "Strike the lyre," opened the second part, which, given by such a nicely balanced quartette, could not fail to be appreciated. "Let roe dream again," by Miss Maud Dennett, was nicely sung, she hav- ing gained more confidence. This was followed by "The pilgrim of love," by Mr. G. Barton, jun., and was most decidedly his best song of the evening, being given with good feelitg and nice finish. "Johnny Schrnoker " by the glee party, quite roused the audience, and received a very 'Andy encore. Miss McCarron, in "Love not," sustained her reputation; and Mr. W. G. Foreman's humorous song, "You know not what I mean," created much amuse- ment ,and was heartily applauded. It is needless to comment on Mr. Dennett's singing of the " Midshipmite," it being sung with nice style and exceedingly good pronunciation. "In the wood," a glee, was the last piece on the pro- gramme. Before the National Anthem was sung Mr. S. Robinson proposed, and the Rev. J. 'Barnacle seconded, a very hearty vote of thanks to the performers. Mr. H. J. Foreman performed the duties of accompanist in a very able manner.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.
The Winsford corps of the Salvation army is marking, the departure of its "Captain " and " Lieutenant " by a series of meetings, among which there have been a tea-meeting and a" holiness convention."

SUNDAY SCHOOL SERMONS—The annual sermons of the Weaver Sunday school connected • with Christ Church ware preached on Sunday last by the incumbent, the Rev. E. Nixon, M.A., in the morning; and by the vicar of Hartford, the Rev. E. Eddowes, M.A., in the evening. The collections amounted to £3O odd.

FAIR.—The winter fair was held on Saturday Jut, when the weather being very fine there was a good gathering. quotations for heifers and stirlis were from £7 to £l2; s.t.)re cows from £9 to £l6, and calving cows from the latter price to £25. Pigs were in abundance at fromlo3. to a guinea for young ones, and store pigs sold at 30s. to 50s. Many changed hands as customers were plentiful. There were a -few Shot- land ponies present, but no sales were made. A NEW UNDERTAKING AT WINSFORD —We' learn that a lease, containing important brine concessions, of land front- ing for near two-thirds of a mile to the Wind/3rd "flashes" on the river Weaver, has been obtained from Mr, George F. Wilbraham, and that operations are shortly to be com- menced near "Stock-stairs" to 'sink for brine, and the erection on the land, by a joint stock company, of large and important salt and other works, and also the making of a shipbuilding yard. A new branch line of railway is also spoken of in connection with the undertaking;. and we bear that a syndicate is now being formed by a firm. of London and Manchester financiers to complete the project. WIGAN.

The Hon. Algernon Egerton, Conservative, and Mr. Walter Wren, Liberal, were nominated on Tuesday for the representation of Wigan. The polling is timed for to-day (Saturday). NATIONAL AND BLUE COAT BOYS' SCIIDOL.—The annual examination of this school took place on the 9th aud 10th of October, 1882, by E. L. Phelps, Esqt, Her Majesty's In-, spector, assisted by Mr. Forster. The rector (the Hon. and Rev. Canon Bridgeman) has just received the following re- port:—" Discipline has improved, and is now very satisfac- tory. Progress.in attainments has been a little impeded by building operations during the year, the teaching staff also is rather too small for the numl:ers, nevertheless excellent work is done in the school. The elementary subjects in the first and second standards, and the class subjects (grammar and geography) in the second and third standards deserve- special praise. Both rooms (boys and girls) have becn thoroughly repaired, and additional class-rooms constructed, which greatly increase the efficiency of the schools." The head master's certificate has ..been endorsed as follows : Mr. Langshaw has been working with rather a small staff, of teachers„but has maintained -his- school in every high state of efficiency." During the last, three years nine boy&have been allowed from this scbeol to compete for free scholar- ships for three years at the Wigan Grammar Schoolot whom eight have been successful. • ITEMS OR CHESHIRE NEWS.

Cheshire huntsmen will learn with regret that neither Carnbermere Abb3y nor any other place in England has been engaged with a view, to a pending visit of the Empress ci austria during the-hunting season. The 'Vienna Presse ,states emphatically that her Majesty is not coaling to 'England. CREWE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the Crewe Agricultural Society was held on Monday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. Willi:4m Wright. The hon. secrethey (Mr.W. Eardley) submitted the accounts for the past year,, which showed an adverse b.4lance of £34. The year began with a balance to the credit bf the seciety of £25, and the subscriptions amonnted to £264, and other receipts, entrance fees, and gAte money brought up the total. to £617. The expenses, howeyor, had been £651. The accounts ware passed, and the committee and hon. secretary were re-elected. A discussion then took place on a sugges- tion to invite the Cheshire Amalgamated Society to hsld a two days' show at Crewe next year, in which case the Crewe society would amalgamate. Councillor Welch pro- posed that the Crewe Society should offer the Cheshire Society £l5O and a free site to be selected by the County Committee. The resolution was carried unanimously, and a deputation was appointed to urge the claims of Crewe at the forthcoming anal meeting of the Cce.enty Society.
