div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF -GUAIiDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF -GUAIiDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse I on'Tuesday, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were pcesent the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, John Lock- wood, Messrs. T. Nurman, J. Mclntyre, J. Darbyshire, E. A. Wallington, G. S. Haeeharst, Robert Ashton, C. Rigby, W. Jackson, J. Carnpkin, J. Knowles, Joseph Stokes, W. Pickering, Regal Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linker (clepu'y clerk).
A SETTLED DISPUTE. The DEPUTY CLunt read the following letter from Mr. Sutton, the as3istant secretary to the Local government Board:—

- Sir,—l an diceeted br the roc d Government Board to s ate that they have hat under con-lidera-ion the enquiry onn-ained In your letter of the 27,11 September is t, r speetiog the arrangement for the re-iesption int ) the Infections flos provided by the Runeorn improvement Oommissi.m,r=, of cases of Infectious disease amongst paupers, from the tow ships comprised in the Ralcorn tne.iiell relief distlet. I arts directed to laform the Guar :tans thtt in tne opinion of the Board it forms sus part of the duty of the medical officer for the Itunc-sra district to attend nova persons who may be treated In the Infectious Hoszltal, As it appears to the Board that he cannot be "lawfully required" by any of the pers ,ns meri. tioned in Article 206, No. 1 of the Gene al Consolidated Order, to furnish attendance or tnecl eines in such hospitals. The Board, at the same time desire to slate that it appears to thlm that the most satisfact ry ar:angement would b that the chargs for the me -deal treatment of pauper cases, as w 11 as that for the other atteocian..es required by the sick in the hospital, should be ineMded in the payment to be made by the Guardians under toe agreement with the hospital authorities. It was decided that a copy of the letter should be forwarded to the Board of Commissioners. THE WORICHIOUSE SCHOOL.

The DEPUTY CLERIC said Her Majesty's inspector of ichools had reported that 96 per cent. of the boys and 85 per cent. of the girls at the Workhouse school had passed the examination. The knowledge, of the various subjects exhibited by the scholars was on the whole" very fair."

div.head: WORICHOrSI3 DRAINAGE.
div.p: THE WORICHOrSI3 DRAINAGE.

Mr. Illchms,E; presented a report from the committee appointed to consider the question of land required for Workhouse drainage. It stated the committee had inspected the land proposed to be the site of the irrigation works, and after careful censideration they had resolved to recommend the Guardians to arrange for about four statute acres of land for irrigation, such land to be enclosed with a quick fence. Mr. Mclntyre proposed the adoption of the report, and impressed upon the Board the necessity for the work being efficiently done if it were to be of,any benelit.—Mr. NORMAN seconded the motion.—Mr. HAZLEiII7RST asked if the drainage would not pass down the sewerage pipes in sufficient volume to c)ntaminate the canal .—dr. MclsTrus replied that the sewage would be properly filtered, as the pipes would be placed three feet below the surface of the soil. The water which would enter the canal woald be almost fit to drialz.—The motion was tarried.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.
Rev. J. LOCKWOOD reported that the Finance Committee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £736 105 Bd.
THE RUNCORN RELIEVING OFFICER CENSURED: ALLEGED NEGLEC r.

Mr. R. ASHTON, referring to the circumstances of the death at the Workhouse of Thomas Bettley, formerly a fishmonger at Runcorn (which were reported in The Examiner Cast iiiatairday), said it seemed that this man' who walked from Runcorn to the Workhouse, apalied to Mr. Wright for an order. It bad not transpired whether Mr. Wright had refused the order, still there must be blame attaching to someone. If Mr. Bettley applied for an order ts the house, it was Mr. Wright's business to give hint one, and secure a conveyance to convey him thither. It was not the first time cases of this kind had been brought before the Board from Runcorn throngh Mr. Wright's negligence, and he for one strongly recommended that an investigation be made into the present case. (Hear, hear,)—The Rev. J. W. N. TANNER said he supposed Mr. Jones could not receive a case into the house without an order.—The CLERK Wee under- stood to say that that depended upon the nature of the caee. —Mr. ASHTON asked the reason why Mr. Bettley did not receive- an order.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD said he lied asked Mi. Wright about the case, and he said that Mn Bett- ley called at his (Mr. Wright's) office on Xuesday afternoon about half-past three, and a.eked for an order of adinittence to the Workhouse. Mr. Wright did not give him one, but said "Oh, wait until to-morrow morning, and then I will give you one," adding, "I am wanted at Weston, and I must go ; my time is up.: Come again 'to-morrow morning." Bettley replied, "I must go, for I have made all my arrange- ments." Mr. Wright could not see what arrangements were necessary. It appeared that soon after Mr. Bgttley took the train to Sutton Weaver and walked to the Work- house. That was Mr. Wright's explanation.—The DEPUTY CLERK read the masters report, which stated Bettley arrived at the Workhouse about five p.m. without an order, but said Mr. Wright would send ,rie on. Bettley said ho ' was tired and poorly, and the- master sent him to the in- firmary, where he had tea and was properly treated. After- wards he appeared much . better, but at 9-35 he became worse, and messengers were despatched for the medical officer. He however died at ten o'clock before the doctor's arrival. The nurse said the deceased died from heart dis- ease, an opinion which wag afterwards coufirmea by the medical officer.—The Rev. J. LOCKWOOD : He 'made no re- mark to Mr. Wright about feeling ill.—Mr. RIGBY : It seems to me to be very gross negligence on the part of Mr. Wright. —Mr. R. Aserroet: No doubt about it. If this was the first case I could excuse it. But it is not the first case by many. —Mr. RIGBY : I think the Board ought to censure him about it strongly. He is a very cantankeroua old men.— Mr. NORMAN : This else ought to convince us that • we e ought to have a horse belonging to the union.— Mr. Wright was called Lao the room, and the CHAIRMAN aSked: When did Mr. Bettley app'Y to you for an order? —Mr. WRIGHT: A week to-day, sir.—What time was it? It would be a little before two o'clock.—What was your reason for not granting it? I had come out of the office and was on my way to Weston when he asked me for it, and I asked him to see me in the morning.—Mr. R. ASHTON : Had you just come out of the office? Yes.—Were you close I to the door? No; not close to the door exactly.—The ' Cuaaame.N: You were not far away? No.—Watt condition did he appear to be in ? He seemed to be right enough, as far as I could see. He was lame, but he did not complain of being ill or anything of that.—lf you had given him an order then, should you have ordered a conveyance? No, sir.—What did • you say to him: I said, " You must see me in the morning?' I was going to Weston and I wished to get there so that I could get back before dark. Bettley said "I am obliged to go. I have made all arrangements ready for going, and I must go." I slid, "See me in the morning;" but he still stuck to the statement that ha must go, as he had made all arrangements. I didn't understand what arrangements he had mede.—The CHAIRMAN: He might have paid up to that day at his ledgings.—The. DEPUTY Ceanx: Did you :Jay that you would send Mr. Jones the • outer? No.—Mr. LINAYER : It is on the book—Roy. J. LOCKWOOD : He would say that to get in.—The DEPUTY CLERIC: I think that would get over the difficulty.—Mr. WP-IGHT : If I had given him an order it would not have saved his life.—Mr. NORMAN: That is not the question. When a person applies to you for an order, and you know the circumstances, I think you ought to give him an order at once. You knew Bettlev had been in the house often before.—Mr. WRIGHT admitted that fact; and Mr. NORMAN asked if Mr. Jones had refused to take Bettley into the house, and the latter had died, what position would 1F... Wright have been in ?—Mr. WRIGHT: I Joh% know.— Mr. DARBYSIIIRE: If he had not had sufficient money to pay his railway fare he would have had to walk the whole distance.—Mr. WRIGHT: It appears he had money.—Mr. RIGBY : That is not the question.—Mr. WRIGHT: Am I bound to give an order to everyone who applies? The CHAIRMAN: You are obliged to exercise a certain amount ef discretion.—Mr. WRIGHT : I was doing then.—Mr. LOCKWOOD : But you admit that if it had not been incon- venient to go to the office and get the oirler, you would have given him one.—Mr. : Most likely I should. If he had come to the office when I was in the office I shotild have given him one.—Mr. LOCKWOOD: It was not a question of his right to one.—Mr. NORMAN: Why dou't you confess at once? When qaestioned by Mr. Rigby you say "Am I to give an order to anyone who asks," and here Mr. Lockwood drags it out of you that if it had not been inconvenient to you you would have given him an order.— Mr. 'WRIGHT: Don't I tell you be didn't appear ill ? Mr.. NORMAN : I met him on the Monday before he applied for the order' and I am sure that man was in such a state that I was glad to get away from him. I gave him some money, and was very thankful I got past him, I was so afraid of the man dying as he stood beside me. Any per- son, I am sure, would have given him an order into the house. If he had told me that he was going to the Work- house, I should have taken him is a cab.—Mr. WRIGHT made a remark, to which the CHAIRMAN replied: You are mistaken. It would not have taken you a minute to give I him the order, and you knew it would be right.—Mr. WRIGHT: Yes: I quite see now. At the same time, I thought it would be better if he started in the morning.— Mr. NORMAN: There is no doubt in my mind but that the mats had settled everything, and had no money to pay his lodgings.—Mr. Wiwi= : Ile didn't say that.—Mr. Non- MAN: But he said, "I have settled everything and must go." —Mr. WRIGHT: Yes, I told you he said he must ge.—The CILLIRMAIT : lie showed that by going in spite of the order. I Mr. WRIGHT : I don't know anything more than he said. He did not complain of being badly ill at all. He asked for • nothing more than the order. Mr. Wright then left the room, and Mr. IL /est:Igo:1 said the Board had heard Mr. Wright's excuse. This was not the first case. Only about a month ago a man might have died but for some lodging. house keeper taking care of him; Mr. Wright never asked a question about it, and was never near the place since the man was hurt. He thought this case ought to be investigated further.—The CHAIRMAN : I don't think we have a very good case. There is nothing to inveetigate. We have elicited all that we can. It is really a mistake simply. ma Wright thought next morning would do just as well.—Mr. ASHTON: I beg-to move that Mr. Wright be reported to the Local Government Board. The CHAIRMAN : I think we had better-have a better case to report. It is merely an error of judgment.—Mr. RIGBY : I think it is gross negli- gence.—ha CHAIRMAN: I am looking at how the Local Government Board will lcok at it. Mr. RIGBY : They will look in the Paine light as I do. Mr. Nonnew : Suppose we try him once more. (Laughter.) —Mr. R. AsuroN : It will never have any effect upon hien., —Mr. Noetereer Blessed are the merciful. (Laughter.)— Mr. Aserrote : We have had niercy too long.—Mr. NORMAN:' I think that if the chairman just tells him that we shall have to report him if there are any other complaints about him, it will be quite sufficient.—At the request of the Board the nurse, Mrs. Janet Ball, was called into the room and

questioned by the chairman. She -stated that she perceived that Bettley was suffering from heart disease when she first saw him, but she did not anticipate that be would die so soon. The walk to the Workhouse no doubt made him a great deal worse.—Mr. C. RIGZY ROW seconded Mr. Ashton's motion that Mr. Wright be reported.—The motion, however, was not pat to the meeting, and after a little conversation Mr. Wright was again called into the room.—The CHAIRMAN said: I am directed by the Board to express their great disatisfaction at your negligence in this case It is quite clear that if Bettley had been a minute or two sooner you could have given him an order, but you would not take the trouble to go back to the office or house to write it out. It is not merely this case, but there are so many other cases of negligence against you. It is with great difficulty the Board have let you off and not reported you b the Local Government Board. The reeson they have not done so is that there is a black mark against you already, and we:don't know what the consequences might be if we were to report to them this time. We should be sorry if at your age and after your service you should be "sacked," but we do hope sincerely that you will be more careful in these cases for the future, and show a little more sympathy and kindness for the poor people. As I have often told you civility costs nothing, and a kind word goes a long way with poor people. The Board has also a very strong feeling that the next case should be reported what- ever the consequences may be and not let you off so easily. —Mr. ASHTON : Can you hEar that Mr. Wright ?—Mr. WRIGHT: I can hear sir.—The CHAIRMAN: You have heard a good many such things, do you take any nstice.—Mr. WRIGHT: I will try to think on.

div.head: FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH,
div.p: FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH,
RE-OPENING SERVICES.

An important event in the annals of Frodsham took place on Thursday, when the well-known Parish Church was re- opened for Divine service, after being closed for nearly 21 years for the much needed ,work of restoration. Before noticing the opening services, it may be of interest to our readers if we very briefly review the history of the work. The general style of the present structure, according to Ormerod, is that of the fifteenth century, but the porch and a considerable part of the south side was re-built in 1715. The fabric is built of red stone, sad consists of a nave, chancel, side aisles, and tower containing six bells. The arches In the nave, and the pillars supporting the arches ; the chancel, with the Kingsley or mother chapel ; and a piscina on the south side of the 'altar under a Gothic arch, with a trefoil head and canopy between two pillars terminating in crotchets, have been referred to ,as among the most interesting features in the old structure. It will now be about ten years since the restoration was first proposed. At that time the church was surveyed and plans prepared, but the matter was allowed to remain in abeyance until the year 1879, when the parishioners, at a meeting held on the 22nd December' decided that it was desirable and necessary that the Parish Church should be restored. A working committee was appointed, consisting of the following gentlemen, viz.:—Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., vicar; Messrs. Charles Reynolds, JP., John Robinson, John Ashton, J. R. Pickering, William Hayes, Henry Linaker, Charles E. Linaker, and Thomas Lewis. The services of Messrs. Bodiey and Garner, of Lon-. don, the well-known ecclesiastical architects, were secured, and plans were at once prepared, and the work proceeded with. The outline of the church has not been interfered with, and, viewed from a distance, its noble proportions show to advantage. The roof has been elevated to the point indicated on the tower as its original position, and the alteration adds grace and dignity to the fabric. The character of the south side has been entirely changed. The factory-like windows which for- merly existed, have given place to others with beautiful and delicate tracery; an important feature has been added by a turret at the south-west corner; and we venture to say that when the tower and porch have been restored the eleva- tion of the south side of the church will present an ap- pearance of great architectural beauty. The interior of the church has received very careful attention, and after noticing that the unsightly galleries have been removed, we were struck by the effective appearance of the restored pillars and arches. The old Norman pillars, with their richly-carved caps, in the nave have been cleared and partly restored, the south arcade of the nave completed, a new Norman arch, two pillars and a smaller pointed arch being • substituted for the old wide arch, and the old pier of the south side of the chancel arch. The clerestery windows have also been restored. The east window is now extended to its original size, and I contains an artistic design in stained glass representing the I Ascension. The drapery and arrangement of the figures are carried out in the highest style of art, and the general excellence of the work is mare apparent the closer it is observed. Mr. J. R. Pickering is the generous donor of this ornament to the church. Messrs. Burliss6n and Gill are the artists for the east window, and have also executed the small stained glass window oh the south side presented by Miss M'Key, of Liverpool. Tie reof of the church is entirely new, and is substan- tially carried out in oak, the roof of the chancel and ag'es being also in richly carved oak. Mr. leichard Beckett, of Hartford, has had the contract for the oak roofs. The following very handsome presents have been given, viz : Pulpit and lectern, by Mr. James Reynolds, Fox Hill; font, by the children of Mr. Hayes, of Ashton Hayes; east window by Mrs. Rigby Pickering; small south window by Blies M‘Kay; service books by Miss Lithom ; trays for communion by Dr. Robinson and Mr. Henry Linaker; two oak screens by Mrs. Rigby Pickering; one oak screen by Mr. Charles Iteynolde, of Netherton ; altar cover by ladies of Fiodsham ; candlesticks and ornaments for the com- munion table by the architects, Messrs. Bodley and Garner. It shotll€l be stated that Mr. Speechley has acted as clerk of the works, and the church is intended to accommodate 700 worshippers. Messrs. Binns, of Broarborough, near e Leeds, are engaged building a splendid and powerful organ for the church, and it iv expected to be completed in about three months. In conclusion, we would observe that the very liberal donations eguaranteed at the first meeting of the parishioners foreshadowed that the "poor expedient of a niggardly repair" vas not cantemplated,, and sub- sequent events have proved that wlfat has been attempted by the committee has been to "aim at reinstating the main features of the church to the latest date of what can be acknowledged as a true and genuine building, and sweeping away 'what is obviously mean and worthless." , The appearance of the church on Thursday showed that the above lines had been faithfully followNl, and although there yet remains much to be done before the work is completed. The main features of the restoration were apparent, and re- flected great credit on 'Messrs. Bedley and Garner, the architects, and will hand down to future ages the names of , the gentlemen who have devoted their time and energies in superintending i.nd conducting the work. . The re-opening services were preceded by the ceremony of the consecration of the land added to the graveyard of the church, which took place at eleven o'clock. Half an hour before that time the bells in the tower broke their long silence, and poured forth from their iron'throats a " liqeid I ditty," to once more call the parishioners to their devotions. Despite the extreme coldness of the weather, there was an extensive response, and people were continually entering the sacred edifice until the commencement of the service. The new burial ground, Which is on the 'east side of the church, his an area of 3,337 square yards. In one regard, in which the old ground is lamentably lacking—effective drainage— it will be most favourably placed. For this purpose, and wan, 17.1.c.1 is .n course of also for building a boundary erection, Mr. E. A. Wright has given the sum of £250. Mr. William Haves has contributed £4O towards the purchase of the land from the Marquis of Chohnondeley. Biehop Kelly, of Macclesfield, performed the consecration ceremony, which was witnessed by a considerable number of spectators. He was received in the church by the church xardens, Mr. John Ashton and Dr. Robinson, and the clergy, who were attired in their surplices. A precession was then formed. In front were the churchwardens, followed by the Revs. Canon Heron, Spooner, Hoole' Canon Upperton, E. A. Campbell, J. J. Bryant, J. H. Acherson, Nixon, Canon Dodd, L. Garnett, Spencer Stanhope, It. C.. Garnett, Hague, Whytehead, John Lockwood, Havard, Bleecowe, Cogswell, Penrose, Motherley' Crerner, Ramsden, Grier, Canon Cooper, Archdeacon Darby, Dean Howson', Bishop Kelly, and the Vicir (the Rev. H. B. Blo,gg, M.A.). Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. Henry Linaker (representatives of the Building Conemittee) brought up the rear. They proceeded round the burial ground, the bishop and clergy repeating a .verse, alternately, of the 49th Psalm. Other formalities having been gone through, they returned to the church, where, preceded by the choristers, who were attired in their long white surplices, they walked up the centre aisle to the chancel, the Rev Canon Barclay having meanwhile taken his position amongst them. The choristers were singing the proces- sional hymn commencing—
Lift the strain of high thanksgiving Tread with songs the hallowed way

Before it was concluded, the golden light of the winter's sun broke through the grey mists of the morning, and flooding into the chancel invested it with a beauty almost indescrib- able, the rich, though mellowed colours of the large stained window, the artistic tracery of the oaken screens, and the ornamental stone work, affording a charming picture to the view of the crowded congregation. To those who were acqusinted with the ancient edifice in its former state the view must indeed have been a striking contrast. It was pleasing•to notice the familiar form of Mr. Samuel Aston, the sexton (who, it is said, has been employed In the church in some capacity since the battle of Waterloo), once more moving about the aisles, for without him the church would scarcely seem complete. The service, with the exception of several special prayers, was that for St. Andrew's Day. The Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., read the prayers. The first lesson was read by the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., the second by the Rev. Canon Upper- ton, and the ante-communion office by Bishop Kelly. The anthem, "0, how amiable are Thy dwellings," was sung by the choristers in good style. Mr. Thomas Riley presided at the organ. The very rev. the Dean of Chester preached the sermon from the 14th verse of the Ist chapter and the Bth verse of the 6,th chapter of the Gospel according to St. John, taking the words "Andrew, Simon, Peter's brother." He described Bethesda, where Andrew was called by the Lord from his vocation of a fisherman to be a fisher of men, spoke of the apostle's Christian virtue as a pattern for the ministry, and, having referred to his character,, said there was no greater blessing in a parish than a cheerful Christian parishioner. Speaking of Herod's restored temple at Jerusalem, Dean Howson observei that architecture was the expression of the collec- tive concourse and worship of mankind. Their earliest wish must be that that restored church in which they were gathered might be a place of happy and constant concourse

that it might be an effectual Ad eloquent admonition to all men around that they take "heed that they forsake not the assembling of themselves together" on Sundays in the manner of all men, alike in the country and in the town. An offertory was then taken. EVENING SERTICE.

AT WIDNES- A MAN KILLED. Yesterday morning, about half-past nine, an accident of:a horrible nature occurred to a man named Thomas Howell, near the goods station on the Midland and Sheffield Rail- way, near Widnes. Howell had 3nly come from Dukinfleld that morning, and was proceeding from the Central Station, Widnes, in the direction of the tarn table, situate on the railway, near Mr. Brook's works. He was carrying a heavy bag of cement on his back, and did not perceive the approach of the 9-30 train from Widnes to Warrington, which was travelling with a speed of about 20 miles an hour. The unfortunate man appears to have heard the ' approach of the train when close upon him, and stepped into the four-foot, as he thought, perhaps, to avoid it. He was instantly knocked down by the engine, and carried by the train for a distance of 60 yards. The train also passed over him, inflicting injuries of a frightful description. He was literally dismembered, his head being crushed to a pulp, his limbs scattered about the line, and the metals bespat- tered with his brains and blood, Mr. Patten, the station- master, had the remains removed, and such was the state of the body that while the trunk was removed on a hand cart, the limbs, eec., were conveyed away in a basket to the Golden Ball Inn, Moss Bank, Widnes,

The hearty peal of the bells on Thursday evening was pleasant music to the parishioners of Frodsham, and a large congregation assembled to do honour to the Parish Church, which lost none of its grandeur when lighted up. The ministers present were Rev. H. B. Blogg, M A., vicar, Revs. A. P. Reynolds and Alfred Grier, curates, and the Revs. S. Wilkinson, H. Havard, J. Whytehead, J. Lockwood, and J. Penrose. The prayers were read by the Revs. A. P. Rey- nolds and A. Grier, and appropriate lessons, psalms, and hymns bad been selected. The anthem was taken from the 122nd Psalm, verses 1,5, 6, and 7, and was given in excel- lent style by the choir, the rendition being char- acterised by a crispness and Itrict ,observance of time; the parts were well balanced, and harmonised together in a very satisfactory manner. The success was doubtless due to careful training, and the excellent acoustic properties of the grand old church added much to the effect. The sermon was preached by the vicar, the Rev. H. B. Blozg, M.A.. who took for his text the Ist verse of the 122nd Psalm, " I was glad when they said unto me, we will go into the house of the Lord."

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT,
HOUSE OF COMMONS. - NEW WRIT.—A new writ was ordered to be issued for Liverpool. •

Mainciascan.—Sir C. DUKE promised to communicate with the Admiralty with a view of producing Admiral Jones's official report of his visit to Madagascar last year. Tun CHERI CONVENTION.—Answering Mr. CROPPER, who inquired whether matters in debate in the Chefu Conven- tion had been settled, Mr. C. DUKE said he had to reply in the negative. THE TRIAL OF ARABI. Mr. LABOUCHERB asked whether it was true as reported in the papers that all the charges except those of participating in the late military operations were to be withdrawn against Arabi, and that he was to be condemned to banishment.—Sir C. DILKE said no communication had been received from the Egyptian Government. Lord Dufferin had sent information, but be could not speak for the Egyptian Government. Replying to Sir W. Lawsoiv, he said the Egyptian Government had applied to Her Majesty's Government to send out a British general and officers to command the Egyptian army. The communi- cation was under consideration. MARINES FOR IRELAND.—Mr. TREVELYAN, replying to Mr. PARNELL, said it was true that thO Marines had been asked to volunteer for duty in Ireland tb assist the police. He could not say more on the subject. GRAND COMMITTEES. The adjourned debate on the resolutions for the appointment/of two standing committees was resumed.—Mr. DODSON moved the second resolution, which provided that each committee should consist of not less than 60 or more than 80 members, to be nominatki by the committee of selection, who should have rogat'd to the nature of the bills and the qualification of the, members selected, and should have power to add and die, charge members from time to time, provided the number of 80 be not exceeded.—Lord R. CHURCHILL moved as an amendment to omit the latter part of the resolution in orderl to insert words providing that the standing committees should consist of forty members who should be elected by the whole House 'by ballot.—,:he amendment was with- drawn—At this point it appeared that further opposition was withdrawn, and after the resolution bad been amended to provide committees of selection with power to add to and discharge membersirom standing committees, it was agreed to:, The third and fourth resolutions, which provided for the appointment of chairman, and commitment and report_ of bills, were agreed to. The last resolution, providing that the preceding.four resqlutione be standing orders until the, end of next session, waA agreed to amid slight cheers.—The House adjourned at a quarter to nine until" to-day (Satur- day),at a quarter to four. ,

div.head: ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT AT RITNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED EMBEZZLEMENT AT RITNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, before Mr. Willard Bankes, two young men named Thomas Hicks and Wm. Hodgkinson were charged, on remand, with having on the 27th November stolen is. and one serge jacket, the property of Horatio Syred, pawnbroker, Church-street. They were also charged with receiving the same. Hicks was further charged with embezzling three sums of money, amounting to 55. Bd., the property of Mr. Syred. Hicks, it appeared, was employed by Mr. Syred to manage his shop at Run- corn, and slept on the premises. The prisoner, contrary to the instructions of Mr. Syred, had allowed Hodgkinson to lodge with him. Suspecting that things were not going on a right, a number of marked coins were placed in the till. On the 27th November inspector Hollingworth went to the shop of the prosecutor, where he found the pri- soners. He searched them both. On the prisoner Hicks he found the shilling produced, which he identified as one be had seen in the office before. Subsequently, he searched the house, and found the jacket produced in the kitchen. It bore evidences of having been worn by Hodgkinson at his work of cleaner at Widnes. When charged with the theft, Hutchinson said "I bought it, but I ought to have paid for it to-night." Hicks satid " Yes; that is true."— Superintendent Williamson said the case had assumed a more serious aspect than he thought it would, and as these cases were very difficult to work up, he asked for the pri- soners to be remanded until Tuesday.—The prisoners were remanded.

The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported that there were 492 inmates in the Workhouse as compared with 49 last week, and 487 in the corresponding week last year.

Mr. HARTLEY intimated that the overseers of Eccleaton township had a meeting last Monday, which he attended and examined Mr. Dunn's books, and found that the whole of the money collected by him had been placed in the hands of the overseers' bankers to the credit of the township.

div.head: RAILWAY CATASTROPHE.
div.p: A RAILWAY CATASTROPHE.

Mr. HARTLEY said that some time ago he was ordered to obtain a milk testing apparatus so as to ensure a pure sup- ply. He had sent for one, but it had been broken in the transit, and he now asked the Board to leave it in his hands to make a claim against the London and North-Western Railway Company for 14s. 6d., the value of the apparatus. —This was agreed to.—ln answer t) Mr. Newsome, Mr. HARTLEY said there had been a great improvement in the milk supplied to the Workhouse—Lhe cream had risen from 4,1.- to 9 per cent.

A letter was read asking the Board to pay ss. which it had been agreed should be subscribed by the members of Boards of Guardians towards the expenses in connection with the Poor Law Conference.—Mr. TYttuiz : I propose the chairman subscribe the. ss. div.p: THE SrPPLY OF COFFiNS.

Mr. HArtmEy submitted a list of a number of articles, including coffins, for the Workhouse, contracts for which he suggested should be advertised for.—Mr. SADLER said be had heard some complaints at Widnes about all tbe coffins being supplied by one p2rs3n. He did not think it was quite fair that the supply should be monopolisal in this way.—Mr. HAIITLEY said the coffirie he proposed to advertise for were for the Workhouse ;those for the districts were obtained by the relieving efficers. There was only 7s. or 83. a piece paid for them, and he did not suppose they should want a coal at Il'idnes once a fortnight, but he would give instructions to the relieving oficer to distribute his favours.—The subject then dropped.

div.head: SUTTON 7.IEDICAL OFFICERSTIIP.
div.p: THE SUTTON 7.IEDICAL OFFICERSTIIP.

Mr. HARTLEY said the Relief Committee of the Sutton and Windle districts, appointed to consider the appointment of a medical officer for the Sutton district, did not think it advis- able to make any re-arrangement of the present relief dis- tricts of St. Helens and Sutton, and recommended that a medical officer for the Sutton district be advertised for.— Mr. JACKSON moved, and Mr. IN-Ewsoura seconded, ths con- firmatidn of these minute..—The;Jtev. T. CHAMBERS said he had received; letter from a brother clergyman residing in that district, asking him, in vie.iv of that appointment, to exprgss a hope that the medical officer might reside ither at Peasley Cross or Sutton.---The Rev. Mr. BARNACLE, who had previously said that he wished to make a few remarks on the appointment of the medical officer, said th3t was just whit he was going to say.—Mr. JACKSON said he thought it was explained at the committee meeting that where the doctor at present resided was more central than Peas* Cross.—Mr. CHAMBERS said he would not b 3 guilty of any breach of confidence if he just read a part of what his friend wrote, which was that the "medical officer for Sutton dis- trict should reside either at Peasley Cross or St. Helens. It would be a gross wrong if he were to live at St. Helens junction, more than three miles from his patients. The poorest parts of the township were about Grove's colliery and the glass works of Messrs. Pilkington."—Mr. JACKSON said that letter should not be brought before the Board unless tl-ey knew the originator of it.—Mr. CHAMBERS said he heard some member of the Board say that he should have the name of the writer. He (Mr. Chambers) did not see it in that light at all, and he, refused to give up the gentleman's name, though he (the writer) himself worddprobably not have the slightest objection to it. It was a piece of rudeness to ask such a thing.—The Rev. Mr. BARNACLE said he strongly supported Mr. Chambers. He himself had received a note probably from the same gentleman that wrote to Mr. Chambers who simply wished thbm to do something which would be of benefit to the district.—Mr. CHAMBERS Said nobody knew his own district better than a clergyman, an?. belied a -perfect right to write that letter.—After a little further talk it was resolved to appoint a medical officer by motion at the next meeting. TILE RIGHT OF GUARDIANS TO VISIT THE WORKHOUSE.

Mr. MEADOWS said there had been a House Committee formed, which was no doubt working very well, but he should like to know whether there would be any objection to any Guardian going through the Workhouse at any time. The question was, as far as he was concerned, that the House Committee mk.t on Tuesdays, a day on which he was engaged at Manchester, and therefore he should like to know whether the Board would object to any member going through the house without being appointed to do so.—The CHAIRMAN: I should think not.—Mr. MEADOWS said he thought it was the duty of eviky Guardian to visit the house occasionally.—Mr. HARTLEY said the orders said a Guar- dian must be a member of the Visiting Committee, or he had no right to go into the Workhouse. A Guardian could bring nothing before the Board about what he saw in the Workhouse unless he visited it as one of the Visiting Com- mittee.—Mr. P. Lowarost said a Guardian might pick up some information he might bring forward.—Mr. HARTLEY. pointed out that they bad appointed a committee,-which they made -responsible for the minagement of the Workhouse. Mr. Donna asked if a mem- ber of the Visiting Committee • could come to the house at anytime.—Mr. HARTLEY: I think not.— Mr. NEWSOME said there waS a Visiting Committee of about' 21, but there were never more than five or Six went through the house on tbe committee meeting day, and he wantcd to know if any member of the committee could go through the house on any other day.—Mr. HARTLEY said , all he could say was that they had not the right; if they came, theycame as private individuals, and could only visit by the consent of the master, but not as members of the Visiting Committee. He then referred back to the minutes of the first meeting of the Visiting Committee, at which Tuesday was fixed upon As the day of meeting, and stating that the committee could appoint sub-committees of not less than three members who could Visit the Workhouse without notification to the Workhouse officials.—The Rev. R. FINEGAN said it was desirable that surprise visits should be made occasionally.—Mr. TYRER pointed out that the sub-committees could do that.—lt was stated that the master was always,willing to allow any of the members to look through the premises, after which the subject dropped.

div.head: WIDNES BOARD SCHOOLS.
div.p: WIDNES BOARD SCHOOLS.
DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES LAST NIGHT.

Last evening, Widnes Drill Hall was crowded with an audience gathered to witness the presentation to those children attending the schools of the Widnes School Board who had succeeded in securing the prizes generously offered by Mr. T. Sutton Timmis ; (the chairman of the Board) and Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P. The room was packed in every part by the parents of scholars and the scholars themselves, while some youths, more venturesome than the rest, perched themselves rather insecurely on the ledges of the windows. An extensive platform had been erected, and en this were assembled several hundred scholars who, during the evening, sang a number of songs in good style, under the conductorship of Mr. Showan. Amongst those present were—Mr. T. Sutton Timmis (chairman), Mrs Timmis, Mr. J. Brock, J.P., Mr. Robert Shaw, Mr. H. W. Deacon, Rev. J. Wright-Williams, M.A.; Rev. George Bond, M.A.; Mr. E. Carey, Mrs. Carey, Mr. Thomas Balmer, Mr. John Hough, Mr. William Crabtree, Messrs. Showan, Snoddy, Hunter; Misses Clayden, Broad, Strong, Hender- son, Strickland, Mrs. Comes, and Mrs. Todd. The CHAIRMAN said many of the friends of education in Widnes had thought it desirable that the prizes which had been earned during the last school year for good attendance should be given in public, and they were therefore asked to be present that evening. The prizes to be give were for good and regular attendance. To every child who had attended every time the schools had been open, which meant every possible attendance, the whole of the school fees would be paid—(applause) ; and to those children who had only missed five times half the fees would be paid. (Applause.) It was extremely gratifying to find that such a number of children, considering the cir- cumstances, had come forward to claim these prizes. At Simms Cross 10 children had attended every time; at War- rington-road,7 ; at West Bank, 7; making a total of 22 children who had attended school every time the school had been open. (Applause.) At Simms Cross 42 had attended, 5 times, at Warrington-road 11, and West Bank 31. (Applause.) He wished to explain that the promise to give these prizes was only made known in May of this year, and inasmuch as the school year commenced in September, 1881, it was evident that the children who had gained the prises, would have put in as great a number of attendances without the incentive, a thing which he regarded with great satisfacticn, and as very creditable to the children. The object in giving these prizes for good attendance was to remove an evil which all teachers and managers of elementary schools recognised as one of the greatest with which they had to contend, and that was irregular attendance. Now the ratepayers of Widnes had found the money to build the fine Board schools they had in Widnes, and the Board had provided good teachers, good managers, and good apparatus, but unless the parents sent their children to school, all this money was wasted. And this was not only an injury to those who did not attend, but it was a positive injury done to those who did attend. If the teacher prepared a lesson and gave. it to the class when some were not present, and absent, perhaps, the next day, he had either to* work hack again, or the children had to pick it up as best they could. It was with the hope that this attendance might be stimulated that these prizes were given. The idea of doing so was borrowed from the proceedings of the Liverpool Council of Education, an association which had done a great deal of gooll in Liverpool, not only in denominational, but in Board schools also. But the prizes were not given exactly on the saute .lines. In Liverpool al[ the money was paid to the parents. It was proposed that in Widnes "that half the money should be given •to the parents, and that the other half should be invested in the Post Office Saxings Bank for the benefit of the children. (Applause.) It was evident the children could not make their regular attendance without they were sent by their parents. If the parents would not get their children ready, or if they kept them at home on any frivolous pretences, why the children could not go. On the other hand be the parents ever so willing, if the child Was not properly attended to, it would not go. And, therefore, the idea was that both parents and chlhdren should partici- pate in the benefit, that they should both pull together with the hopeful result that the children would go. The money might na be a great deal, but he hoped it would be something anpreciable to the parents and to the children. He believed it might prove most valuable to the children, not only for its money value alone, but by teaching them two lessons—one was thrift and the other self denial. (Applause.) Thrift meant the gradual accumulation of .emall savings. If children got into the habit of saving, he thought the habit might grow and strengthen in after life, and that spell nucleus which tlfey had in the savings' balik might fortes the basis of large future savings. It was also desired and hoped that it would teach the children self- denial, and to recognise that it was their duty to go to schoel, and when the children grew up in life and became workmen or employers, the habit would grow, and they would becomo thrifty men and women, always found at the post of duty. Having made an appeal to the parents to send their children to school OTI every possible occasion, the Chairman conclu- ded by r,eading letters of apology from Fattier Clarke and Father Finegan, for their non-attendance through previous engagements..

Ttie presentations concluded, • Mr. JOHN Enoex said it was his duty to ask the audience to present a cordial vote of thanks to Mrs. Timmis ft), her kindness hi coming there that evening and presenting the prizes to the children. (Applause.) It must have been a grand sight to them all to see the children go to the table to receive' their prizes. They all knew that the great aim of the pates was to get the chil- dren to attend school regularly. It was only feir to, the teachers that they should do so. They could not expect a teacher to succeed with a pupil if that pupil only attended halt of hie or her time. It was only fair to the children that tkey should attend regularly. They could not succeed in learning if they did not go the whole of their time. These children, as they knew, were the future men and woman of Widnes, and if they were to grotv up intelligent, they must be educated, and if they'were to be properly educated they must attend regularly. It might interest some of them to know what had been the progress in the average attendance at all schools in Widnes daring the. last five,years. In 1878 the average attendance was 71.5; in 1879 they seemed to have receded a little, and the average attendance was 68 1 ; in 1830 the average attendance was 71.2; in 1882, partly owing to the efficiency of the school board officers, and greatly to the stimulus given by the very liberal offer of Mr. itimmis and Mr. Gossage, the avenge attendance had risen to 75.8. div.head: LATEST NE WS.
div.p: LATEST NE WS.

The funeral of the late Lord Berwick took place yesterday at Akham Church, Shrewsbury, which is near Attingham Hall, the family seat. There was a large number present at the ceremony. At Sheffield yesterday morning, a fire broke out in •a dwelling-house, and a whole family had a narrow escape, six children having to jump from the bedroom windows. According to present arrangements Mr. Davitt will leave Dublin next,Mouday, he having engaged to deliver lectures on Irish qu..sstions in various Eaglish towns during the pre- sent month., •

A shocking case of supposed child murder was discovered at Wibsev, Bradford, on Thursday. The body of an infant was found in an ash-pit dreadfdly burnt, its arm and back being broken, and a, glass' bottle driven into its head. - Madame Nilsson's first appearance in New York was made to a crowded, fashionable audience in Steinway Hall, and was entirely successful. All the critics agree that her voice is as powerful and charming as ever. Lille had a most enthusiastic greeting,,

Yesterday the thirty-eighth birthday of the Princess of Wales was celebrated at Windsor with the customary honours. The bells of St. George's Chapel and the parish churches rang merrily at intervals. Royal salutes were fired from thS Long Walk and Virginia Waters. The Prin- cess' was born on the Ist December, 1844. A fire discovered in Forest's old-established music ware- house, High-st ,Shrewsbttry,about six o'clock yesterday morn- ing, and in a verrshort space of time the building was com- pletely gutted. The place is closely surrounded by other property, occupied by Mr. Robinson, jeweller, Mr. Chancellor, bookseller, and several others.

Considerable excitement has been caused in Birmingham by another case' of armed burglars. Early yesterday morn- ing, a servant girl at Spring Hill, a suburb of the town, saw two men with blackened faces getting through the window of a house into the street. She called for the assistance of a labourer who was naar, when one of the men presented a revolver at them, and both the giil and the labourer fled. The burglars escaped.
WRECK OF A SCHOONER IN THE DEE.-LOSS OF FOUtt LIVES.

The name-board, hatches, and wheel of the Accrington Lass, a schooner belonging to Connah's quay, Chester, have been picked up in the "wild roads,' at the mouth of the Dee. The Accringlon Lass left Douglas, laden with ore, on Monday, and has .not since been beard of. Two of her crew. of four, named Griffiths, resided at Connah's Quay. YELLOW '?EVER ON BOARD SHIP.—TWELVE DEATHS.

_ A Lloyd's teletram -received from Havana, states that the barque Caterina gas put into that port uuder quaran- tine, while on a voyage from Pensacola, to Greenock with a full cargo. The whole of the crew, excepting the captain, mate, cook,, and steward died of yellow fever whilst the vessel lay at Pensacola' and soon after sailing the captain and cook also died. The ship will be fumi- gated, and a new captain and crew shipped, to enable her to proceed.

EXCITING CO4FLICT WIT ARMED,BUR.GLARS. An exciting affray with armed burglars took place in the Harborne-road, near Birmingham, at four o'clock yester- day morning. Two men with suspicious-looking parcels were observed by two pelice-officers on duty, and challenged to stop and explain their reason for being out at such an hour. They 'hurried on, and the codstables following Made a dash at them, upon which one of the men turned round, and, pointing a revolver at them, fired. The bullet whizzed past one of the officer's heads: The other policeman then ran forward with .a view •to effect an arrest, when the second of the two ruffians pro- duced another revolver and firbd- at him, but again the bullet fortunately missed its mark. By keeping the officers covered by their revolvers, tha burglars managed to escape. Every effort is being made to capture them, the polite scouring the district for miles round.
THE MILES PLATTING RITUAL CASE. MORE TROUBLE BREWING.

A Manche4ter correspondent telegraphs :—All the papers necessary for the institution of the Rev. Harry Cowgill to the rectory of St. John's, Miles Platting, Manchester, have for several days been in the hands of the Bishop of Mao- chester, who, however, has not taken any steps in the matter. It is understood that the bishop will refuse to in- stitute Mr. Cowgill unless he promises to bring the ritual and observance down to the Manchester Cathedral standard, and this, it ia an open secret, Mr. Cowgill will not do. •

PROPOSED OLDHAM BRANCH OF THE SHIP CANAL. A project is being mooted in Oldham for taking a Whit- tary of the ship canal extending to that town. The proposed canal would be a branch of the main stream, and theater- way would be partly fed in the district through which it runs and by the main canal. It is held that boats of two hundred to three hundred tons burden could be brought along the waterway to Oldham. A COLLIERY CLOSED THROUGH:I. A BOYS'

THE AFFAIRS OF A WIDNES SOLICITOR,—At the Liver- pool Court of Bankruptcy, yesterday, before Mr. J. F. Col- lier. judge, Thomas Beasley, solicitor, of Widnes, passed his public examination, and the trustee, Mr. BoHand, submitted terms of an arrangement under, which the creditora were to receive 3s. in the pound. Mr. Thomas Martin, solicitor, of Liverpool, appeared and, objected to the amend- ment of the bankruptcy, which was-a condition of the pro- posed arrangement, on the ground ,that he was a purchaser of certain property, part of the debtor's estate, the tranefer of which had not been completed,, and the effect el the annu,lment of the bankruptcy would be to re-vest that pro- perty in the bankrupt—his Honow was of opinion- that Mr. Martin's objection was premature, and that the-proper time for' him to raise it would be when the questioefof annul- ment came formally before the oeurt, such annulment -being conditional upon the composition being duly paid: CHIRQE AGAINST A HALTON BEERHOUSE KR,F,PEV.—On Thursday, at the Occasional, Court, 13ank-street, Warring- ton, before Mr. James Marson, Joseph Taylor, beerhouse keepee, Halton, and Robert Haddock, of the same place, were charged with s'ealing four fowls, a hamper, and a bag, the property of John Weir .and farther with, stealing four fowls, a hamper, and a bag, the property of Henry Weedall. —Mr Moore appeared for the prisoners. From the evidence it appeared that the prisoners drove over to Stretton, :along with Mr. Peter Lever, to attend a sa.le on the farm. of Mr. Philip Darbyshke. They put up at a house a short distance from the farm, and about halt-past three o'clock went to the sale. Mr. Weir and Mr. Weedall also attended the sale, and bought some fowls which they put in hampers, and left them in the yard until othe; things had been sold, but when they, came to look for the fowls again they found they were gone. The prisoners naked a boy named Glover to help them to carry the hampers. to the trap, and he did so, and saw them take the fowls out of one hamper and put them into the other, and then drive off. Information was given to the police, who we to Taylor's bouse and found all the fowls except one.ee-Taylor was:, remanded to the Daresbury Petty Sessieens, bail being allowed, himself in £lOO and a surety in £5O, but Haddock was diecharged, ft:Zee not being set-ftietet evidence nqinst hit,
